SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA
COUNTY OF SACRAMENTO
BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI,
Petitioner,
v.
JEFFREY MACOMBER, in his official
capacity as Secretary of the California
Department of Corrections and
Rehabilitation,
Respondent.
Case No. 26WM000028
FIRST AMENDED VERIFIED 
PETITION
FOR WRIT OF MANDATE
(No Substantive Changes)
(Code Civ. Proc. § 1085)
[Alternative Writ Requested]
FIRST AMENDED VERIFIED PETITION FOR WRIT OF MANDATE
(No Substantive Changes)
Petitioner Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi respectfully petitions this Court for a writ of mandate 
pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 1085 to compel Respondent Jeffrey Macomber, in 
his official capacity as Secretary of the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation 
(CDCR), to perform the ministerial duty to conduct an individualized parole discharge 
determination in accordance with California Penal Code sections 3008(d)(2), 3000 et seq., and 
related statutes, and to set aside Respondent’s denial of early discharge from parole dated 
December 1, 2025 (the “Discharge Review Report”). Petitioner does not seek a court-ordered 
discharge, but only a lawful determination conducted under the correct statutory standards.
I. NATURE OF THE ACTION
This action challenges CDCR’s unlawful application of categorical policy bars that override the 
individualized, case-by-case statutory criteria that must govern parole discharge decisions. 
Specifically, CDCR denied Petitioner’s discharge based on two categorical rules unsupported by 
statute:
1. A rigid rule under Policy 19-03 (Amended) that parolees with 10-year parole terms are 
ineligible for early discharge until serving at least 6.5 years; and
2. A policy requiring “completion” of sex offender treatment that CDCR itself defines as 
impossible to achieve before parole discharge.
Neither categorical bar appears in the governing statutes; in fact, both contradict the express 
statutory range (“not less than one year, up to the entire period of parole”) and individualized 
assessment mandate. By substituting bright-line policies for individualized statutory analysis, 
CDCR has violated its ministerial duty under California law, exceeded its statutory authority, 
and rendered the words “up to” surplusage in violation of the canon that every word in a statute 
must be given effect.
II. PARTIES
A. Petitioner
1. Petitioner Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi (CDC # BF3571) is currently on parole supervision in 
San Joaquin County under the jurisdiction of CDCR’s Division of Adult Parole Operations 

Page 2 of 9
(DAPO), Stockton 2 GPS unit. Petitioner was originally released on parole on December 2, 2020 
following conviction for violations of Penal Code section 289(a)(1)(A) (Penetration 
w/Force/Violence/Fear of Immediate Bodily Injury) and section 220(a)(1)(01) (Assault with 
Intent to Commit Specified Sex Offense). Petitioner is subject to PC 290 registration 
requirements and has been assigned a 10-year parole term with a controlling discharge date of 
December 2, 2030. Petitioner has been directly and concretely harmed by CDCR’s categorical 
policies: despite serving approximately five years of continuous parole supervision under the 
operative term (December 2020-December 2025), with low risk scores, stable residence, and 
substantial compliance, he has been denied discharge consideration based solely on mechanical 
application of unauthorized time-based bars and an impossible-to-satisfy treatment completion 
standard. This constitutes ongoing unlawful restraint of liberty. Petitioner has a clear, present, 
and beneficial right to a parole discharge determination conducted in accordance with statutory 
requirements.
B. Respondent
Respondent Jeffrey Macomber is the Secretary of the California Department of Corrections and 
Rehabilitation, the official with ultimate authority over parole operations and discharge 
determinations. Respondent is sued in his official capacity as the officer who has the ministerial 
duty under Penal Code sections 3008(d)(2) and 3000 et seq. to ensure that parole discharge 
determinations are conducted in accordance with statutory requirements. Code Civ. Proc. § 1085.
III. JURISDICTION AND VENUE
1. This Court has jurisdiction pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 1085, which 
authorizes this Court to issue writs of mandate to compel the performance of an act which the 
law specially enjoins as a duty resulting from an office.
2. Venue is proper in Sacramento County Superior Court pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure 
section 401, as Sacramento County is the seat of state government and the location where 
Respondent, as Secretary of CDCR, maintains his principal office and formulates the challenged 
statewide policies. This venue is consistent with Alliance for Constitutional Sex Offense Laws v. 
Macomber (Sacramento Super. Ct. Case No. 23STCP02378), which successfully challenged 
identical CDCR policies in this Court. In the alternative, should the Court find venue more 
appropriate in San Joaquin County where Petitioner is supervised, the proper remedy is transfer 
under Code of Civil Procedure section 397, not dismissal.
IV. EXHAUSTION OF ADMINISTRATIVE REMEDIES
3. Exhaustion of administrative remedies is not required, or in the alternative, is excused for the 
following reasons:
A. Futility
4. Petitioner can “positively state what the administrative agency’s decision in his particular case 
would be.” In re Thompson (1985) 172 Cal.App.3d 256, 262. The Discharge Review Report 
dated December 1, 2025 (Exhibit A hereto) specifically cites categorical policy criteria as the 
sole bases for denial. The Unit Supervisor Comments state:
“Based on Sex Offender Management Program Earned Discharge Criteria, 
Policy 19-03 (Amended), Newanforbi is not eligible for EDC at this time due to 
having a 10-year parole term. Newanforbi has only completed approximately 4 
years of the required 6.5 years of supervision.”

Page 3 of 9
5. This language establishes that CDCR applies a fixed departmental criterion—the 10-year/6.5-
year rule—that operates mechanically without regard to individual circumstances. Any 
administrative appeal would be denied based on the same categorical formula.
6. Similarly, CDCR officials have admitted under oath that CDCR policy prohibits completion of 
sex offender management programs prior to discharge from parole. In In re Dwyer (San Mateo 
Super. Ct. Case No. SC-080355A/HC-3020, Order Mar. 20, 2023) (Exhibit B hereto), CDCR 
representatives testified that “a sex offender cannot successfully ‘complete’ a sex offender 
management treatment program while on parole.” This admission establishes that any 
administrative appeal challenging the “incomplete treatment” ground would be denied based on 
the same unlawful categorical policy.
7. Both categorical bars reflect fixed CDCR policies, not individualized statutory analysis. 
Further administrative proceedings would be futile.
B. No Adequate Administrative Remedy
8. The administrative grievance process cannot provide adequate relief because Petitioner 
challenges the legality of statewide CDCR policies that exceed statutory authority. The CDCR 
602 administrative grievance process is designed to address individual factual disputes, not to 
invalidate regulations or declare agency policies ultra vires. Horn v. County of Ventura (1979) 
24 Cal.3d 605, 611 (“One need not exhaust inadequate remedies in order to challenge their 
sufficiency.”). Administrative reviewers lack the authority to declare departmental policies 
unlawful or to invalidate criteria adopted by agency headquarters.
9. The Board of Parole Hearings has no administrative appeal process for discharge denials 
issued by DAPO. According to the Roadmap to Reentry legal guide: “To challenge a BPH 
decision or a parole condition set by the BPH, you do not need to file an administrative appeal—
UNLESS the issue involves a disability. Since the BPH has no administrative appeal process, 
you can immediately file a state petition for writ of habeas corpus [or mandate].” The only 
adequate remedy is judicial review.
C. Pure Question of Law
10. This petition presents pure questions of law requiring no further factual development: 
whether CDCR’s categorical policies comply with Penal Code sections 3008(d)(2) and 3000 et 
seq., and whether CDCR exceeded its statutory authority by imposing eligibility criteria not 
found in statute. Courts, not administrative agencies, are the appropriate forum to resolve 
statutory interpretation and ultra vires challenges. County of Contra Costa v. State of California 
(1986) 177 Cal.App.3d 62, 73.
V. STATEMENT OF FACTS
A. Petitioner’s Parole History and Compliance
11. Petitioner was originally released on parole on December 2, 2020. As of the December 1, 
2025 Discharge Review Report, Petitioner had served approximately five years of continuous 
parole supervision under the operative term. He has been classified as Category SA, CSRA 
Score: 2 (low-risk classification). The Report’s reference to having ‘only completed 
approximately 4 years of the required 6.5 years’ reflects CDCR’s internal accounting methods 
not grounded in statute and further illustrates the arbitrary nature of the challenged categorical 
criteria. Regardless of how CDCR internally calculates elapsed time, no statute authorizes a 
minimum time-served requirement for discharge eligibility. The 6.5-year bar is an unauthorized 

Page 4 of 9
addition to statutory criteria. Tidewater Marine Western, Inc. v. Bradshaw (1996) 14 Cal.4th 557 
(agency policies adding requirements not found in statute are invalid).
12. The Parolee Dynamic Profile evaluation demonstrates: (1) stable residence with family in 
Stockton for eight months or longer; (2) compliance with general and special parole conditions; 
(3) participation in sex offender treatment with partial completion and ongoing progress (Core 
Phase, Block 1, Module 4/7); (4) affiliation with pro-social individuals. Despite some parole 
violations during the review period (related to treatment access and GPS charging, not new 
criminal conduct), CDCR did not pursue revocation, and Petitioner has maintained stable family 
residence and low risk scores.
B. The December 1, 2025 Discharge Review Report: Categorical Denial
13. On December 1, 2025, CDCR issued a Discharge Review Report (CDCR Form 1502-DR) 
denying Petitioner’s consideration for early discharge. The Unit Supervisor stated:
“Based on Sex Offender Management Program Earned Discharge Criteria, 
Policy 19-03 (Amended), Newanforbi is not eligible for EDC at this time due to 
having a 10-year parole term. Newanforbi has only completed approximately 4 
years of the required 6.5 years of supervision.”
14. The Report also cites “incomplete sex offender treatment” as a basis for denial. These two 
categorical bars—the 10-year/6.5-year time requirement and treatment noncompletion—
constitute the entirety of the substantive denial reasoning.
15. Critically, nowhere in the Discharge Review Report does CDCR cite or apply the 
individualized statutory criteria set forth in Penal Code sections 3008(d)(2) or 3000 et seq. The 
Report does not reference consultation with certified sex offender management professionals 
regarding individualized program duration under § 3008(d)(2). It does not cite current risk 
assessment scores or evidence-based evaluation of whether continued treatment is necessary for 
public safety. It does not weigh Petitioner’s demonstrated compliance and stability. Instead, the 
denial rests entirely on automatic, policy-based exclusions.
C. CDCR’s Categorical Policies Exceed Statutory Authority
16. The 10-year/6.5-year criterion referenced in the Discharge Review Report derives from 
CDCR’s internal Policy 19-03 (Amended). This categorical bar does not appear in any California 
statute. Penal Code sections 3000 et seq. establish maximum parole terms but do not create 
minimum time-served requirements for discharge eligibility.
17. The “incomplete treatment” criterion flows from CDCR’s longstanding policy that sex 
offender management programs “cannot be completed short of discharge from parole.” In In re 
Dwyer, CDCR witnesses testified under oath that their interpretation of § 3008(d)(2) requires 
parolees to maintain “some connection to treatment” for the entire period of parole until 
discharge, making early completion structurally impossible. (San Mateo Super. Ct. Order at 4-5, 
7.)
18. Following litigation in Alliance v. Macomber, CDCR adopted new regulations effective 
April 17, 2025 (15 Cal. Code Regs. § 3574) that explicitly state: “Supervised persons may 
complete a sex offender management program before discharge from parole, as contemplated by 
PC section 3008(d).” Critically, section 3574(f) requires that retention determinations be 
“supported by good cause” as defined in Penal Code section 3000, stated in writing on Form 
CDCR 3043, signed by both the treatment provider and parole agent, and delivered to the parolee 

Page 5 of 9
within 30 days. The December 1, 2025 Report contains no such written good cause 
determination, no Form 3043, no Containment Team Meeting (CTM) findings as required by 
section 3574(e), and no risk-based rationale tied to statutory criteria. This regulatory adoption 
constitutes an admission against interest that prior policies (and current application) were 
unlawful. The agency cannot simultaneously concede in regulations that early completion is 
possible while denying it in practice. This demonstrates bad-faith continued enforcement despite 
regulatory changes and constitutes arbitrary and capricious agency action.
VI. STATEMENT OF LAW
A. Code of Civil Procedure § 1085: Ordinary Mandate
19. Code of Civil Procedure section 1085 authorizes this Court to issue a writ of mandate to 
compel “the performance of an act which the law specially enjoins, as a duty resulting from an 
office, trust, or station.” The writ runs against the officer who holds the legal duty. Code Civ. 
Proc. § 1085.
20. Two essential elements must be shown: “(1) a clear, present and usually ministerial duty on 
the part of the respondent… and (2) a clear, present and beneficial right in the petitioner to the 
performance of that duty.” California Ass’n for Health Services at Home v. Dep’t of Health Care 
Services (2012) 204 Cal.App.4th 676, 683.
21. A ministerial duty arises when the law specially enjoins an act. Even if discretion is involved 
in applying statutory criteria, mandate lies where the agency exercises discretion under an 
unlawful standard or substitutes categorical rules for required individualized analysis. Pomona 
Police Officers’ Ass’n v. City of Pomona (1997) 58 Cal.App.4th 578, 583-84.
22. The duty to apply the correct legal standard is ministerial, even where the ultimate decision 
involves discretion. When an agency is required by statute to apply specific criteria in reaching a 
decision, the agency’s obligation to use those criteria (rather than substitute its own policy-based 
criteria) is a ministerial duty enforceable by mandate. The discretion lies in weighing the 
statutory factors, not in choosing which factors to consider.
23. Mandate also lies to correct an abuse of discretion, which occurs when an agency “has not 
proceeded in the manner required by law.” Code Civ. Proc. § 1094.5(b); Pomona Police, 58 
Cal.App.4th at 583-84. When an agency fails to apply statutory criteria and instead relies on 
unauthorized categorical policies, it fails to proceed in the manner required by law.
B. Penal Code § 3008(d): The Individualized Determination Mandate
24. Penal Code section 3008(d)(2) governs sex offender management programs for parolees 
placed on parole on or after July 1, 2012. It provides:
“Persons placed on parole on or after July 1, 2012, shall successfully complete a 
sex offender management program… as a condition of parole. The length of the 
period in the program shall be not less than one year, up to the entire period of 
parole, as determined by the certified sex offender management professional in 
consultation with the parole officer and as approved by the court.”
25. The statutory phrase “not less than one year, up to the entire period of parole” establishes a 
discretionary range requiring individualized assessment. The word “up to” necessarily implies 
that program duration may be less than the full parole term. CDCR’s interpretation renders the 

Page 6 of 9
words “up to” surplusage, violating the canon of statutory construction that every word in a 
statute must be given effect. People v. Rizo (2000) 22 Cal.4th 681, 685.
26. By defining “completion” as impossible before discharge and applying automatic term-based 
bars, CDCR converts “up to” into “always,” directly contradicting the statute’s plain language 
and violating its ministerial duty to perform individualized determinations.
C. Categorical Rules Eliminating Statutory Discretion Are Invalid
27. In In re Gadlin (2020) 10 Cal.5th 915, the California Supreme Court unanimously struck 
down CDCR regulations that categorically excluded inmates with registerable sex offense 
convictions from nonviolent offender parole consideration. The Court held: “This categorical 
exclusion conflicts with the constitutional directive that inmates… convicted of a nonviolent 
felony offense… shall be eligible for parole consideration.” Id. at 928.
28. The Supreme Court emphasized that “eligibility must be based on an inmate’s current 
circumstances—not categorical rules applied without individual consideration.” Id. CDCR 
cannot create “wholesale exclusions” from statutory rights. Id.
29. Similarly, In re Taylor (2015) 60 Cal.4th 1019 held that blanket parole restrictions are 
permissible only when “based on, and supported by, the particularized circumstances of each 
individual parolee.” 60 Cal.4th at 1037. These precedents establish that when agencies convert 
discretionary statutory authority into categorical rules, mandate relief is appropriate to compel 
compliance with individualized statutory mandates.
D. Superior Court Precedent
30. While not binding appellate precedent, the reasoning of recent Superior Court rulings is 
directly on point and persuasive regarding CDCR’s systemic failure to comply with Penal Code 
§ 3008(d).
31. In In re Dwyer (San Mateo Super. Ct. Case No. SC-080355A/HC-3020, Order Mar. 20, 
2023), the court conducted an evidentiary hearing and found that CDCR’s practice of requiring 
treatment “for the entire term of parole, apparently without reference to the individualized 
performance of each parolee” vitiates the Legislature’s directive. The court found that 
“[d]iscretion exercised in that fashion… effectively requires all parolees participating in this 
program to do so for the entire term of parole.” Order at 11.
32. In Alliance for Constitutional Sex Offense Laws v. Macomber (Sacramento Super. Ct. Case 
No. 23STCP02378, Order Dec. 13, 2023), this Court overruled CDCR’s demurrer, holding that a 
petition alleging these exact statewide policies states a valid cause of action for ordinary mandate 
under § 1085. The Macomber ruling validates both the procedural vehicle and the exhaustion 
arguments presented here, demonstrating that this legal theory has already survived the Attorney 
General’s initial challenges.
VII. CAUSE OF ACTION: VIOLATION OF MINISTERIAL DUTY AND ABUSE OF 
DISCRETION
33. Petitioner re-alleges and incorporates by reference all preceding paragraphs.
34. Respondent has a clear, present, and ministerial duty under Penal Code sections 3008(d)(2) 
and 3000 et seq. to perform the ministerial duty of conducting individualized parole discharge 
determinations based on statutory criteria.

Page 7 of 9
35. Respondent violated this duty by denying discharge based on two categorical bars not found 
in statute: (a) the 10-year/6.5-year Policy 19-03 (Amended) criterion, and (b) the “incomplete 
treatment” criterion based on CDCR’s policy that treatment cannot be completed prior to 
discharge.
36. The Discharge Review Report also references unemployment and parole violations. 
However, even if these factors were proper considerations, they cannot salvage an otherwise 
unlawful decision premised on categorical bars. First, CDCR did not pursue revocation for these 
violations, indicating CDCR itself determined they did not pose a threat to public safety. Second, 
the violations documented in the Report relate to treatment access and GPS charging issues—not 
new criminal conduct or deceptive polygraph responses. Third, under 15 Cal. Code Regs. section 
3574(f), violations do not automatically justify retention; CDCR must demonstrate “good cause” 
tied to individualized risk assessment, which the Report fails to do. Fourth, under the “taint” 
doctrine, when an agency relies on both proper and improper grounds, the court cannot presume 
the agency would have reached the same result using only proper criteria. The appropriate 
remedy is to vacate and remand for a lawful determination applying only statutory and regulatory 
criteria. See California Highway Patrol v. Superior Court (2008) 158 Cal.App.4th 726, 735 
(decision based partly on improper standard must be set aside); cf. Topanga Ass’n for a Scenic 
Community v. County of Los Angeles (1974) 11 Cal.3d 506, 514-515 (agency must articulate 
findings supporting decision under proper legal standard).
37. Respondent exceeded statutory authority by imposing eligibility criteria that do not appear in 
any statute and that effectively rewrite the Legislature’s individualized assessment framework.
38. Petitioner has been directly and concretely harmed by CDCR’s categorical policies. 
Petitioner has served over 5 years on parole with low risk scores, stable residence, and 
substantial compliance, yet has been denied discharge consideration based solely on mechanical 
application of unauthorized time-based bars and an impossible-to-satisfy treatment completion 
standard. This constitutes ongoing unlawful restraint of liberty, creating both standing and 
ripeness for immediate judicial review. The harm is not speculative or future—it occurs each day 
Petitioner remains on parole supervision beyond what the statute authorizes.
39. Petitioner has a clear, present, and beneficial right to a parole discharge determination 
conducted in accordance with applicable statutes. Petitioner has no plain, speedy, or adequate 
remedy in the ordinary course of law other than this writ of mandate.
40. Absent relief from this Court, Petitioner will continue to be subjected to unlawfully 
prolonged parole supervision based on categorical agency rules rather than the individualized 
statutory criteria to which he is entitled.
VIII. RESERVATION OF FEDERAL CLAIMS
41. Petitioner expressly reserves the right to litigate any federal constitutional claims, including 
claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, in a federal forum. This petition seeks relief solely for violations 
of state statutory duties and state administrative law principles. Petitioner does not waive, and 
specifically preserves, any federal claims arising from Respondent’s conduct. England v. 
Louisiana State Bd. of Med. Exam’rs (1964) 375 U.S. 411. This petition seeks to compel 
CDCR’s compliance with state law, creating a judicial record of ultra vires conduct that may 
support later federal claims for pattern-and-practice violations under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. Because 
mandate addresses prospective statutory compliance, while § 1983 targets past constitutional 

Page 8 of 9
violations, the two remedies are distinct and non-duplicative. A favorable ruling will establish 
CDCR’s statutory violations under state law without prejudicing federal constitutional claims. 
Monell v. Dept. of Soc. Servs. (1978) 436 U.S. 658.
PRAYER FOR RELIEF
WHEREFORE, Petitioner respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Issue an alternative writ of mandate or order to show cause directing Respondent to show 
cause, if any, why a peremptory writ of mandate should not issue;
2. Following hearing or submission, issue a peremptory writ of mandate commanding 
Respondent to:
a. Vacate and set aside the December 1, 2025 Discharge Review Report;
b. Conduct a new parole discharge determination for Petitioner applying the individualized 
statutory criteria set forth in Penal Code sections 3008(d)(2), 3000 et seq., and 15 Cal. Code 
Regs. § 3574, without reliance on categorical bars;
c. Specifically, command Respondent to reconsider Petitioner’s discharge eligibility without 
applying CDCR Policy 19-03 (Amended)’s requirement that a parolee with a 10-year term 
serve 6.5 years before discharge eligibility, and without treating ‘completion’ of a sex 
offender management program as a precondition that is definitionally impossible to satisfy 
prior to discharge;
d. Determine sex offender management program length through consultation with certified 
sex offender management professionals and parole agents, as mandated by Penal Code 
section 3008(d)(2), based on Petitioner’s individual progress, risk assessment, and 
compliance history;
e. Apply written retention criteria as required by 15 Cal. Code Regs. § 3574, including 
treatment provider and parole agent assessment of progress and risk, with written 
documentation of good cause for any continued retention;
3. Award Petitioner costs of suit;
4. Retain jurisdiction to ensure compliance with the Court’s orders; and
5. Alternatively, issue a declaratory judgment pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 1060 
declaring that CDCR Policy 19-03 (Amended)’s 10-year/6.5-year time-based eligibility criterion 
is invalid as ultra vires, and that CDCR’s categorical prohibition on treatment program 
completion prior to parole discharge violates Penal Code section 3008(d)(2) and 15 Cal. Code 
Regs. section 3574;
6. Grant such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper.

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
I. INTRODUCTION
This proceeding for a writ of mandate pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 1085 addresses 
an unlawful substitution of categorical criteria by the California Department of Corrections and 
Rehabilitation ("CDCR") in place of the individualized assessment framework established by the 
Legislature for parole discharge. Petitioner Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi challenges the 
Department’s reliance on unauthorized "underground regulations" that override the evidence-
based assessment framework enacted by the California Legislature.1
At the heart of this action lies a conflict between bureaucratic expediency and statutory duty. The 
Legislature, through Penal Code section 3008(d)(2), explicitly designed a flexible, discretionary 
system for sex offender parole supervision, mandating that treatment program duration be 
determined by clinical professionals and the courts—with a range extending "not less than one 
year, up to the entire period of parole." This statutory language reflects a legislative intent to tailor 
supervision to the specific risks and progress of the individual parolee.
The Department, however, has effectively rewritten this statute through internal policy. By 
enforcing a rigid "10-year/6.5-year" time-served requirement under Policy 19-03 (Amended) and 
maintaining a de facto policy that treatment completion is structurally "impossible" prior to 
discharge, the Department has converted the Legislature's discretionary "up to" into a mandatory 
"always." This substitution of fixed departmental criteria for individualized statutory analysis 
constitutes both a failure to perform a ministerial duty and an abuse of discretion under California 
law.
This case also presents a failure to proceed in the manner required by law. Effective April 17, 
2025, the Department promulgated new regulations—15 Cal. Code Regs. § 3574—that formally 
recognize the possibility of early treatment completion and require specific procedural safeguards, 
including written findings of "good cause" for retention, that were absent from the Petitioner’s 
December 1, 2025 Discharge Review Report. The Department’s continued enforcement of its 
legacy policies in direct contravention of its own new regulations is arbitrary, capricious, and 
legally unsustainable.
Critically, this Petition does not ask the Court to substitute its judgment for that of the agency 
regarding the ultimate outcome of discharge. Rather, it seeks to compel the agency to exercise its 
discretion within the lawful boundaries set by the Legislature—free from the constraints of ultra 
vires policies. The California Supreme Court addressed precisely this type of challenge in In re 
Gadlin (2020) 10 Cal.5th 915, holding that categorical exclusions from parole rights are 
impermissible when the governing law mandates individualized assessment. The same principle 
applies here with equal force.
1 "The length of the program shall be . . . not less than one year, up to the entire period of parole." Pen. Code § 
3008(d)(2).
Page 3

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
II. STATEMENT OF THE CASE
A. Factual Background and Parole History
Petitioner Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi (CDC #BF3571) was released on parole on December 2, 
2020, following incarceration for violations of Penal Code section 289(a)(1)(A) (Penetration with 
Force/Violence) and section 220(a)(1) (Assault with Intent to Commit Specified Sex Offense). 
Upon release, he was subject to registration under Penal Code section 290 and assigned a 10-year 
parole term, with a controlling discharge date of December 2, 2030.
For the five years preceding the challenged decision, the Petitioner remained under continuous 
parole supervision. His performance on parole demonstrates a trajectory of stability and 
compliance that the statutory scheme was designed to recognize. As of December 2025, his 
classification was “Category SA,” and his California Static Risk Assessment (CSRA) score was 2
—indicating “low risk” for recidivism. The CSRA score of 2 places Petitioner in the lowest 
recidivism risk category, consistent with CDCR’s own risk assessment protocols and supporting 
discharge under risk-based criteria in 15 CCR § 3574(f).
The administrative record reflects the following key indicators of rehabilitation and stability:
•
Residence Stability: The Petitioner maintained a stable residence with family in Stockton 
for over eight months, satisfying the "Residence Stability" objective of the discharge 
review criteria.
•
Treatment Progress: Despite significant systemic disruptions—including approximately 
seven different clinicians over the five-year parole period and admissions by clinicians that 
completed homework assignments were lost—the Petitioner has actively participated in 
the Sex Offender Management Program (SOMP), advancing to the Core Phase, Block 1, 
Module 4 of 7. These changes interfered with continuity of care and consistent progress 
tracking, yet the Petitioner demonstrated persistence and compliance through ongoing 
engagement.
•
Social Affiliation: He demonstrated affiliation with pro-social individuals and avoided 
new criminal conduct throughout his parole term.
•
Supervision History: While the record notes technical violations related to GPS charging 
and treatment attendance, the Department did not revoke parole based on these violations.
B. The Challenged Discharge Denial
On December 1, 2025, the Division of Adult Parole Operations (DAPO) issued a Discharge 
Review Report (CDCR Form 1502-DR) denying the Petitioner's consideration for early discharge. 
The denial was not based on a holistic evaluation of the Petitioner's low risk score or his five years 
of stability. Instead, the "Unit Supervisor Comments" explicitly relied on two categorical 
barriers:
Page 4

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
•
The Time-Served Bar (Policy 19-03): The report stated: "Based on Sex Offender 
Management Program Earned Discharge Criteria, Policy 19-03 (Amended), Newanforbi is 
not eligible for EDC at this time due to having a 10-year parole term. Newanforbi has only 
completed approximately 4 years of the required 6.5 years of supervision."
•
The "Incomplete Treatment" Bar: The report cited "incomplete sex offender treatment" 
as a concurrent basis for denial—referencing a standard that, as demonstrated below, 
renders completion structurally impossible before discharge.
Crucially, the report failed to incorporate the procedural requirements mandated by the 
Department's own regulations that became effective months earlier in April 2025. There was no 
"Form 3043" outlining good cause for retention, no evidence of a Containment Team Meeting 
finding, and no consultation with a certified sex offender management professional regarding the 
appropriate duration of the program.
C. The Regulatory Landscape: 15 CCR § 3574
To fully appreciate the illegality of the December 2025 denial, one must examine the regulatory 
context. Following litigation in Alliance for Constitutional Sex Offense Laws v. Macomber 
(Sacramento Super. Ct. Case No. 23STCP02378), the Department adopted 15 California Code of 
Regulations section 3574, effective April 17, 2025. These regulations were intended to bring the 
Department into compliance with Penal Code section 3008(d) by formalizing the "Containment 
Model" and explicitly acknowledging that treatment completion is not inextricably linked to the 
discharge date.
The following table illustrates the stark disconnect between the requirements of 15 CCR § 3574 
and what actually appeared in the Petitioner's Discharge Review Report:
15 CCR § 3574 Requirement
Dec. 1, 2025 Report – Actual
Early completion permitted (§ 3574(d))
Denied on categorical "impossibility" policy
Written "good cause" finding required
Absent – only citation to Policy 19-03
CDCR Form 3043 required
No Form 3043 attached or referenced
Treatment provider signature required
No provider signature or input documented
Containment Team Meeting (CTM) required
No CTM documented or referenced
Risk-based retention criteria (§ 3574(f))
No risk scores cited; time-bar dispositive
30-day notice to parolee
No notice provision included
This table is not incidental to the Petition. It is the core of it. Every column on the right represents a 
failure by CDCR to follow its own binding regulations—regulations adopted less than eight 
months before the denial at issue.
Page 5

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
III. STANDARD OF REVIEW
A. Writ of Mandate Under Code of Civil Procedure § 1085
A traditional writ of mandate under Code of Civil Procedure section 1085 is the appropriate vehicle 
to compel a public official to perform a ministerial duty or to correct an abuse of discretion. To 
obtain relief, the petitioner must demonstrate: (1) a clear, present, and usually ministerial duty on 
the part of the respondent; and (2) a clear, present, and beneficial right in the petitioner to the 
performance of that duty. California Ass'n for Health Services at Home v. Dep't of Health Care 
Services (2012) 204 Cal.App.4th 676, 683.
While the ultimate decision to discharge a parolee involves an exercise of discretion, the duty to 
apply the correct legal standard in making that decision is ministerial. Mandate lies where an 
agency exercises its discretion under an unlawful standard or substitutes unauthorized categorical 
rules for the individualized analysis required by statute. Pomona Police Officers' Ass'n v. City of 
Pomona (1997) 58 Cal.App.4th 578, 583–84.
B. Abuse of Discretion and the "Manner Required by Law"
An abuse of discretion is established not only when an agency’s decision is unsupported by 
evidence, but also when the agency "has not proceeded in the manner required by law." Pomona 
Police Officers’ Ass’n v. City of Pomona (1997) 58 Cal.App.4th 578, 583; AIDS Healthcare 
Foundation v. L.A. County Dept. of Public Health (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 693; see also Topanga 
Ass’n for a Scenic Community v. County of Los Angeles (1974) 11 Cal.3d 506, 514. As the 
California Supreme Court held in Yamaha Corp. of America v. State Bd. of Equalization (1998) 
19 Cal.4th 1, while agencies possess expertise in their domains, the judiciary retains the ultimate 
power to interpret statutes. When an agency’s policy contradicts the plain text of a governing 
statute, the agency has abused its discretion, and the court must intervene to enforce the legislative 
will.

IV. ARGUMENT
A. Exhaustion of Administrative Remedies Is Excused
The Department will likely assert, as a threshold matter, that the Petitioner has failed to exhaust 
administrative remedies. This argument fails under three independently sufficient doctrines, each 
of which has been endorsed by the California Supreme Court.
1. The Futility Exception Applies.
The futility exception to the exhaustion requirement applies when the petitioner can "positively 
state what the administrative agency's decision in his particular case would be." In re Thompson 
(1985) 172 Cal.App.3d 256, 262. Here, no inference is required. The December 1, 2025 Discharge 
Review Report explicitly states the basis for denial: "Newanforbi is not eligible for EDC at this 
time due to having a 10-year parole term. Newanforbi has only completed approximately 4 years 
of the required 6.5 years of supervision." This language reflects a fixed, statewide policy—not a 
case-specific exercise of discretion. Any Form 602 administrative appeal would be reviewed by 
the same agency enforcing the same categorical policy. It is futile to ask an agency to overturn its 
own "underground regulation" through a grievance process designed for individual factual 
disputes, not systemic policy challenges.
The factual predicate for this conclusion is not speculative. In In re Dwyer (San Mateo Super. Ct. 
Case No. SC-080355A/HC-3020, Order dated Mar. 20, 2023), CDCR officials testified under oath 
that sex offenders on parole cannot "complete" treatment before discharge. This sworn admission 
establishes CDCR's institutional position—a position that no internal grievance reviewer has the 
authority to override.
2. The Pure Question of Law Exception Applies.
The California Supreme Court has held that "[p]ure questions of law need not be exhausted 
administratively, particularly when the agency lacks authority to grant the relief sought." Coachella 
Valley Mosquito & Vector Control Dist. v. California Public Employment Relations Bd. (2005) 
35 Cal.4th 1072, 1080. The issues presented in this Petition are textbook pure legal questions:
(a)  Does Penal Code section 3008(d)(2) authorize categorical, time-based bars to discharge 
eligibility?
(b)  Does CDCR possess statutory authority to prohibit early program completion?
(c)  Is Policy 19-03 ultra vires to the statutes it purports to implement?
These are questions of statutory interpretation and agency authority. They do not require factual 
fact-finding or the exercise of administrative expertise. They are matters for this Court.
3. The Administrative Remedy Is Inadequate.
Page 7

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
The California Supreme Court has also held that "[o]ne need not exhaust inadequate remedies in 
order to challenge their sufficiency." Horn v. County of Ventura (1979) 24 Cal.3d 605, 611. The 
CDCR Form 602 grievance process cannot invalidate a regulation, declare a policy ultra vires, or 
compel the Department to disregard agency-wide directives. Only a court of law possesses the 
authority to do so. The administrative process is therefore not merely inadequate—it is structurally 
incapable of providing the relief sought here.
Page 8

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
B. CDCR's Categorical Time-Bar Violates Penal Code § 3008(d)(2)
The Department's primary justification for denying discharge—the "10-year/6.5-year" rule 
embedded in Policy 19-03—is a categorical policy that finds no support in the governing statute. 
Penal Code section 3008(d)(2) establishes the framework for sex offender management programs 
on parole. Its text is unambiguous regarding the permissible range of treatment duration:
"The length of the period in the program shall be not less than one year, up to the entire 
period of parole, as determined by the certified sex offender management professional in 
consultation with the parole officer and as approved by the court." Pen. Code § 3008(d)
(2).
1. The Canon Against Surplusage and the Meaning of "Up To."
A fundamental canon of statutory construction requires that "every word in a statute must be given 
effect." People v. Rizo (2000) 22 Cal.4th 681, 685. The Legislature's inclusion of the phrase "up 
to" in section 3008(d)(2) is not ornamental. It creates a discretionary range—a range that, by its 
plain meaning, explicitly contemplates that for some parolees, the appropriate duration of the 
treatment program will be less than the entire parole period.
If the Legislature had intended to mandate that all sex offenders remain in the program for their 
full parole term—or for a fixed percentage thereof (e.g., 6.5 years of a 10-year term)—it would 
have enacted language to that effect. It did not. Instead, it delegated the determination of duration 
to clinical professionals and the courts. By enforcing Policy 19-03, which imposes a mandatory 
minimum of 6.5 years for all parolees with 10-year terms regardless of individual progress, the 
Department renders the words "up to" complete surplusage. This violates the cardinal rule that 
courts—and agencies—must avoid interpretations that make statutory language meaningless. 
Lungren v. Deukmejian (1988) 45 Cal.3d 727, 735.
The point may be stated simply. If CDCR's policy is valid—that treatment duration is effectively 
coterminous with parole until discharge—then the statutory phrase "not less than one year, up to" 
serves no function whatsoever. A court must presume the Legislature intended that phrase to have 
meaning. The only logical meaning is that there exists a subset of parolees for whom the 
appropriate treatment duration is less than the full parole term. Policy 19-03 forecloses even the 
possibility of that subset existing.
2. In re Gadlin and the Prohibition on Wholesale Exclusions.
The California Supreme Court has repeatedly rebuked CDCR for attempting to curtail statutory 
parole rights through categorical administrative rules. In In re Gadlin (2020) 10 Cal.5th 915, the 
Court invalidated CDCR regulations that categorically excluded nonviolent sex offenders from 
parole consideration under Proposition 57. The Court held that "eligibility must be based on an 
inmate's current circumstances—not categorical rules applied without individual consideration." 
Id. at 928. The regulations created, in the Court's words, "wholesale exclusions from a 
constitutional right. That is impermissible." Id.
Page 9

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
Although Gadlin addressed parole consideration for inmates rather than discharge for supervisees, 
its reasoning applies with equal force here. In both contexts, the Department attempted to use a 
blanket exclusion—based on penal status—to override a statutory or constitutional directive for 
flexible, individualized review. The 10-year/6.5-year rule is precisely the type of “wholesale 
exclusion” condemned in Gadlin. It prejudges every parolee with a 10-year term as ineligible for 
discharge until a fixed date, regardless of their “current circumstances,” their individual progress, 
or the “good cause” findings required by law.
This principle was recently reaffirmed in In re Leman (2021) 66 Cal.App.5th 200. The court held 
that CDCR’s reliance on a “one-size-fits-all” policy, rather than an “individualized consideration 
of [the parolee’s] current risk to public safety,” constitutes an abuse of discretion. Id. at 215. The 
court emphasized that an agency substituting generalized classifications for statutorily mandated 
individualized assessment violates its duty to proceed in the manner required by law. The identical 
flaw infects the denial here: CDCR applied categorical time bars and structural impossibility rules 
rather than assessing the Petitioner’s actual risk, progress, and rehabilitation.
3. In re Taylor and the Requirement for Particularized Circumstances.
Similarly, in In re Taylor (2015) 60 Cal.4th 1019, the Supreme Court struck down blanket 
residency restrictions imposed on all sex offenders on parole, holding that such restrictions are 
permissible "only when [they are] based on, and supported by, the particularized circumstances of 
each individual parolee." Id. at 1037. The Court emphasized that while public safety is a 
compelling interest, it does not justify arbitrary administrative barriers that bear no rational 
relationship to an individual's actual risk.
The Petitioner's denial was not based on his particularized circumstances. To the contrary, his 
circumstances—stable residence, low risk score, five years of supervision without revocation, and 
active treatment participation—militated in favor of discharge. He was denied solely because of a 
generalized policy rule applied mechanically to his sentence structure. Under Taylor, this failure 
to conduct an individualized assessment constitutes an invalid exercise of agency power.
Page 10

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
C. CDCR's "Completion Impossible" Policy Violates § 3008(d)(2) and 15 CCR § 3574
The second categorical bar cited in the December 1, 2025 Discharge Review Report—"incomplete 
sex offender treatment"—is not a reflection of the Petitioner's clinical status alone. It is the product 
of a structural policy that renders pre-discharge completion impossible by design. This Court need 
not speculate about the existence of such a policy; it has been established under oath.
1. The Policy Was Established Through Sworn Testimony.
In In re Dwyer (San Mateo Super. Ct. Case No. SC-080355A/HC-3020, Order dated Mar. 20, 
2023), the superior court held an evidentiary hearing at which CDCR officials and treatment 
provider representatives testified. The court found as a matter of fact that CDCR's practice was to 
require every registrant-parolee to participate in the treatment program for the entire term of parole, 
"apparently without reference to the individualized performance of each parolee." The court 
concluded that this practice "vitiates the Legislature's directive" in section 3008(d). The Dwyer 
record further established that no parolee had ever been allowed to "complete" the sex offender 
treatment program prior to discharge under CDCR's unwritten rules.
This is not a relic of the past. The December 1, 2025 Report in this case cited "incomplete sex 
offender treatment" as a basis for denial—while simultaneously applying a framework under 
which completion before discharge is structurally unattainable. The policy persists. Petitioner’s 
treatment provider, HOPE, was the subject of that very testimony in Dwyer. Its "continuous 
connection" mandate is the direct cause of Petitioner’s "incomplete" status cited in the December 
2025 Report, proving the policy’s active application in his case long after the Dwyer court 
condemned it.
2. CDCR's Own Regulations Repudiate the Policy.
Effective April 17, 2025, CDCR adopted 15 Cal. Code Regs. § 3574, which states in subsection 
(d): "Supervised persons may complete a sex offender management program before discharge 
from parole, as contemplated by PC section 3008(d)." This language is a direct and formal 
repudiation of the "completion impossible" stance. It is not ambiguous. It is not incidental. It is the 
regulation's explicit acknowledgment that the law has always permitted—and indeed contemplated
—early completion.
The Department cannot have it both ways. It cannot promulgate a regulation in April 2025 
explicitly permitting early completion, and then deny a parolee in December 2025 on the ground 
that completion is impossible. To do so is the definition of arbitrary and capricious agency action. 
See Yamaha Corp. of America v. State Bd. of Equalization (1998) 19 Cal.4th 1, 7 ("An agency 
regulation that is inconsistent with the statute under which it is adopted is void."); see also Morris 
v. Williams (1967) 67 Cal.2d 733, 737 (courts must strike down agency practices contradicting 
statute).
3. The December 1 Report Violates § 3574's Procedural Requirements.
Page 11

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
Section 3574(f) provides that any decision to retain a supervised person in treatment must be 
“supported by good cause” as defined in Penal Code section 3000, documented in writing on 
CDCR Form 3043, signed by both the treatment provider and the parole agent, and delivered to 
the supervised person within 30 days. The Petitioner’s Discharge Review Report contains none of 
these elements. There is no Form 3043. There is no treatment provider signature. There is no 
articulated “good cause” analysis. There is no delivery. This is not a minor procedural deficiency. 
The requirement for a treatment provider’s signature ensures that clinical experts—not custodial 
agents alone—participate in the duration decision, exactly as section 3008(d)(2) requires. By 
bypassing this check, the Department removed the “certified sex offender management 
professional” from the decision-making loop entirely.
These structural and policy barriers are compounded by failures in treatment delivery attributable 
to CDCR and its contracted providers. The Petitioner’s experience of approximately seven 
clinician changes over five years—coupled with lost homework—demonstrates a profound lack 
of continuity that the California Sex Offender Management Board (CASOMB) guidelines seek to 
prevent. CASOMB’s Guidelines for Transfer of Clients between Programs (July 2024) recognize 
that provider changes “may interfere with the consistency of an individual’s containment team,” 
disrupting treatment plans, prior successes, and motivation, and mandate steps like record 
transfers, discharge summaries, and collaborative decisions with parole to mitigate harm. 
CASOMB’s Treatment Completion Guidelines (April 2018) emphasize that treatment duration 
must be determined through individualized assessment by the containment team, focusing on 
progress in treatment modules, risk reduction, and dynamic factors rather than arbitrary time 
minimums. These standards contemplate flexible duration and support early completion for 
offenders demonstrating sufficient rehabilitation—precisely the individualized framework § 
3008(d)(2) mandates and § 3574 implements. CDCR’s Policy 19-03 ignores this expert guidance, 
and the fragmented care prevented the consistent, evidence-based input from a certified 
professional required by § 3008(d)(2) and § 3574(f), further tainting the denial.
Where treatment records are fragmented, reset, or lost due to repeated provider turnover, CDCR 
cannot establish by substantial evidence that continued treatment is clinically necessary, rather 
than administratively prolonged. The Petitioner’s advancement to Core Phase, Block 1, Module 4 
of 7—despite these systemic disruptions—demonstrates good-faith participation and progress. 
CDCR’s reliance on “incomplete treatment” punishes the Petitioner for deficiencies caused by the 
Department’s own failures in record-keeping and provider continuity, rendering the denial 
arbitrary and unsupported by substantial evidence.

D. Policy 19-03 Is an Invalid "Underground Regulation"
Independent of its conflict with the governing statutes, Policy 19-03 is void as an "underground 
regulation" that was never adopted through the procedures required by the California 
Administrative Procedure Act.
The APA defines a "regulation" as every rule, standard, or order of general application adopted by 
a state agency to implement, interpret, or make specific the law it enforces. Gov. Code § 
11342.600. Regulations must be adopted through a formal notice-and-comment process to ensure 
public transparency and legal vetting. A rule that meets the definition of a regulation but has not 
been formally adopted is an "underground regulation"—and it is void. Tidewater Marine Western, 
Inc. v. Bradshaw (1996) 14 Cal.4th 557, 571.
The California Supreme Court in Tidewater established a two-part test to identify underground 
regulations: (1) Does the rule apply generally, rather than to a specific case? (2) Does the rule 
implement, interpret, or make specific the law enforced by the agency? Policy 19-03 satisfies both 
prongs. First, it applies generally to all parolees with a 10-year term—it is not an adjudication of 
a specific case but a blanket standard. Second, it interprets and "makes specific" the broad "up to" 
language of Penal Code section 3008(d) by imposing a concrete minimum duration (6.5 years) that 
the statute itself does not contain.
Because Policy 19-03 was never adopted through the APA process—unlike the new Section 3574, 
which was—it is an illegal underground regulation. The Department cannot rely on an invalid rule 
to justify the deprivation of the Petitioner's statutory right to an individualized assessment. As the 
Court in Tidewater observed, an agency does not have the power to "add requirements" to a statute 
through internal policy manuals. See also California Hotel & Motel Ass'n v. Industrial Welfare 
Comm'n (1979) 25 Cal.3d 200, 212.

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
E. CDCR Violated Its Ministerial Duty to Apply the Correct Legal Standard
The foregoing arguments converge on a single, controlling principle: the duty to apply the correct 
legal standard is ministerial, even where the ultimate decision involves discretion. AIDS 
Healthcare Foundation v. Los Angeles County Dept. of Public Health (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 693, 
700. When an agency is required by statute to apply specific criteria in reaching a decision, the 
agency’s obligation to use those criteria—rather than substitute its own policy-based criteria—is 
a ministerial duty enforceable by mandate. Id.
As the California Supreme Court held in People v. Superior Court (Laff) (2001) 25 Cal.4th 703, 
734, “the determination of whether to [grant a benefit] is discretionary, but the duty to apply the 
correct criteria in making that determination is ministerial.” Here, the correct criteria are the 
individualized factors set forth in § 3008(d)(2) and § 3574—clinical progress, risk assessment, 
containment team input, and good cause findings. The unauthorized criteria are Policy 19-03’s 
categorical time bars and the structurally impossible completion standard. CDCR’s failure to apply 
the correct, statutorily mandated criteria is a ministerial duty violation remediable by mandate.
This principle has direct application here. CDCR possessed discretion to weigh the Petitioner’s 
risk level, his compliance history, his treatment progress, and the other individualized factors 
contemplated by Penal Code section 3008(d)(2) and 15 CCR § 3574. CDCR did not possess 
discretion to substitute categorical time-based bars for that individualized inquiry. The duty to use 
the statutory factors—rather than Policy 19-03’s mechanical formula—is ministerial. It failed to 
perform that duty. By applying a rigid time-bar and an impossible completion standard, the 
Department abdicated that discretion entirely. A ministerial duty to exercise discretion cannot be 
satisfied by a refusal to exercise it. See Rodriguez v. Solis (1991) 1 Cal.App.4th 495, 502.
The Court of Appeal in Pomona Police Officers' Ass'n v. City of Pomona (1997) 58 Cal.App.4th 
578, 583–84, confirmed that mandate lies to correct an agency that "has not proceeded in the 
manner required by law." Here, the manner required by law was an individualized assessment 
conducted by—or at least in consultation with—a certified sex offender management professional, 
documented through the procedures of 15 CCR § 3574. The December 1, 2025 Report reflects 
none of that. It reflects a mechanical application of a categorical rule. That is not a failure of 
discretion; it is a failure to exercise discretion at all—and mandate is the appropriate remedy. See 
also Rodriguez v. Solis (1991) 1 Cal.App.4th 495, 502 (mandate lies when agency substitutes 
unauthorized criteria for statutory requirements).

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
F. The December 1, 2025 Decision Is "Tainted" and Must Be Vacated
The Department may attempt to argue that the denial should stand because the Petitioner had 
technical parole violations—GPS charging issues and a treatment attendance issue. This argument 
fails under the well-established "taint" doctrine of California administrative law.
1. A Decision Based Partly on Improper Grounds Must Be Set Aside.
The Court of Appeal held in California Highway Patrol v. Superior Court (2008) 158 Cal.App.4th 
726, 735, that when an administrative decision rests on multiple grounds and at least one is 
improper, the decision must be set aside. The reasoning is that a reviewing court cannot determine 
with certainty that the agency would have reached the same result absent the improper 
consideration. The appropriate remedy is vacatur and remand—not judicial speculation about what 
the agency might have done.
Here, the December 1, 2025 denial rests on multiple grounds. Two of them are demonstrably 
improper: the 6.5-year time bar (ultra vires under Tidewater and inconsistent with section 3008(d)
(2)) and the incomplete treatment standard (structurally impossible under the pre-2025 policy, and 
formally repudiated by § 3574(d)). The remaining grounds—technical violations and 
unemployment—may or may not, standing alone, constitute sufficient basis for denial under a 
properly conducted individualized review. But because the decision is inextricably tainted by the 
improper criteria, it cannot be upheld.
2. The Improper Criteria Were Dispositive.
This is not a close case on the application of the taint doctrine. The Report states plainly: 
“Newanforbi is not eligible for EDC at this time due to having a 10-year parole term.” The Report’s 
use of the term “not eligible” is dispositive. It reveals a threshold eligibility determination made 
before any holistic review of Petitioner’s individual circumstances. The Report’s use of “not 
eligible” language confirms the categorical bar was dispositive, not supplementary—precluding 
any meaningful individualized review. Under the taint doctrine, this foundational reliance on 
unlawful criteria requires vacatur without speculation. California Highway Patrol v. Superior 
Court (2008) 158 Cal.App.4th 726, 735. The subsequent notes on technical violations are post-hoc 
justifications for a decision already reached on unlawful grounds. This sequence confirms that the 
taint is not incidental; it is foundational. The Policy 19-03 bar was not a supplementary 
consideration but the determination that foreclosed any individualized analysis from taking 
place.
Because the “incomplete treatment” finding rests on records compromised by CDCR’s own 
failures in continuity and documentation—specifically, seven clinician changes over five years 
and the admitted loss of completed homework—that ground is independently invalid and further 
taints the discharge denial. An agency cannot penalize an individual for deficiencies caused by the 
agency’s own systemic failures. The fragmented treatment records prevent any reliable 
determination of the Petitioner’s actual clinical status, rendering the “incomplete treatment” 
Page 15

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
rationale arbitrary and unsupported. This independent taint reinforces the need for vacatur and 
remand under proper procedures.
Moreover, the technical violations themselves were treated by CDCR as insufficiently serious to 
warrant revocation. If the Department did not consider the violations grave enough to revoke 
parole, it is difficult to conceive how they would, standing alone, justify denial of discharge 
eligibility—particularly for a parolee with a low risk score and five years of stable supervision.
3. The Remedy Is Vacatur and Remand.
Under the taint doctrine, the Court should not attempt to "save" the denial by speculating that the 
Department would have reached the same result using only proper criteria. See JKH Enterprises, 
Inc. v. Dept. of Industrial Relations (2006) 142 Cal.App.4th 1046, 1058. The appropriate remedy 
is vacatur of the December 1, 2025 Discharge Review Report and remand for a new determination
—one conducted under the individualized criteria of Penal Code section 3008(d)(2) and the 
procedural requirements of 15 CCR § 3574. See also Topanga Ass'n for a Scenic Community v. 
County of Los Angeles (1974) 11 Cal.3d 506, 514–15 (agency must articulate findings supporting 
decision under proper legal standard; decision lacking proper legal basis must be set aside).

Newanforbi v. Macomber – Opening Brief
G. Petitioner Has a Clear Beneficial Right to a Lawful Determination
The second element of a mandate action—a clear, present, and beneficial right in the petitioner—
is readily established. Penal Code section 3008(d)(2) creates a right to have the duration of the sex 
offender management program determined through an individualized assessment by a certified 
professional. 15 CCR § 3574 creates correlative procedural rights: to a Containment Team 
Meeting, to written "good cause" for retention on Form 3043, and to 30-day notice. The December 
1, 2025 Report provided none of these.
Moreover, the Petitioner has a liberty interest in freedom from unlawful prolongation of parole 
supervision. While there is no constitutional right to parole discharge per se, once a state 
establishes a statutory scheme for early discharge—as California has done through Penal Code 
sections 3000, 3001, and 3008—it creates a liberty interest that is protected by the Due Process 
Clause. Greenholtz v. Inmates of Nebraska Penal and Correctional Complex (1979) 442 U.S. 1; In 
re Lawrence (2008) 44 Cal.4th 1181. Ongoing parole supervision subjects the Petitioner to GPS 
monitoring, residency restrictions, and the constant threat of re-incarceration for technical 
violations. Prolonging that supervision beyond what the law authorizes—through policies that are 
nowhere in the statute—is not a neutral administrative act. It is a deprivation of liberty that the law 
does not sanction.
This Court, in Alliance for Constitutional Sex Offense Laws v. Macomber (Sacramento Super. Ct. 
Case No. 23STCP02378, Order dated Dec. 13, 2023), overruled CDCR's demurrer to a petition 
presenting these identical legal theories. In doing so, it necessarily found that a parolee has 
standing and a beneficial right to challenge categorical discharge policies as ultra vires. That ruling 
validates both the procedural vehicle and the substantive claims presented here.

V. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER FOR RELIEF
The Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation has engaged in an unlawful substitution of 
categorical criteria for the individualized assessment required by statute. By applying the "10-
year/6.5-year" rule and the "impossible completion" standard, the Department violated the plain 
text of Penal Code section 3008(d)(2), ignored the mandate of In re Gadlin and In re Taylor against 
categorical exclusions, and failed to follow its own binding regulations under 15 CCR section 
3574.
The Petitioner has met all requirements for the issuance of a writ of mandate. The Department has 
a ministerial duty to apply the correct statutory criteria. It failed to do so. The Petitioner has a 
beneficial right to an individualized assessment. He was denied one. The decision is tainted by 
reliance on improper criteria. It must be vacated.

the Discharge Review Report dated December 1, 2025.

time-served bar.

4. Compel Procedural Compliance, specifically requiring that any decision to retain the 
Petitioner in treatment be supported by written "good cause" on CDCR Form 3043, signed 
by a certified treatment provider and parole agent, as required by 15 CCR § 3574(f).
5. Issue a Declaratory Judgment finding that CDCR Policy 19-03 (Amended), to the extent 
it imposes a mandatory minimum time-served requirement for parole discharge, is an 
invalid "underground regulation" adopted in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act 
and is ultra vires to Penal Code section 3008(d).

Information for Judgment Creditor Regarding Service  
If you want to be able to ask the court to enforce the order on the judgment debtor or any third person, you 
must have a copy of the order personally served on the person to be examined by a sheriff, marshal, 
registered process server, or the person appointed in item 3 of the order, and have a proof of service filed 
with the court. You must have the order served at least 30 calendar days before the date of the examination 
if the examination is of the judgment debtor, or at least 10 calendar days before the date of the examination if 
the examination is of a third person. 
If the examination is of a third person, you must also have a copy of the order served personally or by mail 
on the judgment debtor at least 10 calendar days before the date of the examination.

proceeding.

that is yours or owes you a debt. This property or debt is as follows (describe the property or debt):

or your exemption may be waived.

NOTICE TO PERSON SERVED   If you fail to appear at the time and place specified in this order, you

Page 3 of 4

AT-138/EJ-125 [Rev. Oct. 1, 2024]
APPLICATION AND ORDER FOR 
APPEARANCE AND EXAMINATION 
(Attachment—Enforcement of Judgment)
AT-138/EJ-125
APPEARANCE OF A CORPORATION, PARTNERSHIP,  
ASSOCIATION, TRUST, LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY, OR OTHER ORGANIZATION
If the order to appear for the examination on page 1 does not require the appearance of a specified 
individual:
• 
The organization has a duty to designate one or more of the following to appear and be 
examined: officers, directors, managing agents, or other persons who are familiar with the 
organization's property and debts.
• 
Failure to designate such a person familiar with the organization's property and debts to 
appear for examination will result in the order to appear for the examination to be deemed to 
have been made to, and require the appearance of, the following:
• 
If the organization is a corporation registered with the Secretary of State, a natural 
person named as the chief financial officer in the corporation's most recent filing with 
the Secretary of State. If no one is so named, a natural person named as the chief 
executive officer in the corporation's most recent filing with the Secretary of State. If no 
one is so named, a natural person named as the secretary in the corporation's most 
recent filing with the Secretary of State.
• 
If the organization is a limited liability company registered with the Secretary of State, 
the first natural person named as a manager or member in the limited liability 
company's most recent filing with the Secretary of State.
• 
If the organization is a limited partnership registered with the Secretary of State, the 
first natural person named as a general partner in the limited partnership's most recent 
filing with the Secretary of State.
• 
If the organization is not registered with the Secretary of State or the organization's 
filings with the Secretary of State do not identify a natural person as described above, a 
natural person identified by the judgment creditor as being familiar with the property 
and debts of the organization, together with an affidavit or declaration signed by the 
judgment creditor that sets forth the factual basis for the identification of the individual. 
The affidavit or declaration shall be served on the organization together with the order.
• 
Service of an order to appear for an examination upon an organization by any method 
permitted under the Code of Civil Procedure or the Corporations Code, including service on 
the agent of the organization for service of process, shall be deemed effective service of the 
order to appear upon the individuals identified above.

office or go to

I.  PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
1. I am the Plaintiff in the above-entitled action and am over eighteen years of age. The
matters set forth herein are within my personal knowledge unless stated on information and
belief, and if called as a witness, I could and would competently testify to them. I submit this
Declaration in support of my Request for Entry of Default Judgment by the Court (Judicial
Council Form CIV-100) against Defendant ALPINE TRUCK SALES, INC. ("Alpine"),
pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 585, subdivision (b), and California Rules of Court,
rule 3.1800.
2. This Declaration is submitted together with the following companion documents
constituting my prove-up package as to Alpine: (a) the Court's Notice to Filing Party on the prior
default submission (returned with this resubmission as directed); (b) Plaintiff's Request for Entry
of Default and Court Judgment (Form CIV-100), including the Declaration of Nonmilitary Status
at CIV-100 item 8; (c) Plaintiff's Request for Dismissal of Does 1 through 20 (Form CIV-110);
(d) this Declaration; (e) Plaintiff's [Proposed] Judgment by Court After Default (Form JUD-100);
and (f) the exhibits attached hereto, which are the same documentary exhibits previously
submitted in support of the default judgment prove-up against co-defendant Diamond Truck
Sales, Inc. ("Diamond"), attached again here so that this filing is complete and self-contained as
to Alpine. Plaintiff waives costs of suit on CIV-100 item 7f; no Memorandum of Costs (Form
MC-010) is filed with this packet. Plaintiff seeks compensatory relief only and does not request
punitive damages in this filing.

names Alpine as a defendant on the theory that Alpine is Diamond's successor in interest, mere

III.  SUCCESSOR LIABILITY IS DERIVATIVE, NOT ADDITIONAL

for independently committing fraud, misrepresentation, or breach of contract in the underlying
vehicle sale transaction; rather, Alpine is sued as the entity that has, by operation of the
successor-liability and alter-ego doctrines pleaded in the FAC, become answerable for the single
judgment obligation that Diamond itself already owes to Plaintiff by reason of Diamond's own
default.
9. Accordingly, Plaintiff does NOT seek, and this Declaration does NOT request, an
additional or duplicative award of damages against Alpine on top of the judgment sought against
Diamond. Plaintiff instead requests that judgment be entered against Alpine in the same total
amount requested against Diamond, on a joint and several basis, so that Plaintiff may recover the
single judgment sum from either or both defendants, without any double recovery. This is
consistent with the [Proposed] Judgment (Form JUD-100) submitted with this packet, which at
item 8 expressly provides that Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is jointly and severally liable with
Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. as Diamond's successor, mere continuation, alter ego, and/or
fraudulent transferee.

III.  SUCCESSOR LIABILITY IS DERIVATIVE, NOT ADDITIONAL
8. Alpine's liability in this action is derivative of Diamond's liability. Alpine is not sued
for independently committing fraud, misrepresentation, or breach of contract in the underlying
vehicle sale transaction; rather, Alpine is sued as the entity that has, by operation of the
successor-liability and alter-ego doctrines pleaded in the FAC, become answerable for the single
judgment obligation that Diamond itself already owes to Plaintiff by reason of Diamond's own
default.
9. Accordingly, Plaintiff does NOT seek, and this Declaration does NOT request, an
additional or duplicative award of damages against Alpine on top of the judgment sought against
Diamond. Plaintiff instead requests that judgment be entered against Alpine in the same total
amount requested against Diamond, on a joint and several basis, so that Plaintiff may recover the
single judgment sum from either or both defendants, without any double recovery. This is
consistent with the [Proposed] Judgment (Form JUD-100) submitted with this packet, which at
item 8 expressly provides that Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is jointly and severally liable with
Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. as Diamond's successor, mere continuation, alter ego, and/or
fraudulent transferee.

Declaration in support of my Request for Entry of Default Judgment by the Court (Judicial
Council Form CIV-100) against Defendant ALPINE TRUCK SALES, INC. ("Alpine"), pursuant
to Code of Civil Procedure section 585, subdivision (b), and California Rules of Court, rule
3.1800.
2. This Declaration is submitted together with the following companion documents
constituting my prove-up package as to Alpine: (a) Plaintiff's Request for Entry of Default and
Court Judgment (Form CIV-100); (b) this Declaration; and (c) the exhibits attached hereto, which
are the same documentary exhibits previously submitted in support of the default judgment
prove-up against co-defendant Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. ("Diamond"), attached again here so
that this filing is complete and self-contained as to Alpine.
II. PROCEDURAL POSTURE
3. The operative pleading in this action is the First Amended Complaint ("FAC"), which
names Alpine as a defendant on the theory that Alpine is Diamond's successor in interest, mere
continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or a participant in a fraudulent transfer under
the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act (Civ. Code section 3439 et seq.).
4. Alpine was personally served with the Amended Summons, the First Amended
Complaint, and the Notice of Case Assignment and Notice of Hearing on July 1, 2026, at 9:00
a.m., by delivery to Mustaqem Usmani, Manager, at 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California
95380, by San Joaquin County Sheriff's Deputy T. Caldwell, under Code of Civil Procedure
section 416.10. Proof of Service (Form POS-010, Levying Officer File No. 2026002577) was
signed July 2, 2026 by the Sheriff's Authorized Agent and is on file with this Court.

5. Alpine's deadline to respond to the FAC expired thirty (30) days after service, on July
31, 2026. Alpine filed no responsive pleading, demurrer, or other appearance, and no
meet-and-confer contact was received from Alpine at any time before or after that deadline. I
have submitted a Request for Entry of Default (Form CIV-100) against Alpine, and the Court has
entered, or will shortly enter, Alpine's default as reflected in the Court's file.
6. Because Alpine has defaulted, the well-pleaded factual allegations of the FAC
concerning Alpine's liability are deemed admitted. (Steven M. Garber & Assocs. v. Eskandarian
(2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 813, 823; Kim v. Westmoore Partners, Inc. (2011) 201 Cal.App.4th 267,
281.) The well-pleaded allegations include, without limitation: that Diamond rebranded to Alpine
during the pendency of this action; that Alpine has operated from the same locations as Diamond,
including 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California, under the same Osmani family ownership
and management; and that Alpine is therefore liable for Diamond's obligations in this action as its
successor in interest, mere continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or by reason of a
fraudulent transfer of Diamond's business and assets to Alpine.
7. This Declaration addresses only the amount and proof of damages as against Alpine. I
have made no effort to relitigate liability, which is deemed established by the default, nor to
relitigate the underlying fraud and misrepresentation claims against Diamond, which were proved
up separately -- and on the same exhibits reattached hereto -- in the default judgment package
previously submitted as to Diamond.
III. SUCCESSOR LIABILITY IS DERIVATIVE, NOT ADDITIONAL
8. Alpine's liability in this action is derivative of Diamond's liability. Alpine is not sued
for independently committing fraud, misrepresentation, or breach of contract in the underlying
vehicle sale transaction; rather, Alpine is sued as the entity that has, by operation of the
successor-liability and alter-ego doctrines pleaded in the FAC, become answerable for the single

9. Accordingly, Plaintiff does NOT seek, and this Declaration does NOT request, an
additional or duplicative award of damages against Alpine on top of the judgment sought against
Diamond. Plaintiff instead requests that judgment be entered against Alpine in the same total
amount requested against Diamond, on a joint and several basis, so that Plaintiff may recover the
single judgment sum from either or both defendants, without any double recovery. This is
consistent with the [Proposed] Judgment (Form JUD-100) already on file in this action, which at
item 8 expressly provides that "Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is jointly and severally liable with
Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. as Diamond's successor, mere continuation, alter ego, and/or
fraudulent transference."
IV. DAMAGES (SAME SUM AS THE DIAMOND JUDGMENT)
10. The itemized calculation of damages is set forth in full in the Declaration in Support
of Request for Default Judgment previously filed against Diamond, and in Attachment 4b to
Plaintiff's Case Management Statement (Form CM-110) filed July 20, 2026, both of which are
incorporated herein by reference. The supporting documentary exhibits (Exhibits 1 through 10)
are attached to this Declaration for completeness. In summary: documented out-of-pocket losses
of $20,218.65; additional sworn, undocumented out-of-pocket losses of $5,750.00; conservatively
calculated lost commercial income of $23,400.00 (18 weeks x $1,300/week); and prejudgment
interest under Civil Code section 3287(a) (7%, approximately 3.04 years) of $4,302.55 -- for a
compensatory subtotal of $53,671.20.
11. Plaintiff additionally requests punitive damages of $25,000.00 under Civil Code
section 3294, based on the well-pleaded and, as to Diamond, now-admitted allegations that
Diamond's concealment of the DEF/SCR emissions defect was intentional, malicious, fraudulent,

Declaration in support of my Request for Entry of Default Judgment by the Court (Judicial

to Code of Civil Procedure section 585, subdivision (b), and California Rules of Court, rule
3.1800.
2. This Declaration is submitted together with the following companion documents
constituting my prove-up package as to Alpine: (a) Plaintiff's Request for Entry of Default and
Court Judgment (Form CIV-100); (b) this Declaration; and (c) the exhibits attached hereto, which
are the same documentary exhibits previously submitted in support of the default judgment
prove-up against co-defendant Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. ("Diamond"), attached again here so
that this filing is complete and self-contained as to Alpine.
II. PROCEDURAL POSTURE
3. The operative pleading in this action is the First Amended Complaint ("FAC"), which
names Alpine as a defendant on the theory that Alpine is Diamond's successor in interest, mere
continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or a participant in a fraudulent transfer under
the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act (Civ. Code section 3439 et seq.).
4. Alpine was personally served with the Amended Summons, the First Amended
Complaint, and the Notice of Case Assignment and Notice of Hearing on July 1, 2026, at 9:00
a.m., by delivery to Mustaqem Usmani, Manager, at 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California
95380, by San Joaquin County Sheriff's Deputy T. Caldwell, under Code of Civil Procedure
section 416.10. Proof of Service (Form POS-010, Levying Officer File No. 2026002577) was
signed July 2, 2026 by the Sheriff's Authorized Agent and is on file with this Court.
