5. Alpine's deadline to respond to the FAC expired thirty (30) days after service, on July
31, 2026. Alpine filed no responsive pleading, demurrer, or other appearance, and no
meet-and-confer contact was received from Alpine at any time before or after that deadline. I
have submitted a Request for Entry of Default (Form CIV-100) against Alpine, and the Court has
entered, or will shortly enter, Alpine's default as reflected in the Court's file.
6. Because Alpine has defaulted, the well-pleaded factual allegations of the FAC
concerning Alpine's liability are deemed admitted. (Steven M. Garber & Assocs. v. Eskandarian
(2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 813, 823; Kim v. Westmoore Partners, Inc. (2011) 201 Cal.App.4th 267,
281.) The well-pleaded allegations include, without limitation: that Diamond rebranded to Alpine
during the pendency of this action; that Alpine has operated from the same locations as Diamond,
including 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California, under the same Osmani family ownership
and management; and that Alpine is therefore liable for Diamond's obligations in this action as its
successor in interest, mere continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or by reason of a
fraudulent transfer of Diamond's business and assets to Alpine.
7. This Declaration addresses only the amount and proof of damages as against Alpine. I
have made no effort to relitigate liability, which is deemed established by the default, nor to
relitigate the underlying fraud and misrepresentation claims against Diamond, which were proved
up separately -- and on the same exhibits reattached hereto -- in the default judgment package
previously submitted as to Diamond.
III. SUCCESSOR LIABILITY IS DERIVATIVE, NOT ADDITIONAL
8. Alpine's liability in this action is derivative of Diamond's liability. Alpine is not sued
for independently committing fraud, misrepresentation, or breach of contract in the underlying
vehicle sale transaction; rather, Alpine is sued as the entity that has, by operation of the
successor-liability and alter-ego doctrines pleaded in the FAC, become answerable for the single

judgment obligation that Diamond itself already owes to Plaintiff by reason of Diamond's own

9. Accordingly, Plaintiff does NOT seek, and this Declaration does NOT request, an
additional or duplicative award of damages against Alpine on top of the judgment sought against
Diamond. Plaintiff instead requests that judgment be entered against Alpine in the same total
amount requested against Diamond, on a joint and several basis, so that Plaintiff may recover the
single judgment sum from either or both defendants, without any double recovery. This is
consistent with the [Proposed] Judgment (Form JUD-100) already on file in this action, which at
item 8 expressly provides that "Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is jointly and severally liable with
Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. as Diamond's successor, mere continuation, alter ego, and/or
fraudulent transference."
IV. DAMAGES (SAME SUM AS THE DIAMOND JUDGMENT)
10. The itemized calculation of damages is set forth in full in the Declaration in Support
of Request for Default Judgment previously filed against Diamond, and in Attachment 4b to
Plaintiff's Case Management Statement (Form CM-110) filed July 20, 2026, both of which are
incorporated herein by reference. The supporting documentary exhibits (Exhibits 1 through 10)
are attached to this Declaration for completeness. In summary: documented out-of-pocket losses
of $20,218.65; additional sworn, undocumented out-of-pocket losses of $5,750.00; conservatively
calculated lost commercial income of $23,400.00 (18 weeks x $1,300/week); and prejudgment
interest under Civil Code section 3287(a) (7%, approximately 3.04 years) of $4,302.55 -- for a
compensatory subtotal of $53,671.20.
11. Plaintiff additionally requests punitive damages of $25,000.00 under Civil Code
section 3294, based on the well-pleaded and, as to Diamond, now-admitted allegations that
Diamond's concealment of the DEF/SCR emissions defect was intentional, malicious, fraudulent,

2. This Declaration is submitted together with the following companion documents
constituting my prove-up package as to Alpine: (a) Plaintiff's Request for Entry of Default and
Court Judgment (Form CIV-100), including the Declaration of Nonmilitary Status at CIV-100
item 8; (b) this Declaration; (c) Plaintiff's [Proposed] Judgment by Court After Default (Form
JUD-100); and (d) the exhibits attached hereto, which are the same documentary exhibits
previously submitted in support of the default judgment prove-up against co-defendant Diamond
Truck Sales, Inc. ("Diamond"), attached again here so that this filing is complete and
self-contained as to Alpine. Plaintiff waives costs of suit on CIV-100 item 7f; no Memorandum of
Costs (Form MC-010) is filed with this packet.
II. PROCEDURAL POSTURE
3. The operative pleading in this action is the First Amended Complaint ("FAC"), which
names Alpine as a defendant on the theory that Alpine is Diamond's successor in interest, mere
continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or a participant in a fraudulent transfer under
the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act (Civ. Code section 3439 et seq.).
4. Alpine was personally served with the Amended Summons, the First Amended
Complaint, and the Notice of Case Assignment and Notice of Hearing on July 1, 2026, at 9:00
a.m., by delivery to Mustaqem Usmani, Manager, at 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California
95380, by Stanislaus County Sheriff's Deputy T. Caldwell, under Code of Civil Procedure section
416.10. Proof of Service (Form POS-010, Levying Officer File No. 2026002577) was signed July
2, 2026 by the Sheriff's Authorized Agent and is on file with this Court.
5. Alpine's deadline to respond to the FAC expired thirty (30) days after service, on July
31, 2026. Alpine filed no responsive pleading, demurrer, or other appearance, and no
meet-and-confer contact was received from Alpine at any time before or after that deadline. I
have submitted a Request for Entry of Default (Form CIV-100) against Alpine, and the Court has
entered, or will shortly enter, Alpine's default as reflected in the Court's file.
6. Because Alpine has defaulted, the well-pleaded factual allegations of the FAC

concerning Alpine's liability are deemed admitted. (Steven M. Garber & Assocs. v. Eskandarian
(2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 813, 823; Kim v. Westmoore Partners, Inc. (2011) 201 Cal.App.4th 267,
281.) The well-pleaded allegations include, without limitation: that Diamond rebranded to Alpine
during the pendency of this action; that Alpine has operated from the same locations as Diamond,
including 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California, under the same Usmani family ownership
and management; and that Alpine is therefore liable for Diamond's obligations in this action as its
successor in interest, mere continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or by reason of a
fraudulent transfer of Diamond's business and assets to Alpine.
7. This Declaration addresses only the amount and proof of damages as against Alpine. I
have made no effort to relitigate liability, which is deemed established by the default, nor to
relitigate the underlying fraud and misrepresentation claims against Diamond, which were proved
up separately -- and on the same exhibits reattached hereto -- in the default judgment package
previously submitted as to Diamond.
III. SUCCESSOR LIABILITY IS DERIVATIVE, NOT ADDITIONAL
8. Alpine's liability in this action is derivative of Diamond's liability. Alpine is not sued
for independently committing fraud, misrepresentation, or breach of contract in the underlying
vehicle sale transaction; rather, Alpine is sued as the entity that has, by operation of the
successor-liability and alter-ego doctrines pleaded in the FAC, become answerable for the single
judgment obligation that Diamond itself already owes to Plaintiff by reason of Diamond's own
default.
9. Accordingly, Plaintiff does NOT seek, and this Declaration does NOT request, an
additional or duplicative award of damages against Alpine on top of the judgment sought against
Diamond. Plaintiff instead requests that judgment be entered against Alpine in the same total
amount requested against Diamond, on a joint and several basis, so that Plaintiff may recover the
single judgment sum from either or both defendants, without any double recovery. This is
consistent with the [Proposed] Judgment (Form JUD-100) submitted with this packet, which at
item 8 expressly provides that Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is jointly and severally liable with
Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. as Diamond's successor, mere continuation, alter ego, and/or

IV. DAMAGES (SAME SUM AS THE DIAMOND JUDGMENT)
10. The itemized calculation of damages is set forth in full in the Declaration in Support
of Request for Default Judgment previously filed against Diamond, and in Attachment 4b to
Plaintiff's Case Management Statement (Form CM-110) filed July 20, 2026, both of which are
incorporated herein by reference. The supporting documentary exhibits (Exhibits 1 through 10)
are attached to this Declaration for completeness. In summary: documented out-of-pocket losses
of $20,218.65; additional sworn, undocumented out-of-pocket losses of $5,750.00; conservatively
calculated lost commercial income of $23,400.00 (18 weeks x $1,300/week); and prejudgment
interest under Civil Code section 3287(a) (7%, approximately 3.04 years through June 15, 2026)
of $4,302.55 -- for a compensatory subtotal of $53,671.20.
11. Plaintiff additionally requests punitive damages of $25,000.00 under Civil Code
section 3294, based on the well-pleaded and, as to Diamond, now-admitted allegations that
Diamond's concealment of the DEF/SCR emissions defect was intentional, malicious, fraudulent,
and oppressive. Because Alpine's liability for this sum is derivative of Diamond's own default and
admitted misconduct, Plaintiff requests that the same punitive damages figure be included in the
judgment against Alpine on the same joint and several basis, not as a separate punitive award
against Alpine for independent conduct of its own.
12. The resulting total default judgment amount requested -- as against Diamond, and,
jointly and severally on the same sum, as against Alpine -- is not less than $78,671.20. Consistent
with CIV-100 item 7f and Plaintiff's approved fee waiver, costs of suit are waived; no costs
amount is included in the judgment total.

VIII.  PREJUDGMENT INTEREST
26. The documented out-of-pocket losses set forth in Section IV are liquidated and certain,
or capable of being made certain by calculation, and the right to recover them vested on the dates
each charge was incurred. I am therefore entitled to prejudgment interest on those amounts at the
legal rate of seven percent (7%) per annum (Cal. Const., art. XV, section 1) from the date of loss
to the date of judgment, pursuant to Civil Code section 3287, subdivision (a). (See North Oakland
Medical Clinic v. Rogers (1998) 65 Cal.App.4th 824, 828-830.)
27. For purposes of this prove-up I have computed prejudgment interest using a single,
conservative weighted-average start date of June 1, 2023 (the approximate midpoint of the dates
on which the documented charges in Section IV were incurred, from April 4, 2023 through June
23, 2023), applied to the $20,218.65 documented out-of-pocket subtotal through June 15, 2026:
$20,218.65 x 7% x approximately 3.04 years (06/01/2023 to 06/15/2026) = $4,302.55. I treat that
$4,302.55 figure as a conservative fixed amount through June 15, 2026 and do not seek additional
prejudgment interest for the period after that date in this request.
28. I have not sought prejudgment interest on the lost-income component in Section VI,
because lost income is not liquidated within the meaning of Civil Code section 3287, subdivision
(a).

VIII.  PREJUDGMENT INTEREST
26. The documented out-of-pocket losses set forth in Section IV are liquidated and certain,
or capable of being made certain by calculation, and the right to recover them vested on the dates
each charge was incurred. I am therefore entitled to prejudgment interest on those amounts at the
legal rate of seven percent (7%) per annum (Cal. Const., art. XV, section 1) from the date of loss
to the date of judgment, pursuant to Civil Code section 3287, subdivision (a). (See North Oakland
Medical Clinic v. Rogers (1998) 65 Cal.App.4th 824, 828-830.)
27. For purposes of this prove-up I have computed prejudgment interest using a single,
conservative weighted-average start date of June 1, 2023 (the approximate midpoint of the dates
on which the documented charges in Section IV were incurred, from April 4, 2023 through June
23, 2023), applied to the $20,218.65 documented out-of-pocket subtotal through June 15, 2026:
$20,218.65 x 7% x approximately 3.04 years (06/01/2023 to 06/15/2026) = $4,302.55. I treat that
$4,302.55 figure as a conservative fixed amount through June 15, 2026 and do not seek additional
prejudgment interest for the period after that date in this request.
28. I have not sought prejudgment interest on the lost-income component in Section VI,
because lost income is not liquidated within the meaning of Civil Code section 3287, subdivision
(a).

belief, and if called as a witness, I could and would competently testify to them. I submit this

Declaration in support of my Request for Entry of Default Judgment by the Court (Judicial
Council Form CIV-100) against Defendant DIAMOND TRUCK SALES, INC. ("Diamond"),
pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 585, subdivision (b), and California Rules of Court,
rule 3.1800.
2. This Declaration is submitted together with the following companion documents
constituting my prove-up package: (a) Plaintiff's Request for Entry of Default Judgment (Form
CIV-100); (b) Plaintiff's Memorandum of Costs (Form MC-010); (c) Plaintiff's Declaration of
Nonmilitary Service; (d) Plaintiff's [Proposed] Judgment by Court After Default (Form
JUD-100); and (e) the documentary exhibits referenced herein and listed in Section XIII below.
II.  PROCEDURAL POSTURE
3. The operative pleading in this action is the First Amended Complaint ("FAC"), which
asserts eight causes of action against Defendant Diamond: (1) Fraudulent Concealment; (2)
Intentional Misrepresentation; (3) Negligent Misrepresentation; (4) Breach of Contract; (5)
Breach of Implied Warranty of Merchantability (Cal. Comm. Code section 2314); (6) Violation of
the Unfair Competition Law (Bus. & Prof. Code section 17200 et seq.); (7) Rescission and
Restitution; and (8) Declaratory Relief.
4. The FAC was personally served on Diamond on May 12, 2026, and the Proof of
Service was filed with this Court on May 18, 2026. Diamond's deadline to respond to the FAC
expired on June 11, 2026. Diamond filed no responsive pleading, demurrer, or other appearance. I
have submitted a Request for Entry of Default (Form CIV-100) against Diamond, and the Court
has entered, or will shortly enter, Diamond's default as reflected in the Court's file.
5. Because Diamond has defaulted, the well-pleaded factual allegations of the FAC
concerning liability are deemed admitted. (Steven M. Garber & Assocs. v. Eskandarian (2007)

The well-pleaded allegations include, without limitation: that Diamond knowingly sold to me a
2014 Volvo VNL diesel semi-truck (VIN 4V4NC9EH6EN142206) that suffered from an
undisclosed and material defect in its Diesel Exhaust Fluid ("DEF") and Selective Catalytic
Reduction ("SCR") emissions systems; that the defect rendered the truck non-compliant with
California emissions law and unsafe for highway operation; that Diamond had pre-sale
knowledge of the defect and concealed it; and that Diamond's conduct was intentional, malicious,
fraudulent, and oppressive within the meaning of Civil Code section 3294.
6. This Declaration addresses only the amount and proof of damages. I have made no
effort to relitigate liability, which is deemed established by the defaults.
III.  THE TRANSACTION AND THE FAILURE
7. On April 4, 2023, I purchased the subject truck (2014 Volvo VNL, VIN
4V4NC9EH6EN142206) from Diamond. The transaction was documented by a Retail Buyer's
Order reflecting a Cash Price of $26,900.00 and Total Charges of $27,092.75 after document and
title fees. A true and correct copy of the Retail Buyer's Order is attached as Exhibit 1.
8. I paid Diamond a deposit of $12,345.10 by certified funds at the time of sale. This
amount appears in the "DEPOSIT" line and is reflected in the "TOTAL CREDITS" line of the
Retail Buyer's Order (Exh. 1, p. 1).
9. The remaining balance of $14,747.65 was financed through a third-party lender, Dakota
Financial LLC, which was selected, arranged, or facilitated by Diamond in connection with the
sale.
10. In connection with titling the truck I was billed by the California Department of Motor

Vehicles in the amount of $3,442.00 for use tax, weight, transfer, and related fees required to
complete registration. The California DMV "Generated Fees" printout dated May 8, 2023 reflects
Total Fees Due of $3,442.00. I have not yet paid this amount because the truck failed before
registration could be completed, leaving me with an outstanding DMV obligation that continues
to accrue penalties. The California DMV "Generated Fees" printout and the corresponding DMV
Report of Deposit of Fees and Application materials are attached as Exhibit 2. I include this
amount in my damages because it is a real, documented financial obligation owed to the State of
California as a direct consequence of Diamond's sale to me of a defective and non-compliant
truck.
11. In connection with the sale Diamond also enrolled me in a GAP product, for which I
was charged $1,895.00 under a separate GAP Addendum. A true and correct copy of the GAP
Addendum is attached as Exhibit 3.
12. I purchased the truck specifically to use it in commercial freight service under my own
owner-operator authority. On April 27, 2023, twenty-three days after purchase, I executed a
Lease-On Owner Operator Agreement with Gobbato Builders, LLC (MC #1357325) under which
I would haul freight for compensation paid weekly by Friday settlement. The Lease-On
Agreement specifically identifies my truck by VIN. A true and correct copy of the Lease-On
Owner Operator Agreement is attached as Exhibit 4. On the same day, April 27, 2023, my
Amazon Relay driver account was activated, providing me with access to dispatch hauling loads
through the Amazon Relay platform. A true and correct copy of the Amazon Relay driver setup
verification, bearing my signature and the platform's digital verification code of April 27, 2023
9:22 AM PDT, is attached as Exhibit 5.
13. Within days of beginning operations the truck experienced exactly the failure mode
characteristic of the DEF/SCR defect alleged in the FAC: it entered engine derate ("limp mode"),
emitted excessive black smoke, lost power, and became incapable of exceeding approximately 35

V.  ADDITIONAL OUT-OF-POCKET LOSSES -- NO CONTEMPORANEOUS RECEIPT
16. In addition to the documented charges set forth above, I personally paid in cash, from
my own funds, two further amounts for emergency services performed on the truck. Although I
did not retain itemized written receipts -- despite having requested them at the time -- these
payments are facts within my direct personal knowledge, and the surrounding contemporaneous
record corroborates that the truck was in storage, released, transported, and delivered for repair
during this period:
(a) Commercial Towing storage-release fee -- $750.00. On or about May 23,
2023, the truck was towed and stored under California Vehicle Code section 22852 by
Commercial Towing, located at 2609 Texas Street, Bakersfield, California. The
contemporaneous Notice of Stored Vehicle issued under Vehicle Code section 22852 is
attached as Exhibit 10. I paid Commercial Towing $750.00 in cash to release the truck. I
requested a written receipt but the operator did not provide one.
(b) Almaraz Diesel repair -- $5,000.00. After the truck was released from
Commercial Towing, Golden Empire Towing transported it (under the invoice
constituting Exh. 8) to Almaraz Diesel, which at that time was operating out of Diamond's
Bakersfield, California location. Almaraz Diesel performed diagnostic and repair work on
the DEF/SCR system. I paid approximately $5,000.00 for that work. I did not receive an
itemized written receipt.
17. The two undocumented amounts above total $5,750.00. I respectfully request that the
Court consider them on the basis of my sworn testimony, in light of the corroborating
documentary evidence -- specifically, the contemporaneous CVC section 22852 Notice (Exh. 10)
and the Golden Empire Towing invoice (Exh. 8), which together establish the chain of custody

VI.  LOST COMMERCIAL INCOME
18. Because of the truck's failure I was unable to perform under the Lease-On Owner
Operator Agreement with Gobbato Builders, LLC (Exh. 4), and I was unable to dispatch any
meaningful number of loads through the Amazon Relay platform (Exh. 5). The truck was
operational for only a matter of days before catastrophic failure. By late May 2023 it had been
towed and stored under Vehicle Code section 22852. By June 23, 2023 the final attempted repair
(the Western Truck Center lamp work, Exh. 9) had failed to restore commercial operability. The
truck was thereafter rendered permanently commercially unusable.
19. Under the Lease-On Agreement with Gobbato Builders, LLC (Exh. 4, paragraph III), I
was set up to operate at a 10% lease-on fee -- meaning I would have netted approximately 90% of
gross load revenue, less fuel, insurance, and incidental expenses. Based on prevailing rates on the
Amazon Relay platform in 2023 and my reasonable expectations at the time the FAC was filed, I
had projected and pleaded approximately $1,800 in net weekly earnings had the truck been
operational. (FAC, paragraph 31.)
20. For purposes of this prove-up, and recognizing that I do not have month-by-month

VII.  RESCISSION, RESTITUTION, AND DECLARATORY RELIEF
22. I gave notice of rescission within the FAC itself, as permitted by Civil Code sections
1691 and 1693. The truck has been irrecoverably damaged by the underlying defect and the
storage process. Restoration of the truck to its original condition is impossible and is therefore
excused under Civil Code section 1693, and this Court is authorized to adjust the equities
between the parties under that statute.
23. The $14,747.65 financed balance was originated through Dakota Financial LLC,
which is not a party to this action. I do not seek in this Declaration a money judgment in the
amount of the financed balance itself, because that obligation is between me and a non-party
lender and recovering it from Diamond would risk a double recovery if I later resolve the
financing separately.
24. I reserve the right, after entry of judgment, to seek a separate determination of any
indemnification or further restitution remedy as to the financed balance if and as appropriate
under Civil Code section 1693 and the Court's continuing equitable jurisdiction over the
rescission count.

in Sections IV through VIII of this Declaration, I respectfully request that the Court's Judgment
include the following findings and declarations. Each falls squarely within the scope of the FAC's
Seventh Cause of Action (Rescission and Restitution) and Eighth Cause of Action (Declaratory
Relief), and each is supported by well-pleaded allegations of the FAC that are deemed admitted
by Diamond's default:
(a) That the April 4, 2023 purchase transaction between Plaintiff and Diamond
Truck Sales, Inc. -- including the Retail Buyer's Order (Exh. 1) and the GAP Addendum
(Exh. 3) -- is rescinded pursuant to Civil Code section 1689, subdivision (b), and is of no
further force or effect as between Plaintiff and Diamond, so that Diamond may not
enforce any term of, or claim any continuing benefit under, that transaction.
(b) That Diamond's conduct in connection with the sale of the subject truck
constituted unlawful, unfair, and fraudulent business acts and practices within the meaning
of California Business and Professions Code section 17200 et seq., as pleaded in the
FAC's Sixth Cause of Action.
VIII.  PREJUDGMENT INTEREST

or capable of being made certain by calculation, and the right to recover them vested on the dates
each charge was incurred. I am therefore entitled to prejudgment interest on those amounts at the
legal rate of seven percent (7%) per annum (Cal. Const., art. XV, section 1) from the date of loss
to the date of judgment, pursuant to Civil Code section 3287, subdivision (a). (See North Oakland
Medical Clinic v. Rogers (1998) 65 Cal.App.4th 824, 828-830.)

IX.  PUNITIVE DAMAGES
29. The FAC pleads, and Diamond's default admits, that Diamond's conduct was
intentional, malicious, fraudulent, and oppressive within the meaning of Civil Code section 3294.
(FAC, paragraph 47.) Punitive damages are accordingly available on the First Cause of Action
(Fraudulent Concealment) and the Second Cause of Action (Intentional Misrepresentation), and
the well-pleaded factual allegations supporting that conduct are now deemed established for
purposes of this prove-up.
30. I respectfully request that the Court award punitive damages in an amount the Court
finds just, reasonable, and constitutionally appropriate under State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v.
Campbell (2003) 538 U.S. 408, and in no event less than $25,000.00. That figure is supported by
Diamond's admitted fraudulent concealment and intentional misrepresentation, the
multi-jurisdictional commercial scale of Diamond's operations alleged in FAC paragraph 7, and
the post-filing rebrand from Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. to Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. alleged in the
FAC as a badge of consciousness of liability and fraudulent intent. The requested $25,000.00
figure is also well below a 1:1 ratio with the compensatory damages requested in this Declaration,

2. This Declaration is submitted together with the following companion documents
constituting my prove-up package as to Alpine: (a) Plaintiff's Request for Entry of Default and
Court Judgment (Form CIV-100); (b) this Declaration; and (c) the exhibits attached hereto, which
are the same documentary exhibits previously submitted in support of the default judgment
prove-up against co-defendant Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. ("Diamond"), attached again here so
that this filing is complete and self-contained as to Alpine.
II. PROCEDURAL POSTURE
3. The operative pleading in this action is the First Amended Complaint ("FAC"), which
names Alpine as a defendant on the theory that Alpine is Diamond's successor in interest, mere
continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or a participant in a fraudulent transfer under
the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act (Civ. Code section 3439 et seq.).
4. Alpine was personally served with the Amended Summons, the First Amended
Complaint, and the Notice of Case Assignment and Notice of Hearing on July 1, 2026, at 9:00
a.m., by delivery to Mustaqem Usmani, Manager, at 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California
95380, by San Joaquin County Sheriff's Deputy T. Caldwell, under Code of Civil Procedure
section 416.10. Proof of Service (Form POS-010, Levying Officer File No. 2026002577) was
signed July 2, 2026 by the Sheriff's Authorized Agent and is on file with this Court.

5. Alpine's deadline to respond to the FAC expired thirty (30) days after service, on July
31, 2026. Alpine filed no responsive pleading, demurrer, or other appearance, and no
meet-and-confer contact was received from Alpine at any time before or after that deadline. I
have submitted a Request for Entry of Default (Form CIV-100) against Alpine, and the Court has
entered, or will shortly enter, Alpine's default as reflected in the Court's file.
6. Because Alpine has defaulted, the well-pleaded factual allegations of the FAC
concerning Alpine's liability are deemed admitted. (Steven M. Garber & Assocs. v. Eskandarian
(2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 813, 823; Kim v. Westmoore Partners, Inc. (2011) 201 Cal.App.4th 267,
281.) The well-pleaded allegations include, without limitation: that Diamond rebranded to Alpine
during the pendency of this action; that Alpine has operated from the same locations as Diamond,
including 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California, under the same Osmani family ownership
and management; and that Alpine is therefore liable for Diamond's obligations in this action as its
successor in interest, mere continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or by reason of a
fraudulent transfer of Diamond's business and assets to Alpine.
7. This Declaration addresses only the amount and proof of damages as against Alpine. I
have made no effort to relitigate liability, which is deemed established by the default, nor to
relitigate the underlying fraud and misrepresentation claims against Diamond, which were proved
up separately -- and on the same exhibits reattached hereto -- in the default judgment package
previously submitted as to Diamond.
III. SUCCESSOR LIABILITY IS DERIVATIVE, NOT ADDITIONAL
8. Alpine's liability in this action is derivative of Diamond's liability. Alpine is not sued
for independently committing fraud, misrepresentation, or breach of contract in the underlying
vehicle sale transaction; rather, Alpine is sued as the entity that has, by operation of the
successor-liability and alter-ego doctrines pleaded in the FAC, become answerable for the single

additional or duplicative award of damages against Alpine on top of the judgment sought against
Diamond. Plaintiff instead requests that judgment be entered against Alpine in the same total
amount requested against Diamond, on a joint and several basis, so that Plaintiff may recover the
single judgment sum from either or both defendants, without any double recovery. This is
consistent with the [Proposed] Judgment (Form JUD-100) already on file in this action, which at
item 8 expressly provides that "Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is jointly and severally liable with
Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. as Diamond's successor, mere continuation, alter ego, and/or
fraudulent transference."
IV. DAMAGES (SAME SUM AS THE DIAMOND JUDGMENT)
10. The itemized calculation of damages is set forth in full in the Declaration in Support
of Request for Default Judgment previously filed against Diamond, and in Attachment 4b to
Plaintiff's Case Management Statement (Form CM-110) filed July 20, 2026, both of which are
incorporated herein by reference. The supporting documentary exhibits (Exhibits 1 through 10)
are attached to this Declaration for completeness. In summary: documented out-of-pocket losses
of $20,218.65; additional sworn, undocumented out-of-pocket losses of $5,750.00; conservatively
calculated lost commercial income of $23,400.00 (18 weeks x $1,300/week); and prejudgment
interest under Civil Code section 3287(a) (7%, approximately 3.04 years) of $4,302.55 -- for a
compensatory subtotal of $53,671.20.
11. Plaintiff additionally requests punitive damages of $25,000.00 under Civil Code
section 3294, based on the well-pleaded and, as to Diamond, now-admitted allegations that
Diamond's concealment of the DEF/SCR emissions defect was intentional, malicious, fraudulent,

Brief Statement of the Case (CM-110, Item 4b):
On or about April 4, 2023, Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi purchased a 2014 Volvo VNL diesel
semi-truck, VIN 4V4NC9EH6EN142206, from Defendant Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. for a total
price of $27,092.75, including a deposit of $12,345.10. Diamond knowingly concealed a material
defect in the truck's Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) and Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR)
emissions systems, rendering the truck non-compliant with California emissions law and unfit
for the lawful commercial highway operation for which it was purchased.
Shortly after purchase, the truck experienced engine derate (limp mode), emitted excessive
black smoke, and lost the ability to exceed approximately 35 mph, rendering it commercially
useless. The defect was pre-existing and known to Diamond through the prior owner's disclosure.
Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is sued as Diamond's successor in interest, mere continuation, de facto
merger, alter ego, and/or as a participant in a fraudulent transfer under the Uniform Voidable
Transactions Act (Civ. Code 3439 et seq.). Diamond rebranded to Alpine during the pendency
of this action, operating from the same locations with the same Osmani family ownership.

Equitable relief sought: Rescission of the purchase transaction pursuant to Civil Code
sections 1689 and 1691; restitution of all monies paid; declaratory relief regarding the
enforceability of sale document provisions and Alpine's liability for Diamond's obligations;
injunctive relief under Bus. & Prof. Code 17200.

sale.

of the first page, it has already been filed and you do not need to file it with the court.

diligence) that tells you that service was unsuccessful and will give details about when the sheriff tried to serve the

next steps.

INTRODUCTION
1. Plaintiff and Petitioner BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI ("Plaintiff") brings this
action to challenge a systemic pattern and practice by the California Department of Corrections
and Rehabilitation ("CDCR") of imposing and enforcing parole conditions that lack the
constitutionally required nexus to a parolee's commitment offense—and then leveraging those
facially invalid conditions to manufacture detention without probable cause, due process, or
judicial oversight.

2. This action arises from—and seeks to prevent the recurrence of—a five-day unlawful
detention imposed on Plaintiff on or about November 1-6, 2024, when Defendant GLENN
URREA placed a parole hold on Plaintiff at the precise moment Plaintiff was otherwise eligible
for release from custody on an unrelated DUI booking. The hold was predicated on a purported
violation of Special Condition No. 063, a categorical "Halloween curfew" imposed without any
individualized nexus to Plaintiff's commitment offense—which involved an adult victim and bore
no connection whatsoever to Halloween, minors, or holiday-related conduct.
3. The unconstitutionality of CDCR's practice has been clearly established for decades. 
People v. Lent (1975) 15 Cal.3d 481 requires every parole condition to bear a rational nexus to
the offender's crime or future criminality. In re Ricardo P. (2019) 7 Cal.5th 1113 reaffirmed and
tightened that requirement. Yet CDCR continues to impose Special Condition No. 063 on PC §
290 registrants categorically, without individualized assessment, and to enforce it through
statewide "Operation Boo" detention sweeps. Plaintiff's detention was not an isolated clerical
error—it was the foreseeable product of policy.
4. Plaintiff remains on parole supervision into 2026 and beyond. Special Condition No.
063 has not been removed from his Conditions of Parole. Defendants' "Operation Boo" is an
annual enforcement event. Absent declaratory and injunctive relief, Plaintiff faces a concrete and
ongoing risk of repeated arbitrary detention every Halloween season.
5. Plaintiff seeks: (a) a writ of mandate compelling CDCR to remove Special Condition
No. 063 from Plaintiff's Conditions of Parole or, in the alternative, to conduct and document an
individualized nexus determination; (b) declaratory relief that Defendants' conduct violated the
California Constitution and California statutory law; (c) prospective injunctive relief requiring
CDCR to implement constitutionally adequate procedures governing the imposition and
enforcement of special parole conditions and parole holds; (d) damages under the Tom Bane Civil
Rights Act and California common law for the unlawful detention; and (e) attorney's fees, costs,

JURISDICTION AND VENUE
6. This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction over this action under Article VI, Section 10
of the California Constitution and Code of Civil Procedure §§ 410.10, 1060, and 1085.
7. Venue is proper in San Joaquin County under Code of Civil Procedure § 395(a) because
this action arises out of the imposition and ongoing enforcement of Special Condition No. 063
against Plaintiff in San Joaquin County, where Plaintiff resides and is under active parole
supervision. Plaintiff remains subject to "Operation Boo" enforcement in San Joaquin County
each year, and the prospective harm and ongoing violation of his constitutional rights are centered
in San Joaquin County. The continuing imposition and enforcement of Special Condition No. 063
by CDCR personnel supervising Plaintiff in San Joaquin County constitutes a substantial part of
the wrongful conduct and the prospective harm to which the requested writ, declaratory, and
injunctive relief is directed. Additionally, venue is proper in Sacramento County under Code of
Civil Procedure § 393(b) because the underlying policy and practice giving rise to this
action—"Operation Boo" and the categorical imposition of Special Condition No. 063 on PC §
290 registrants—were formulated, ratified, and are enforced at CDCR headquarters in
Sacramento County. Defendant JEFF MACOMBER, Secretary of CDCR, and Defendant
BRYAN BISHOP, Director of the Division of Adult Parole Operations, both maintain their
official offices in Sacramento County. Plaintiff respectfully elects San Joaquin County as the
forum, where the concrete and ongoing harm to his liberty occurs.

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. Plaintiff's Commitment Offense and the Critical Absence of Nexus
20. Plaintiff was convicted of a felony offense in January 2018 and sentenced to six years
in state prison. Plaintiff's commitment offense involved an adult victim.
21. Plaintiff's commitment offense had no connection whatsoever to Halloween,
Halloween activities, trick-or-treating, costumes, candy, decorations, minors approaching

residences, or any holiday-specific scenario. Plaintiff's criminal history contains no offenses
involving minors, no offenses involving children, and no offenses with any connection to
Halloween-related conduct.
22. Plaintiff is required to register pursuant to California Penal Code § 290. Registration
status alone does not automatically authorize the imposition of any and all sex-offender-related
parole conditions. California law—and CDCR's own forms—require that special parole
conditions be reasonably related to the parolee's commitment offense, criminal conduct, and/or
future criminality. See People v. Lent (1975) 15 Cal.3d 481; In re Ricardo P. (2019) 7 Cal.5th
1113; 15 Cal. Code Regs. § 2616.
23. The distinction between sex offenses involving minors and those involving adults is
constitutionally and regulatorily significant. A Halloween curfew—designed to prevent contact
with children during trick-or-treating hours—has a rational basis only for offenders whose
histories involve minors. Applying such a condition to an offender whose offense involved an
adult victim, without individualized assessment, is arbitrary, pretextual, and unlawful.
B. Special Condition No. 063 and Its Facial Invalidity As Applied
24. On or about August 4-5, 2025, CDCR imposed updated Special Conditions of Parole
on Plaintiff (CDC No. BF3571), which were approved and signed by Defendant Noguchi on
August 5, 2025. Special Condition No. 063 was also previously imposed on Plaintiff no later than
November 19, 2020, as part of pre-release procedures at California Health Care Facility,
demonstrating the condition's long-standing categorical application without documented nexus.
25. Special Condition No. 063 (the "Halloween curfew") states, in full: "You shall observe
the following curfew on Halloween 5:00 p.m. to 5:00 a.m. and remain within your approved
residence or location determined by your Agent of Record. The exterior lights of your approved

residence or location shall remain off for the duration of the Halloween curfew. You shall not
participate or engage in Halloween activities (e.g., trick or treating, offering of Halloween candy,
decorations, or parties). In addition, during the Halloween curfew, you shall not open the door of
your residence to any persons with the exception of law enforcement personnel, adult family
members, or emergency needs."
26. Special Condition No. 063 was assigned Reason Code 08 on the form. According to
CDCR's own "Reasons for Special Conditions of Parole" table on the same form, Reason Code 08
is defined as: "Based on behavior displayed by offenders convicted of similar crimes, or
displaying similar criminal behavior, imposition of this condition may regulate conduct that is
not in itself criminal, but rather reasonably related to future criminality."
27. The same CDCR form further articulates the legal standard governing all special
conditions: "Special conditions can be imposed if there is a nexus or the conditions reasonably
related to the subject's commitment offense, criminal conduct, and/or future criminality. A special
condition that bars lawful activity is valid only if the prohibited conduct either: 1. Has a
relationship to the crime of which the offender was convicted. 2. Is reasonably related to deter
future criminality."
28. Because Reason Code 08 expressly references "similar crimes" or "similar criminal
behavior," and because Plaintiff's commitment offense involved an adult victim in a non-holiday
context, the imposition of Special Condition No. 063 was not merely a discretionary error—it was
a violation of the plain text of CDCR's own regulatory framework, rendering the condition
facially invalid as applied to Plaintiff.
29. Defendant Noguchi, as the approving Unit Supervisor, performed the ministerial act of
authorizing a facially invalid condition without conducting or documenting the required
individualized nexus assessment. Noguchi's approval created the instrumentality—a void

C. Plaintiff's Lawful Activity on October 31, 2024
30. On October 31, 2024, Plaintiff attended a concert in Oakland, California. Plaintiff was
engaged in lawful activity at an adult entertainment venue. Plaintiff was not at his residence, was
not interacting with trick-or-treaters, was not in proximity to minors, and was not engaged in any
activity that Special Condition No. 063 purported to regulate.
D. DUI Arrest, Booking, and the Moment of Releasability
31. In the early morning hours of November 1, 2024, Plaintiff was arrested by the
California Highway Patrol on suspicion of driving under the influence and transported to Santa
Rita Jail in Dublin, California.
32. Plaintiff was booked into Santa Rita Jail and placed in a holding tank pending
processing of his release.
33. Later that morning, on November 1, 2024, jail personnel informed Plaintiff that he
was otherwise eligible for release from custody on the DUI arrest. Jail personnel further informed
Plaintiff that his DUI-related custody was ending and that he would be released.
34. At approximately 10:30 a.m. on November 1, 2024, a correctional officer informed
Plaintiff: "There has been a prior hold that's been placed on you." This was the first and only
notice Plaintiff received of the parole hold.
35. At the moment jail personnel informed Plaintiff he was otherwise releasable,
Plaintiff's right to liberty vested. The CHP and/or jail officials had already processed Plaintiff's

36. The parole hold placed by Defendant Urrea constituted a new seizure of Plaintiff's
person. It was imposed at the precise moment of Plaintiff's scheduled release and functioned as
the sole but-for cause of Plaintiff's continued confinement. The hold was not a continuation of the
DUI arrest but a distinct act of restraint imposed by parole authorities at the precise moment when
no judicial order, warrant, or lawful basis for detention existed.
37. Plaintiff was not provided paperwork identifying the author of the hold, the factual
basis for the hold, the specific condition allegedly violated, any evidence supporting the alleged
violation, or any opportunity to challenge it.
38. Following notification of the parole hold on November 1, 2024, Plaintiff was
processed into a jail housing unit rather than being released. Plaintiff remained confined at Santa
Rita Jail with a dangerous cellmate who menaced and intimidated Plaintiff for the duration of
Plaintiff's time in custody. Plaintiff feared for his safety and endured psychological strain and
hypervigilance throughout the confinement.
E. Court Appearance, Charging Deadline, and Overridden Release
39. On November 5, 2024, Plaintiff was transported to the courthouse and held in a cold,
dingy holding tank for an entire day pending a court appearance.
40. Plaintiff did not appear before a judge. Plaintiff received no judicial review of the
parole hold.

41. At approximately 3:30 p.m. on or about November 5, 2024, correctional officers told
Plaintiff, in substance: "The judge said the District Attorney has until 4:30 p.m. today to press
charges on you. If not, they must release you today."
42. The 4:30 p.m. deadline on November 5, 2024, passed without the District Attorney
filing charges. At that moment, no lawful basis existed for Plaintiff's continued detention on the
DUI arrest.
43. Despite the passage of that timeframe without charges being filed, Plaintiff was not
released because the parole hold continued to override the release that would otherwise have
occurred. The parole hold functioned as an administrative veto of Plaintiff's entitlement to liberty.
At no point did any neutral judicial officer ratify, review, or authorize the parole hold as a lawful
basis for continued custody.
F. Five Days of Arbitrary Detention
44. Plaintiff remained incarcerated from November 1 through November 6, 2024—five
days of continuous confinement based solely on the parole hold.
45. During this period, Plaintiff received: no written notice of the specific parole condition
allegedly violated; no disclosure of the evidence against him; no preliminary probable-cause
hearing; no opportunity to appear before a neutral decision-maker; no written statement of
reasons for continued detention; and no opportunity to contest either the validity of the underlying
Halloween curfew condition or its application to him.
46. Plaintiff repeatedly attempted to resolve the hold and obtain release, including
contacting multiple bail bond companies. Plaintiff was forced into a desperate posture: calling
outward for help to undo a hold whose basis was not disclosed and whose continuation was not

47. Plaintiff was ultimately released on November 6, 2024, only after one bail bond
company contacted the jail and informed jail personnel that the hold had been lifted. No CDCR
official proactively notified Plaintiff of the hold's termination. Plaintiff's release occurred not
because due process worked, but because an outside party intervened.
G. Employment Jeopardy and Economic Harm
48. Plaintiff was scheduled to begin employment as a commercial truck driver with
Centerline Drivers on the evening of November 1, 2024. This was Plaintiff's first day with a new
employer. Plaintiff's position required a valid CDL and medical card, paid $33.35 per hour
regular rate and $50.03 per hour premium rate, and was subject to DOT regulations.
49. Plaintiff's unlawful detention prevented him from reporting to work on his first
scheduled shift and on subsequent scheduled shifts on November 4, 5, and 6, 2024. Plaintiff
suffered direct economic loss in the form of lost wages ranging from approximately $1,534 to
$2,301, and suffered additional reputational and professional harm in the commercial
transportation industry, where reliability and background clearances are critical.
H. The Halloween Condition Was Used as a Detention-Triggering Device

probable cause, and detention predicated on such a condition was per se unreasonable.

STATUTORY AND REGULATORY FRAMEWORK
21. Penal Code section 3001(a)(2) mandates discharge after one year. Penal Code
section 3001(a)(2) provides that a person required to register under Penal Code section 290 who
has been on parole continuously for one year "shall be discharged" unless the supervising agency
recommends retention and the Board of Parole Hearings, "for good cause, determines that the
person will be retained on parole." The Legislature's use of the word "shall" imposes a
mandatory, not discretionary, duty. (See Haggis v. City of Los Angeles (2000) 22 Cal.4th 490,
498–499 ["shall" is ordinarily mandatory for purposes of Government Code section 815.6].)
22. Penal Code section 3008(d) requires individualized treatment determinations.
Penal Code section 3008(d) authorizes sex-offender-management-program participation as part of
parole supervision but does not authorize retention for the entire term of parole as a matter of
blanket policy. In In re Dwyer, San Mateo Super. Ct. Case No. SC-080355A/HC-3020 (Mar. 20,
2023) (Exh. B), the court held that CDCR's policy of retaining all registrants in a management
program "for the entire term of parole, apparently without reference to the individualized
performance of each parolee," vitiates the Legislature's directive.
23. Title 15, California Code of Regulations section 3574 specifies the required
procedure and documentation. Section 3574, as amended effective April 17, 2025 and made
permanent by the Office of Administrative Law's Notice of Approval of Certificate of

Compliance, OAL Matter No. 2025-0321-01, effective April 28, 2025 (Exh. D), requires that,
before CDCR may recommend retention on parole of a sex-offender registrant beyond the
one-year threshold, it shall: (a) convene a Containment Team Meeting ("CTM") at specified
intervals under subdivision (e); (b) prepare and execute a CDCR Form 3043 (Rev. 11/24)
documenting the CTM and any earned-discharge-consideration findings, and deliver the
completed Form 3043 within 30 calendar days of the CTM; (c) obtain a treatment-provider
signature where required; (d) articulate a written, individualized "good cause" determination
under subdivision (f) tied to documented risk assessment, not to blanket noncompletion of
treatment; and (e) serve the decision on the supervised person. Section 3574(f)(1), as amended,
expressly provides that treatment completion and parole discharge are "legally separate
decisions," displacing the prior practice—condemned in Dwyer—that tethered discharge to
treatment completion as an automatic matter. The amendments also expressly provide that
"supervised persons may complete a sex offender management program before discharge from
parole, as contemplated by Pen. Code section 3008(d)."
24. Government Code sections 815.2, 815.6, and 820(a) govern liability. Government
Code section 815.6 makes a public entity liable for its breach of a mandatory duty imposed by an
enactment designed to protect against the kind of injury suffered, unless the entity exercised
reasonable diligence. Government Code section 815.2(a) makes a public entity vicariously liable
for the injuries an employee causes within the scope of employment. Government Code section
820(a) makes public employees personally liable to the same extent as private persons for injuries
caused by their acts or omissions. Discretionary immunity under Government Code section 820.2
is unavailable where, as here, the duties breached are ministerial—i.e., the statutes and
regulations use mandatory "shall" language, specify the precise conditions of discharge, and leave
no room for policy judgment once those conditions are met. (Kavanaugh v. West Sonoma County

Chelsea’s Law and Development of the Containment Model 
20. 
Since July 1, 2012, Registrants on parole are supervised pursuant to the Containment Model, 
which is codified in Section 3008(d) and related statutes.  The Containment Model is the product of 
reforms enacted through the Chelsea King Child Predator Prevention Act of 2010, known as 
“Chelsea’s Law.”  (Stats. 2010, ch. 219, A.B. 1844 (2009-2010 Reg. Sess.  See also People v. 
Douglas M. (2013) 220 Cal. App. 4th 1068, 1076.)   
21. 
The Containment Model sought to establish “a unified strategy” for the supervision of 
Registrants on post-conviction supervision statewide, rather than the “patchwork of management 
strategies” that had previously existed in California’s 58 counties.  (People v. Garcia (2017) 2 Cal. 
5th 792, 800-01.)  The Containment Model incorporates uniform “best practice for community 
supervision of sex offenders” pursuant to recommendations from the California Sex Offender 
Management Board (CASOMB), the entity charged with setting policy and practice for the 
supervision of Registrants in California.  (Ibid.  See also Cal. Penal Code § 9002.)   
22. 
  As the California Supreme Court has explained, “the Containment Model adopted by the 
Legislature depends on three interrelated elements: [1] supervision and monitoring of the sex 
offender while on [parole]; [2] sex offender-specific assessment and treatment; and [3] the use of 
static, dynamic, and future assessments of the risk of reoffending, including the State Authorized

25. 
The Containment Model took effect on July 1, 2012, and all Registrants on parole became

pursuant to Sections 290 to 290.023, inclusive, shall, while on parole . . ., participate in an approved

The Containment Model in Practice 
27. 
Upon information and belief, the management program called for by the Containment Model 
involves successive phases that require progressively less participation over time.  When first 
released on parole, a Registrant is assessed using SARATSO-approved risk assessment instruments 
and assigned a particular treatment plan by the treatment provider, in consultation with parole 
authorities.   
28. 
Upon information and belief, a Registrant’s initial involvement in the management program 
is time intensive.  A typical Registrant newly released on parole must participate in a weekly group 
therapy session in which curriculum is discussed and completed, plus separate individual counseling 
sessions that do not involve curriculum.  Upon information and belief, the Registrant also 
participates in polygraph examinations to verify compliance with the treatment program as well as 
other conditions of parole.  Upon information and belief, the polygraph examinations are 
administered under the supervision of the treatment provider.   
29. 
Upon information and belief, as a Registrant progresses through and completes the 
curriculum-based group treatment phase of the management program, and otherwise achieves 
treatment goals, a Registrant is eligible to transition to phases of treatment that require less frequent 
group and/or individual sessions.  Upon information and belief, these latter phases are usually called 
“maintenance” or “after care,” consistent with having completed the treatment curriculum and 
needing only “maintenance” of the progress achieved.  Upon information and belief, in most if not 
all treatment programs, the post-curriculum “maintenance” or “after care” phases involve materially 
less frequent group and/or individual sessions than the earlier curriculum-based treatment phases.  
Maintenance and aftercare phases can be as infrequent as one quarterly individual meeting with a 
therapist.

CDCR Regulations, Policy, and Practice Do Not Allow Registrants to Complete and 
Discontinue the Management Program Prior to Discharge from Parole 
31. 
As noted above, the Legislature did not intend the management program for Registrants to 
endure for the entire duration of parole in every case.  To the contrary, Section 3008 expressly 
contemplates that the management program can be “completed” prior to discharge of parole, and 
that its duration can be as short as “one year.”  
32. 
The only CDCR regulation that expressly implements Section 3008 and the management 
program it requires as a condition of parole is Title 15, Section 3573, of the Code of Regulations.  
Section 3573 provides that:  
The Department shall conduct on-going supplemental risk assessments pursuant to 
sections 3573(d) and (e), which are used for designing treatment programs and 
determining supervision levels for sex offenders during their parole terms at the 
direction of the Director of CDCR or their designee.  These assessments are not for 
use in determining whether an offender qualifies as a HRSO, but rather to determine 
the frequency of treatment and the level of supervision needed for monitoring the 
sex offender while in the community.   
(15 C.C.R. § 3573, subd. (c).)  Notably, no provision of Section 3573 or any other regulation allows 
for the “completion” of the management program.  Nor does Section 3573 or any other regulation 
allow for termination of a Registrant’s participation in the management program prior to discharge 
from parole, as Section 3008(d) contemplates.

3574. Sex Offender Treatment 
 
(a) The requirement for a supervised person to attend sex offender treatment is 
established pursuant to Penal Code (PC) section 3008(d), persons released to parole 
and required to register pursuant to PC sections 290 to 290.023 shall participate in a sex 
offender management program. The sex offender management program is comprised of 
three treatment phases (Curriculum Phase, Maintenance Phase, Aftercare Phase), 
Containment Team Meetings (CTMbegin strikethrough, s, end strikethrough,), and polygraph examinations. Sex offender 
treatment providers (whobegin strikethrough, m, end strikethrough, are trained and certified pursuant to PC 290.09) shall be 
subject to the terms of the California Sex Offender Management Board. 
(1) Curriculum Phase, also known as the active phase, is when the supervised person 
attends individual and group therapy sessions, at the prescribed hours per week, as 
determined by the sex offender treatment provider. These sessions focus on the goals 
and objectives of the treatment plan determined by the sex offender treatment provider 
through the sex offense specific treatment curriculum. It also involves the completion of 
mandated State Authorized Risk Assessment Tools for Sex Offenders (SARATSO) and 
the participation in polygraph assessments.  
(2) Maintenance Phase is a phase where the supervised person works to maintain the 
gains made in the curriculum phase. Maintenance phase occurs when a supervised 
person has addressed the underlying issues related to their offending behavior, 
developed skills to lead a pro-social life, and mitigated their dynamic risk factors 
(according to the SARATSO assessment tools), as determined by the sex offender 
treatment provider, allowing for adjustment of treatment requirements. While in the 
maintenance phase, the supervised person is expected to continue to work towards their 
prescribed treatment plan goals, complete SARATSO assessments, participate in 
polygraph assessments, and attend group sessions as determined by the sex offender 
treatment provider. The supervised person may be required to attend in person sessions

2 
weekly, monthly, or quarterly, based on their predetermined needs and assessments by 
the sex offender treatment provider. 
(3) Aftercare Phase is a voluntary phase in the format of a support group with the sex 
offender treatment provider. This phase is for supervised persons who voluntarily 
continue their participation in the sex offender management program after they have 
successfully completed the curriculum and maintenance phases or persons who have 
been discharged from parole supervision.  
(A) Persons voluntarily participating in the aftercare phase are responsible for any costs 
associated with participation.  
(4) Containment Team Meeting is a meeting with all involved parties, as referenced in 
subsection 3574(a)(4)(A), whose purpose is to review the supervised person’s treatment 
progress, dynamic risk factors, polygraph results, community reintegration, response to 
parole supervision, supervision category, and relevant individual case factors to evaluate 
the supervised person’s readiness for sex offender management program completion.   
(A) The Containment Team shall normally be comprised of a parole agent, unit supervisor 
or assistant unit supervisor, supervised person, contracted clinician (licensed psychiatrist, 
psychologist, or psychiatric social worker directly treating the supervised person), and 
victim advocacy representative. In the event all members of the Containment Team are 
not available to meet, the Containment Team shall minimally consist of a contracted 
clinician, parole agent, unit supervisor or assistant unit supervisor, and the supervised 
person. The Containment Team may also include other relevant stakeholders (e.g. 
Division of Adult Parole Operations and community program managers, polygraph 
examiner, etc.), family members of the supervised person, or any person in the 
supervised person’s life that wishes to participate and can provide a first-hand account of 
the positive progress the supervised person is making.  
(5) A Polygraph is a machine that measures a person’s physiological responses when 
they respond to questions. Polygraph assessments are completed or contracted by the 
sex offender treatment provider as required by PC section 3008(d)(3). 
(b) Persons placed on parole on or after July 1, 2012, required to register pursuant to PC 
sections 290 to 290.023, inclusive, shall successfully complete a sex offender 
management program in accordance with PC section 3008(d). Program participation shall 
be no less than one year, up to the entire period of parole. Participation in the sex offender 
management program is required, regardless of when the qualifying offense was 
committed. 
(c) The sex offender treatment provider prescribes the number of treatment hours per 
week as determined by the supervised person’s risks, needs, responsivity, and offense-
free time in the community.  
(d) Supervised persons may complete a sex offender management program before 
discharge from parole, as contemplated by the PC section 3008(d).

FINAL STATEMENT OF REASONS  
The Initial Statement of Reasons (ISOR) is incorporated by reference.  
UPDATES TO THE INITIAL STATEMENT OF REASONS:  
On January 3, 2025, the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation  
(CDCR or the department) published the Notice of Change to Regulations for Sex 
Offender Treatment, which began the public comment period. The department’s Notice 
of Change to Regulations #25-01 was mailed the same day to individuals who had 
requested to be on the department’s mailing list for regulation changes, was posted on 
the department’s website, and copies were posted in CDCR institutions. Five written 
public comments were received during the public comment period. The comments are 
summarized and responded to below under the heading Summaries and Responses to 
Written Public Comments Received During the Initial Comment Period. A public hearing 
was held on February 20, 2025. The department received no comments during the public 
hearing.  
DETERMINATIONS, ASSESSMENTS, MANDATES, AND FISCAL IMPACT:  
The department has determined that no alternative considered would be more effective 
in carrying out the purpose for which this regulation is proposed or would be as effective 
and less burdensome to affected private persons or would be more cost effective to 
affected private persons and equally effective in implementing the statutory policy or other 
provision of law than the action proposed. No such alternatives were proposed or brought 
to the department’s attention during the adoption of this rulemaking action.  
The department has made an initial determination that the action will not have a significant 
adverse economic impact on business. Additionally, there has been no testimony or other 
evidence provided that would alter the department’s initial determination.  
The department has determined that this action imposes no mandates on local agencies 
or school districts, or a mandate which requires reimbursement pursuant to Part 7 
(Section 17561) of Division 4 of the Government Code (GC).  
The department has determined that no reasonable alternatives to the regulation have 
been identified or brought to the attention of the department that would lessen any 
adverse impact on affected private persons or small businesses than the action planned.  
The department, in proposing the adoption of these regulations, has not identified nor has 
it relied upon any technical, theoretical, or empirical study, report, or similar document.  
The department has relied upon the results of the Economic Impact Assessment, which 
can be found in the Notice of Proposed Regulations and is available for review as part of 
the rulemaking file.  
NOTE REGARDING CDCR FORMS INCORPORATED BY REFERENCE (CCR,  
TITLE 1, SECTION 20):  
This note explains the department’s justification for incorporating forms by reference. The 
department uses over 1,500 forms, most of which are regulatory. It would be unduly

cumbersome, expensive and impractical to print all of these forms in the CCR text, 
therefore the department has always incorporated forms by reference, except in specific 
circumstances which do not apply in the case of these regulations.  
The adopted, amended, and/or repealed forms included in this rulemaking action were 
made available to the public for review and were included in the notice of rulemaking sent

SUMMARIES AND RESPONSES TO WRITTEN PUBLIC COMMENTS RECEIVED 
DURING THE INITIAL COMMENT PERIOD: 
Commenter #1  
 
Comment 1: Pursuant to Section 3573, a Stable-2007 score of "four or higher for males 
only" shall be, amended to include but not limited to Transgender Men and Transgender 
Women.  In addition, to include any sexual predator who is a biological person whose 
identity includes not soley Male or Transgender Female, or nonbinary.  A stable score 
shall also be applicable to former biological males that now identify with an identity other 
than male.    
 
In addition, it is imperative that the Aftercare Phase is a Mandatory Outpatient phase in 
the format of a support group with the sex offender treatment provider. The phase shall 
be for supervised persons and shall be mandated for no less than one, continuous year, 
to continue the sex offender's participation in the sex offender management program after 
the sex offender has successfully completed the curriculum and maintenance phases, or 
persons who have been discharged from parole supervision. 
 
Response 1:  
 
California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 15, Section 3574 Sex Offender Treatment (f) 
(2) references reasons to retain a supervised person in a sex offender management 
program. Pursuant to this section, a Stable-2007 score of four or higher for males only is 
a factor. The California Sex Offender Management Board (CASOMB) has established 
State Authorized Risk Assessment Tools for Sex Offenders (SARATSO). These 
assessments are validated, and sex offender management professionals utilize the 
appropriate coding manual and addendums for determining scoring. The Stable-2007 is 
for males only and utilizes the appropriate coding. Gender identity is not a factor in the 
validation or application of the tool.  
 
Regarding part two of the comment, CCR Title 15, Section 3574, Sex Offender Treatment, 
provides for a comprehensive evaluation of risk and needs for each supervised person. 
Sex Offender Treatment (SOT) participation is based on risk of re-offense to a level likely 
to lead to a risk to public safety. When the supervised person has successfully completed 
the maintenance phase it has been determined that their risk and needs have decreased 

Final Statement of Reasons NCR 25-01 
4/17/25 
3 
sufficiently to complete treatment. Additionally, requiring a person to attend a phase of 
treatment after it has been determined that they have successfully completed contradicts 
the purpose of the regulation. Lastly, aftercare phase is also voluntarily, attended by those 
who have discharged parole. The Division of Adult Parole Operations (DAPO) does not 
have the authority to require a person attend treatment if that person is no longer under 
the jurisdiction of DAPO. 
 
Commenter #2  
 
Comment: Commenter is an incarcerated person from High Desert State Prison. 
Commenter wants to know if there is a part from the proposed regulations for incarcerated 
persons who plead “no contest.” Commenter states these people were accused of 
horrible charges and had no choice but to accept deals. Commenter states these groups 
should be able to live their life without watching their backs. These incarcerated persons 
should be reviewed on a case-by-case basis, including review of the programs complete 
while incarcerated, and the evidence for the crime accused of, upon their release. 
 
Response 2:  
 
The requirement for persons placed on parole, that are required to register pursuant to 
Penal Code (PC) sections 290 to 290.023, inclusive, attend sex offender treatment as 
required by PC 3008(d). Specifically, PC 3008(d)(2) states, “Persons placed on parole on 
or after July 1, 2012, shall successfully complete a sex offender management program, 
following the standards developed pursuant to Section 9003, as a condition of parole. The 
length of the period in the program shall be not less than one year, up to the entire period 
of parole, as determined by the certified sex offender management professional in 
consultation with the parole officer and as approved by the court. Participation in this 
program applies to every person described without regard to when his or her crime or 
crimes were committed.” 
 
These regulations only establish parameters for the existing PC and are unable to alter 
the existing requirements set forth by PC. 
 
Commenter #3  
 
Comment 3: Commenter is an incarcerated person who provides some background 
information to their incarceration and sentencing. Commenter states that there are no 
rehabilitation efforts for incarcerated persons who are sentences as sex offenders, only 
punitive efforts. Commenter provides support for the proposed sex offender treatment 
program, but states that sex offender treatment efforts should be offered before release 
and completed during incarceration not after release, due to different life circumstances 
after release.  
 
Response 3:

4 
These regulations only establish parameters for the existing PC and are unable to alter 
the existing requirements set forth by PC. DAPO must abide by PC 3008(d)(2), which 
states, “Persons placed on parole on or after July 1, 2012, shall successfully complete a 
sex offender management program, following the standards developed pursuant to 
Section 9003, as a condition of parole. The length of the period in the program shall be 
not less than one year, up to the entire period of parole, as determined by the certified 
sex offender management professional in consultation with the parole officer and as 
approved by the court. Participation in this program applies to every person described 
without regard to when his or her crime or crimes were committed.” 
 
Additionally, the proposed regulations are regarding Sex Offender Treatment after the 
release from incarceration. The proposed regulations do not address institutional sex 
offender treatment programs or their availability. Therefore, the department cannot speak 
to or address this subject matter at the moment. 
 
Lastly, your comment identifies concerns for potential costs associated with a supervised 
person’s request for a voluntary re-referral to SOT. PC 3008(e) states, “Any defendant 
ordered to be placed in an approved sex offender management treatment program 
pursuant to subdivision (d) shall be responsible for paying the expense of their 
participation in the program. The department shall take into consideration the ability of 
the defendant to pay, and no defendant shall be denied discharge onto parole because 
of their inability to pay.” 
 
Commenter #4 
 
Comments 4 and 5 are duplicative: Commenter is a sex offender treatment provider 
and is responding to NCR 25-05 to solicitate their services and be considered as a 
contractor to provide sex offender treatment services. 
 
Response 4: The comment is either insufficiently related to the specific action or actions 
proposed, or too generalized or personalized to the extent that no meaningful response 
can be formulated by the department in refutation of or accommodation to the comment. 
Therefore, the comment is being dismissed.  
 
Additionally, the department responded to the commenter with resources on how to bid 
on state contracts.

Stockton 2 GPS Parole Unit (Parole Agent Long Moua, Badge #7472, sued herein as a non-party
actor, not as a defendant) authored a CDCR Form 1502-DR Discharge Review Report that, on its
face, (a) applied mutually exclusive statutory parole-term frameworks, (b) relied on a
non-existent "6.5 years of supervision" eligibility rule, (c) applied a non-existent "10-year parole
term" exclusion attributed to an internal "Policy 19-03," (d) omitted every mandatory

2. Plaintiff had been eligible for discharge from parole since December 2, 2021—one year
after his release to parole on December 2, 2020. (Pen. Code § 3001(a)(2).) On information and
belief, no good-cause retention finding by the Board of Parole Hearings under Penal Code section
3001(a)(2) has been articulated, documented, served on Plaintiff, or otherwise provided to him on
request. The statewide policies and practices that drove this result—including CDCR's continued
insistence that sex-offender-management-program participation must continue through the entire
parole term—were judicially condemned in In re Dwyer, San Mateo County Super. Ct. Case No.

applied the pre-amendment framework to Plaintiff anyway.

STATUTORY AND REGULATORY FRAMEWORK
21. Penal Code section 3001(a)(2) mandates discharge after one year. Penal Code
section 3001(a)(2) provides that a person required to register under Penal Code section 290 who
has been on parole continuously for one year "shall be discharged" unless the supervising agency
recommends retention and the Board of Parole Hearings, "for good cause, determines that the
person will be retained on parole." The Legislature's use of the word "shall" imposes a
mandatory, not discretionary, duty. (See Haggis v. City of Los Angeles (2000) 22 Cal.4th 490,
498–499 ["shall" is ordinarily mandatory for purposes of Government Code section 815.6].)
22. Penal Code section 3008(d) requires individualized treatment determinations.
Penal Code section 3008(d) authorizes sex-offender-management-program participation as part of
parole supervision but does not authorize retention for the entire term of parole as a matter of
blanket policy. In In re Dwyer, San Mateo Super. Ct. Case No. SC-080355A/HC-3020 (Mar. 20,
2023) (Exh. B), the court held that CDCR's policy of retaining all registrants in a management
program "for the entire term of parole, apparently without reference to the individualized
performance of each parolee," vitiates the Legislature's directive.

24. Government Code sections 815.2, 815.6, and 820(a) govern liability. Government
Code section 815.6 makes a public entity liable for its breach of a mandatory duty imposed by an
enactment designed to protect against the kind of injury suffered, unless the entity exercised
reasonable diligence. Government Code section 815.2(a) makes a public entity vicariously liable
for the injuries an employee causes within the scope of employment. Government Code section
820(a) makes public employees personally liable to the same extent as private persons for injuries
caused by their acts or omissions. Discretionary immunity under Government Code section 820.2
is unavailable where, as here, the duties breached are ministerial—i.e., the statutes and
regulations use mandatory "shall" language, specify the precise conditions of discharge, and leave
no room for policy judgment once those conditions are met. (Kavanaugh v. West Sonoma County
Union High School Dist. (2003) 29 Cal.4th 911, 916 [discretionary immunity does not apply to
ministerial acts].) Government Code section 820.4 does not exonerate a public employee from
liability for false arrest or false imprisonment.

(Against All Defendants)
59. Plaintiff incorporates paragraphs 1 through 50 as though fully set forth herein.
60. Elements. The elements of false imprisonment are: (1) the nonconsensual, intentional
confinement of a person; (2) without lawful privilege; and (3) for an appreciable period of time,
however brief. (Fermino v. Fedco, Inc. (1994) 7 Cal.4th 701, 715.) Government Code section
820.4 does not exonerate a public employee from liability for false imprisonment.
61. Nonconsensual confinement. Plaintiff did not and does not consent to continued
parole supervision beyond the statutory discharge point. Since November 19, 2025, he has been
subjected, without consent, to the following concrete restraints: continuous 24-hour-per-day GPS
monitoring; a nightly curfew; geographic restrictions; mandatory treatment-attendance
obligations consuming six to eight hours per week; warrantless searches of his person, residence,
and vehicle; restrictions on association and employment; and the threat of reincarceration for any
technical violation.
62. Absence of lawful privilege. The confinement described in paragraph 61 is without
lawful privilege. On information and belief, each of the following—any one of which alone
suffices to negate privilege—is true: (a) no good-cause retention finding by the Board of Parole
Hearings under Penal Code section 3001(a)(2) has been made with respect to Plaintiff, served on
him, or provided to him on request; (b) the "6.5 years of supervision" rule relied upon in Exhibit

decision; and (f) adopted a non-completion characterization of treatment that is the automatic
output of a blanket-retention policy rather than an individualized clinical judgment.
