CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION
Cal. Evid. Code § 1152 / Fed. R. Evid. 408
BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI
1455 Cat Tail Drive • Stockton, CA 95204
Telephone: (209) 801-4442 • E-mail: bnn.cdla@gmail.com
July 12, 2026
VIA ELECTRONIC MAIL
Allison Aguirre Kray, Esq. (Cal. Bar No. 312544)
Counsel -- Federal Express Corporation
2061 Main St, Ste 1100
Irvine, CA 92614
E-mail: allison.kray@fedex.com
Re: Pre-Filing Demand for Settlement -- Newanforbi v. Federal Express Corporation
Unlawful Use of California Sex Offender Registry Information for Employment in Violation of Cal.
Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E); Failure to Hire in Violation of Public Policy; ICRAA Violations;
Demand for $85,000.00 and Injunctive Relief
Dear Ms. Kray:
I write, pro per, to demand pre-litigation settlement of claims arising from Federal Express
Corporation (hereinafter 'FedEx') -- its decision to deny Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI
NEWANFORBI employment based, on information and belief, on his registration in the
California Sex Offender Registry -- in direct violation of California Penal Code section 290.46,
subdivision (j)(2)(E), which categorically prohibits the use of Megan's Law registry information
for any employment purpose.
A complete Draft Complaint for Damages, prepared for filing in the Superior Court of
California, County of San Joaquin, is enclosed as Exhibit A. The Draft Complaint asserts six
causes of action against Federal Express Corporation, demands trial by jury, and is in final form.
I am currently appearing pro per and am actively seeking to retain employment counsel on a
contingency basis. The fee-shifting provision in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) makes this
matter economically attractive to contingency counsel. Settling now eliminates that attorney fee
exposure entirely.
I.   THE DOCUMENTED FACTS
The adverse action is established by First Advantage's own sequential notifications, each
transmitted from DoNotReply@fadv.com and attached hereto as Exhibits 1 through 8:
• March 10, 2025, 1:44 p.m.: First Advantage transmitted to Plaintiff a 'FedEx Pre-Adverse
Employment Action Notice' -- the statutorily required pre-adverse notification before final
adverse action based on a background report -- expressly identifying the subject employer as
'FEDEX GROUND HR.' (Exhibit 1.)

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
• March 11, 2025, 7:48 a.m.: First Advantage re-transmitted the same pre-adverse notice to
Plaintiff's alternate email address. (Exhibit 2.)
• March 11--16, 2025: First Advantage transmitted five separate written reminders urging Plaintiff
to review the pre-adverse notification, each reaffirming the subject employer as 'FEDEX
GROUND HR.' (Exhibits 3--7.)
• March 19, 2025, 1:47 p.m.: Nine days after the initial pre-adverse notice -- and following five
written reminders -- First Advantage transmitted to Plaintiff a 'FedEx Adverse Employment
Action Notice,' confirming that FedEx had taken final adverse action and denied Plaintiff
employment. (Exhibit 8.)
On information and belief, the background screening report compiled by First Advantage
and provided to FedEx contained information derived from California's Megan's Law sex
offender registry identifying Plaintiff as a registrant. On information and belief, FedEx's decision
to deny Plaintiff employment was based, in whole or in substantial part, on that registry status.
No other known basis for disqualification existed in Plaintiff's application or background history.
The pattern of pre-adverse notice, five escalating reminders, and final adverse action -- all
transmitted by First Advantage on FedEx's behalf -- is consistent with an employer acting on a
registry-based background report flag.
On information and belief, the First Advantage report transmitted to FedEx included a
statutory notice informing FedEx of the prohibition in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E).
Background screening vendors routinely include such warnings in reports provided to California
employers. Despite that warning, on information and belief, FedEx used the registry information
to deny Plaintiff employment.
II.   THE LAW IS UNAMBIGUOUS
California Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j), provides in pertinent part:
"(1) A person is authorized to use information disclosed pursuant to this section only
to protect a person at risk.
(2) Except as authorized under paragraph (1) or any other provision of law, use of
any information that is disclosed pursuant to this section for purposes relating to ...
(E) Employment ... is prohibited."
The prohibition is categorical. It is not a balancing test. It contains exactly one narrow
exception -- 'to protect a person at risk' -- which requires an identified individual exposed to a
specific risk of a sex offense in the particular job context. General delivery and package handling
positions do not qualify, and nothing in FedEx's adverse action materials purports to invoke the
exception.
The California Court of Appeal confirmed in Mendoza v. ADP Screening & Selection
Services, Inc. (2010) 182 Cal.App.4th 1644 that section 290.46's civil-liability provisions target
the entity that uses registry information for a prohibited purpose -- not merely the background

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
vendor that reports it. FedEx, as the employer that used the information to deny employment, is
precisely the entity the statute targets.
III.   THE STATUTORY REMEDIES
Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) provides:
"Any use of information disclosed pursuant to this section for a purpose other than
that provided by paragraph (1) or another provision of law ... is subject to a civil
action for actual damages or twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), whichever is
greater, by any person whose information was used for the prohibited purpose. The
person whose information was wrongfully used may also bring an action for
attorney's fees."
In addition to the $25,000 statutory floor:
• Wrongful failure-to-hire tort damages (Tameny claim): compensatory and punitive damages
under Civil Code section 3294.
• ICRAA actual and punitive damages (Civ. Code § 1786.50).
• Invasion of privacy damages (Cal. Const., Art. I, § 1).
• Unfair business practices -- restitution and injunctive relief (Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200).
• Mandatory attorney fees if counsel is retained (§ 290.46(j)(4)(A)). Settling now eliminates this
exposure.

V.   WHY SETTLEMENT NOW IS IN FEDEX'S INTEREST
1. The Pilot precedent is already docketed. Plaintiff filed and served a substantially
identical action against Pilot Travel Centers LLC -- Newanforbi v. Pilot Travel Centers LLC,
Case No. STK-CV-UWT-2026-0007649 -- in the Superior Court of California, County of San
Joaquin. That action is in active litigation and arises from the same statute, the same theory, and
the same documentary pattern. Resolution of this matter before filing prevents it from being
docketed alongside a live, served case presenting identical claims.
2. Discovery will produce the background report. Upon service, Plaintiff will serve
document requests for the First Advantage screening report, FedEx's employment screening
policies for California candidates, and all communications between FedEx Ground HR and First
Advantage concerning Plaintiff's application. That discovery will confirm what is pleaded on
information and belief.
3. Fee exposure escalates immediately upon filing. The fee-shifting provision in Penal
Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) makes this matter economically attractive to contingency
employment counsel -- a guaranty of fees upon judgment means no financial risk to retained
counsel. Once Plaintiff retains counsel, FedEx's total exposure increases by the full amount of
those fees. Settling now eliminates that exposure entirely.
4. Pattern-and-practice risk. If FedEx Ground HR uses First Advantage's background
reports systematically for California candidates, and those reports routinely include sex offender
registry hits that FedEx uses as the basis for adverse action, discovery and UCL litigation could
expose a pattern-and-practice claim with class action potential. Pre-filing resolution forecloses
that risk.
VI.   THE DEMAND
To resolve all claims arising from the matters described herein without litigation, Plaintiff
demands the following:
SETTLEMENT PAYMENT: $85,000.00
(Eighty-Five Thousand U.S. Dollars)
Payment method: Wire transfer to Plaintiff's designated bank account, within seven (7)
calendar days of the execution of a mutually acceptable written settlement agreement. Wire
transfer instructions will be provided upon written acceptance of these terms.
In addition to the monetary payment, the following non-monetary terms are each material to
settlement:
(a) No re-application bar. Written confirmation that Plaintiff's name, identity, and registry status
shall not be used as a basis for denial of any future employment application with Federal

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
Express Corporation or any FedEx-affiliated entity.
(b) Policy acknowledgment. Written acknowledgment, signed by an officer of Federal Express
Corporation, that California sex offender registry information is not a permissible basis for
employment decisions under California law.
(c) Neutral reference. A commitment that any future employer inquiry regarding Plaintiff's 2025
application to FEDEX GROUND HR will receive no response other than confirmation that no
employment relationship was established.
(d) Confidentiality of amount only. The fact of settlement may be disclosed; only the dollar
amount will be confidential. No non-disparagement clause. Release limited to claims arising
from the March 2025 adverse action.
VII.   FORMAL LITIGATION HOLD NOTICE
This letter operates as formal notice of FedEx's duty to preserve evidence under
Cedars-Sinai Medical Center v. Superior Court (1998) 18 Cal.4th 1 and applicable federal
authorities. FedEx is directed to immediately suspend any auto-deletion, archive-purge, or
document-retention schedule that would result in the destruction, alteration, or loss of:
• All documents, e-mails, system entries, and communications concerning Plaintiff's application to
FEDEX GROUND HR, the First Advantage background screening report for Plaintiff, the
pre-adverse action notice of March 10, 2025, all subsequent reminder notices, and the final
adverse action notice of March 19, 2025;
• All policies, procedures, training materials, and decision matrices used by FedEx or FedEx
Ground HR for California employment candidates flagged with sex offender registry results on
background reports, in effect at any time between January 1, 2024 and the present;
• All communications between FedEx (including FEDEX GROUND HR) and First Advantage

'Megan's Law website.'

apprising employers of the prohibitions in section 290.46(j)(2)(E). Despite such warnings, some

violation of the statute.
15. FedEx is a large national employer and one of the country's largest ground parcel
delivery networks, operating hundreds of facilities throughout California. FedEx regularly orders

connection with employment applications. On information and belief, FedEx's background
screening policies and practices result in the regular access to, and use of, sex offender registry

law enforcement and authorizes the California Department of Justice to make certain registrant
information available to the public through an online database commonly referred to as the
'Megan's Law website.'
11. Section 290.46(j)(1) provides that a person is authorized to use information disclosed
pursuant to that section only to protect a person at risk. Section 290.46(j)(2) enumerates uses of
such information that are prohibited. Subsection (j)(2)(E) specifically prohibits use of Megan's

accessible through the Megan's Law website may not be used in employment decisions.

by paragraph (1) or another provision of law is punishable as a misdemeanor, and subject to a
civil action for actual damages or twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), whichever is greater,

information was wrongfully used may also bring an action for attorney's fees.'
14. Background screening companies that compile investigative consumer reports for
employment purposes routinely access and include sex offender registry information in their
reports. On information and belief, these companies also routinely include statutory warnings
apprising employers of the prohibitions in section 290.46(j)(2)(E). Despite such warnings, some
employers nonetheless use the registry information in their employment decisions, in direct
violation of the statute.
15. FedEx is a large national employer and one of the country's largest ground parcel
delivery networks, operating hundreds of facilities throughout California. FedEx regularly orders
background screening reports from third-party vendors—including First Advantage—in
connection with employment applications. On information and belief, FedEx's background
screening policies and practices result in the regular access to, and use of, sex offender registry
information in employment decisions, notwithstanding the prohibition in Penal Code section
290.46(j)(2)(E).

Penal Code and backed by civil and criminal penalties, that employers must not use sex offender
registry information in employment decisions. This prohibition reflects a legislative
determination that the unrestricted use of Megan's Law data in employment gatekeeping is
harmful to individual registrants and to the public interest in meaningful rehabilitation and
reintegration.

requirements of the Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act: (a) the requirement under
Civil Code section 1786.16 to provide Plaintiff with a clear and conspicuous written disclosure
that an investigative consumer report would be obtained, and to obtain Plaintiff's written consent;
(b) the requirement to provide Plaintiff with a complete copy of all investigative consumer reports
obtained, including any compliance materials, concurrent with or prior to the adverse action;
and/or (c) other requirements of ICRAA governing the procurement and use of investigative
consumer reports in employment decisions.

actual damages, including loss of the employment opportunity, lost wages, and emotional
distress. Pursuant to Civil Code section 1786.50, Plaintiff is entitled to actual damages, and, for

Find out if you need to pay a fee for service by asking the court’s self-help center, a lawyer, or the sheriff’s office. 
Here are some situations where you do not need to pay for service: 
If you have a fee waiver in your case (fee waiver granted by a judge on form FW-003 or FW-005). 
If you are serving a domestic violence, elder abuse, or gun violence restraining order. 
If you have a civil harassment, workplace violence, or school violence restraining order based on a credible threat of
violence or stalking.
Give this form and a copy of all the court papers you need served to the sheriff or marshal, including a copy of a fee 
waiver (if you have one). You can turn in your papers in person or send them electronically. 
You should get a form back from the sheriff. 
If the sheriff was able to serve your court papers, you should receive a form (called a proof of service). Make sure 
you get a copy from the sheriff and file it with the court. Note that if there is a court stamp at the top right corner 
of the first page, it has already been filed and you do not need to file it with the court. 
If the sheriff was unable to serve your court papers, you should receive a form (sometimes called declaration of due 
diligence) that tells you that service was unsuccessful and will give details about when the sheriff tried to serve the 
person. If the sheriff was unable to serve your papers, you can ask a lawyer or court’s self-help center about your

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil action for damages and other relief arising from Defendant United Parcel
Service, Inc.'s ('UPS') violation of California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E), which
categorically prohibits any person or entity from using information derived from California's
Megan's Law public sex offender registry for purposes relating to employment.
2. In connection with Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI's application for
employment, UPS procured a background screening report through its third-party background

as a registrant on California's sex offender registry. On information and belief, UPS accessed and
used that registry information—in whole or in substantial part—as the basis for its decision to
deny Plaintiff employment, in direct violation of Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E).
3. The Legislature enacted section 290.46(j) to protect registered sex offenders from a
specific category of harm: the use of Megan's Law registry data—which is made publicly
available for a narrow protective purpose—to blackball them from employment. The civil remedy
provision, section 290.46(j)(4)(A), authorizes a civil action for the greater of actual damages or
$25,000, plus attorney fees. Plaintiff seeks those remedies, together with all other relief this Court
deems just and proper.

JURISDICTION AND VENUE
7. This Court has unlimited civil jurisdiction over this action because the amount in
controversy exceeds $35,000, exclusive of interest and costs.
8. Venue is proper in San Joaquin County pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section
395(a) because Plaintiff resides in the City of Stockton, San Joaquin County, California, and the
injuries giving rise to this action were suffered by Plaintiff in this County.
9. This Court has personal jurisdiction over UPS because UPS is authorized to transact,
and does transact, business in the State of California, including in San Joaquin County, and has
purposefully availed itself of the privilege of conducting activities in this State, thereby subjecting
itself to the jurisdiction of California courts.
FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. General Allegations Regarding California Penal Code Section 290.46(j)
10. California Penal Code section 290.46 requires certain sex offenders to register with
law enforcement and authorizes the California Department of Justice to make certain registrant
information available to the public through an online database commonly referred to as the
'Megan's Law website.'
11. Section 290.46(j)(1) provides that a person is authorized to use information disclosed
pursuant to that section only to protect a person at risk. Section 290.46(j)(2) enumerates uses of
such information that are prohibited. Subsection (j)(2)(E) specifically prohibits use of Megan's

Law registry information 'for purposes relating to . . . [e]mployment.'
12. The prohibition in section 290.46(j)(2)(E) is categorical and admits no exception for
private employers, background check companies, or any private actor making employment
decisions. The Legislature's determination was explicit: sex offender registry information
accessible through the Megan's Law website may not be used in employment decisions.
13. California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) provides a civil remedy for violations:
'Any use of information disclosed pursuant to this section for a purpose other than that provided
by paragraph (1) or another provision of law is punishable as a misdemeanor, and subject to a
civil action for actual damages or twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), whichever is greater,
by any person whose information was used for the prohibited purpose. The person whose
information was wrongfully used may also bring an action for attorney's fees.'
14. Background screening companies that compile investigative consumer reports for
employment purposes routinely access and include sex offender registry information in their
reports. On information and belief, these companies also routinely include statutory warnings
apprising employers of the prohibitions in section 290.46(j)(2)(E). Despite such warnings, some
employers nonetheless use the registry information in their employment decisions, in direct
violation of the statute.
15. UPS is a large national employer that regularly orders background screening reports
from third-party vendors—including First Advantage—in connection with employment
applications. On information and belief, UPS's background screening policies and practices result
in the regular access to, and use of, sex offender registry information in employment decisions,
notwithstanding the prohibition in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E).
B. Plaintiff's Application for Employment with UPS

16. In or around mid-2024, Plaintiff submitted an application for employment with UPS
for a position in UPS's delivery and logistics operations in California. Plaintiff was qualified for
the position sought.
17. As part of its standard pre-employment screening process, UPS initiated a background
check on Plaintiff through First Advantage (operating under the domain 'fadv.com'), a third-party
investigative consumer reporting agency that provides background screening services to
employers nationwide.
18. On or about July 22, 2024, Plaintiff received, at his email address, an electronic
notification from First Advantage (sent from DoNotReply@fadv.com) bearing the subject line:
'Pre Adverse Action Notification regarding your application with UPS.' The notification advised
Plaintiff to review the pre-adverse action notification for his background screening report for
'UNITED PARCEL SERVICE' via a link to First Advantage's portal.
19. The pre-adverse action notice sent to Plaintiff on July 22, 2024 constitutes the
pre-adverse action notification required under the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C.
section 1681b(b)(3)(A), and the California Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, Civil
Code section 1786.40, before an employer takes adverse action based in whole or in part on a
background screening report.
C. Background Check Process and Contents of the Screening Report
20. On information and belief, First Advantage conducted a background screening report
on Plaintiff and transmitted that report to UPS on or before July 22, 2024—the date of the
pre-adverse action notice.

Advantage and provided to UPS contained information derived from California's Megan's Law

22. On information and belief, the First Advantage background screening report
transmitted to UPS included a statutory notice or disclaimer informing UPS of the existence and
requirements of California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E) and expressly warning UPS that
the sex offender registry information contained in the report was prohibited from use in
employment decisions. Background screening companies routinely include such statutory
warnings in reports provided to California employers.
23. Despite any such warning, on information and belief, UPS reviewed, accessed, and
considered the sex offender registry information contained in the First Advantage background
screening report in making its employment decision regarding Plaintiff.
24. On or about July 22, 2024, Plaintiff received a link via First Advantage's portal
through which Plaintiff could access the background screening report. That link has since expired,
and Plaintiff no longer has access to the underlying report or its attachments. Plaintiff therefore
pleads on information and belief as to the specific contents of the report insofar as those contents
relate to sex offender registry information and the basis for UPS's adverse action.

received, at his email address, a second electronic notification from First Advantage (sent from
DoNotReply@fadv.com) bearing the subject line: 'Final Adverse Action Notification regarding
your application with UPS.' This notification confirmed that UPS had taken final adverse action

29. As a direct and proximate result of UPS's unlawful conduct, as alleged herein, Plaintiff

(b) lost career opportunity and professional advancement in the delivery and logistics industry;
and (c) severe emotional distress, including anxiety, humiliation, shame, and mental anguish
arising from being unlawfully denied employment because of his registry status.
30. Plaintiff has experienced significant financial hardship as a direct result of losing the
UPS employment opportunity, which caused immediate and ongoing economic harm to Plaintiff
and his household.

FIRST CAUSE OF ACTION
Violation of California Penal Code Section 290.46(j)(2)(E)
Unlawful Use of Sex Offender Registry Information in Employment Decisions
(Against All Defendants)
32. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 31 as though fully set forth
herein.
33. California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(1) authorizes persons to use information
disclosed pursuant to that section only to protect a person at risk. Section 290.46(j)(2)(E)
categorically prohibits any use of such information 'for purposes relating to . . . [e]mployment.'
There is no exception for private employers making general hiring decisions.
34. Plaintiff is a registrant on California's sex offender registry within the meaning of
Penal Code section 290.46. On information and belief, Plaintiff's registry status was disclosed in
the background screening report compiled by First Advantage and provided to UPS in or about
July 2024.
35. On information and belief, UPS accessed, reviewed, and used the sex offender registry
information contained in Plaintiff's First Advantage background screening report for purposes
relating to employment—specifically, in making the decision to deny Plaintiff employment on or
about July 31, 2024.
36. UPS's use of Plaintiff's sex offender registry information for employment purposes
was not authorized under Penal Code section 290.46(j)(1) or any other provision of law. The
position at issue was in UPS's general delivery and logistics operations, and no facts suggest that
any specifically identified vulnerable person at risk was exposed to any particular risk from

37. Pursuant to Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A), Plaintiff is entitled to bring a civil

SECOND CAUSE OF ACTION
Failure to Hire in Violation of Public Policy
(Tameny Claim)
(Against All Defendants)
38. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 31 as though fully set forth
herein.
39. California recognizes a tort claim for wrongful failure to hire where an employer
refuses to hire an applicant for reasons that violate a fundamental public policy of the State of
California. (See Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167; City of Moorpark v.
Superior Court (1998) 18 Cal.4th 1143.)
40. California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E) embodies a fundamental public policy
of the State of California. The Legislature has expressly declared, in a statute codified in the
Penal Code and backed by civil and criminal penalties, that employers must not use sex offender
registry information in employment decisions. This prohibition reflects a legislative
determination that the unrestricted use of Megan's Law data for employment gatekeeping is
harmful to individual registrants and to the public interest in meaningful rehabilitation and
reintegration.

41. On information and belief, UPS denied Plaintiff employment based, in whole or in
substantial part, on Plaintiff's status as a registrant on California's sex offender registry, as
disclosed in the First Advantage background screening report, in direct violation of the public
policy embodied in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E).
42. By refusing to hire Plaintiff for a reason that violates the fundamental public policy of
the State of California, UPS is liable to Plaintiff for all damages resulting from its unlawful
failure to hire, including lost wages and benefits, emotional distress, and other damages according
to proof at trial.
43. UPS's conduct was willful, malicious, and in conscious disregard of Plaintiff's rights
and of the public policy of the State of California. Plaintiff is therefore entitled to an award of
punitive damages pursuant to Civil Code section 3294.

background screening reports, for employment purposes in California. On information and belief,
First Advantage is an 'investigative consumer reporting agency' within the meaning of Civil Code
section 1786.2(d), and the background screening report prepared by First Advantage and provided

to UPS constitutes an 'investigative consumer report' within the meaning of Civil Code section

46. On information and belief, UPS's procurement and use of the First Advantage
background screening report, which contained sex offender registry information prohibited from
employment use under Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E), constituted a violation of ICRAA and
the public policies incorporated therein. The inclusion of legally prohibited information in an
investigative consumer report prepared for employment purposes, and its use in employment
decision-making, violates the spirit and purpose of ICRAA.
47. On information and belief, UPS failed to comply with one or more of the following
requirements of the Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act: (a) the requirement under
Civil Code section 1786.16 to provide Plaintiff with a clear and conspicuous written disclosure
that an investigative consumer report would be obtained, and to obtain Plaintiff's written consent;
(b) the requirement to provide Plaintiff with a complete copy of all investigative consumer reports
obtained, including any compliance materials, concurrent with or prior to the adverse action;
and/or (c) other requirements of ICRAA governing the procurement and use of investigative
consumer reports in employment decisions.
48. As a direct and proximate result of UPS's violations of ICRAA, Plaintiff suffered
actual damages, including loss of the employment opportunity, lost wages, and emotional
distress. Pursuant to Civil Code section 1786.50, Plaintiff is entitled to actual damages, and, for
willful noncompliance, punitive damages not to exceed $5,000 per violation, plus attorney fees
and costs.

(Cal. Const., Art. I, § 1)
(Against All Defendants)
49. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 31 as though fully set forth
herein.
50. The California Constitution, Article I, Section 1, guarantees every person an
inalienable right to privacy. The Legislature has recognized a legally protected privacy interest in
sex offender registry information by strictly limiting its authorized use under Penal Code section
290.46(j) to the singular purpose of protecting persons at risk, and by prohibiting all other
uses—including use in employment decisions.
51. On information and belief, UPS accessed, reviewed, and used information from
California's sex offender registry pertaining to Plaintiff for the unauthorized and prohibited
purpose of making an employment decision, in violation of Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E).
This unauthorized access and use constituted a serious invasion of Plaintiff's legally protected
privacy interest.
52. UPS's invasion of Plaintiff's privacy was not justified by any legitimate, competing
interest of sufficient weight to override the statutory and constitutional privacy protections. The
position at issue—in general delivery and logistics operations—did not implicate any specific risk
to any identified vulnerable person. The invasion was not authorized by law and could not be
consented to by UPS's unilateral act.
53. As a direct and proximate result of UPS's invasion of Plaintiff's privacy, Plaintiff
suffered humiliation, embarrassment, emotional distress, and other damages in an amount to be
proven at trial.

FIFTH CAUSE OF ACTION
Negligence Per Se
(Against All Defendants)
54. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 31 as though fully set forth
herein.
55. California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E) is a statute enacted for the protection of
a specific class of persons—registrants on the Megan's Law sex offender registry—against the
specific harm of having their registry information used to deprive them of employment
opportunities. Plaintiff is a member of the class of persons the statute was designed to protect, and
the harm Plaintiff suffered—denial of employment, lost wages, and emotional distress—is
precisely the type of harm the statute was enacted to prevent.
56. On information and belief, UPS violated Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E) by
accessing and using Plaintiff's sex offender registry information in making its decision to deny
Plaintiff employment on or about July 31, 2024.
57. Pursuant to Evidence Code section 669, UPS's violation of Penal Code section
290.46(j)(2)(E) constitutes negligence per se. UPS's negligence was a proximate cause of
Plaintiff's damages.
58. As a direct and proximate result of UPS's negligence per se, Plaintiff has suffered
damages in an amount to be proven at trial, including lost wages, lost employment benefits, and
emotional distress.

Unlawful Business Practices
(Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200 et seq.)
(Against All Defendants)
59. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 31 as though fully set forth
herein.
60. California Business and Professions Code section 17200 prohibits 'any unlawful,
unfair or fraudulent business act or practice.' Each prong is independently actionable.
61. UPS's conduct as alleged herein constitutes an 'unlawful' business practice because it
violates California Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E), a statute prohibiting the use of sex
offender registry information in employment decisions. An employer's act that violates a statute is
per se unlawful under Business and Professions Code section 17200.
62. UPS's conduct also constitutes an 'unfair' business practice because it harms
employment applicants—including Plaintiff—and the public interest in the enforcement of
legislative prohibitions, without any justification that outweighs those harms. The Legislature's
policy judgment that registry information must not be used in employment decisions reflects a
considered determination that such use causes harm disproportionate to any benefit.
63. As a direct and proximate result of UPS's unlawful and unfair business practices,
Plaintiff has suffered loss of money and property, including lost wages and employment benefits,
constituting injury in fact and loss of money or property causally connected to UPS's unlawful
conduct, within the meaning of Business and Professions Code section 17204.
64. Plaintiff is entitled to restitution of lost wages and benefits, injunctive relief

If you are serving a domestic violence, elder abuse, or gun violence restraining order. 
If you have a civil harassment, workplace violence, or school violence restraining order based on a credible threat of
violence or stalking.
Give this form and a copy of all the court papers you need served to the sheriff or marshal, including a copy of a fee 
waiver (if you have one). You can turn in your papers in person or send them electronically. 
You should get a form back from the sheriff. 
If the sheriff was able to serve your court papers, you should receive a form (called a proof of service). Make sure 
you get a copy from the sheriff and file it with the court. Note that if there is a court stamp at the top right corner 
of the first page, it has already been filed and you do not need to file it with the court. 
If the sheriff was unable to serve your court papers, you should receive a form (sometimes called declaration of due 
diligence) that tells you that service was unsuccessful and will give details about when the sheriff tried to serve the 
person. If the sheriff was unable to serve your papers, you can ask a lawyer or court’s self-help center about your 
next steps.

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION

BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI
1455 Cat Tail Drive • Stockton, CA 95204

July 12, 2026
VIA ELECTRONIC MAIL
Norman M. Brothers Jr., Esq.
Counsel -- United Parcel Service of America, Inc.
55 Glenlake Parkway NE
Atlanta, GA 30328
E-mail: norman.brothers@ups.com
Re: Pre-Filing Demand for Settlement -- Newanforbi v. United Parcel Service of America, Inc.
Unlawful Use of California Sex Offender Registry Information for Employment in Violation of Cal.
Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E); Failure to Hire in Violation of Public Policy; ICRAA Violations;
Demand for $85,000.00 and Injunctive Relief
Dear Mr. Brothers:
I write, pro per, to demand pre-litigation settlement of claims arising from United Parcel
Service of America, Inc. (hereinafter 'UPS') -- its decision to deny Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI
NEWANFORBI employment based, on information and belief, on his registration in the
California Sex Offender Registry -- in direct violation of California Penal Code section 290.46,
subdivision (j)(2)(E), which categorically prohibits the use of Megan's Law registry information
for any employment purpose.
A complete Draft Complaint for Damages, prepared for filing in the Superior Court of
California, County of San Joaquin, is enclosed as Exhibit A. The Draft Complaint asserts six
causes of action against United Parcel Service of America, Inc., demands trial by jury, and is in
final form. I am currently appearing pro per and am actively seeking to retain employment
counsel on a contingency basis. The fee-shifting provision in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A)
makes this matter economically attractive to contingency counsel. Settling now eliminates that
attorney fee exposure entirely.
I.   THE DOCUMENTED FACTS
The adverse action is established by First Advantage's own sequential notifications, each
transmitted from DoNotReply@fadv.com and attached hereto as Exhibits 1 through 4:
* July 22, 2024, 9:57 AM: First Advantage transmitted to Plaintiff the Pre-Adverse Action
Notification regarding her/his application with UPS -- the statutorily required pre-adverse
notification before final adverse action based on a background report -- expressly identifying the
subject employer as 'UNITED PARCEL SERVICE.' (Exhibit 1.)

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
* July 23 and July 27, 2024: First Advantage transmitted two written reminders urging Plaintiff to
review the pre-adverse notification, each reaffirming the subject employer as 'UNITED
PARCEL SERVICE.' (Exhibits 2 and 3.)
* July 31, 2024, 9:57 AM: Nine days after the initial pre-adverse notice -- and following two
written reminders -- First Advantage transmitted to Plaintiff the Final Adverse Action
Notification regarding his application with UPS, confirming that UPS had taken final adverse
action and denied Plaintiff employment. (Exhibit 4.)
On information and belief, the background screening report compiled by First Advantage
and provided to UPS contained information derived from California's Megan's Law sex offender
registry identifying Plaintiff as a registrant. On information and belief, UPS's decision to deny
Plaintiff employment was based, in whole or in substantial part, on that registry status. No other
known basis for disqualification existed in Plaintiff's application or background history. The
pattern of pre-adverse notice, five escalating reminders, and final adverse action -- all transmitted
by First Advantage on UPS's behalf -- is consistent with an employer acting on a registry-based
background report flag.
On information and belief, the First Advantage report transmitted to UPS included a
statutory notice informing UPS of the prohibition in Penal Code section 290.46(j)(2)(E).
Background screening vendors routinely include such warnings in reports provided to California
employers. Despite that warning, on information and belief, UPS used the registry information to
deny Plaintiff employment.
II.   THE LAW IS UNAMBIGUOUS
California Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j), provides in pertinent part:
"(1) A person is authorized to use information disclosed pursuant to this section only
to protect a person at risk.
(2) Except as authorized under paragraph (1) or any other provision of law, use of
any information that is disclosed pursuant to this section for purposes relating to ...
(E) Employment ... is prohibited."
The prohibition is categorical. It is not a balancing test. It contains exactly one narrow
exception -- 'to protect a person at risk' -- which requires an identified individual exposed to a
specific risk of a sex offense in the particular job context. General delivery and package handling
positions do not qualify, and nothing in UPS's adverse action materials purports to invoke the
exception.
The California Court of Appeal confirmed in Mendoza v. ADP Screening & Selection
Services, Inc. (2010) 182 Cal.App.4th 1644 that section 290.46's civil-liability provisions target
the entity that uses registry information for a prohibited purpose -- not merely the background
vendor that reports it. UPS, as the employer that used the information to deny employment, is
precisely the entity the statute targets.

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
III.   THE STATUTORY REMEDIES
Penal Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) provides:
"Any use of information disclosed pursuant to this section for a purpose other than
that provided by paragraph (1) or another provision of law ... is subject to a civil
action for actual damages or twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), whichever is
greater, by any person whose information was used for the prohibited purpose. The
person whose information was wrongfully used may also bring an action for
attorney's fees."
In addition to the $25,000 statutory floor:
• Wrongful failure-to-hire tort damages (Tameny claim): compensatory and punitive damages
under Civil Code section 3294.
• ICRAA actual and punitive damages (Civ. Code § 1786.50).
• Invasion of privacy damages (Cal. Const., Art. I, § 1).
• Unfair business practices -- restitution and injunctive relief (Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200).
• Mandatory attorney fees if counsel is retained (§ 290.46(j)(4)(A)). Settling now eliminates this
exposure.
IV.   THE DAMAGES MODEL

V.   WHY SETTLEMENT NOW IS IN FEDEX'S INTEREST

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
1. The Pilot precedent is already docketed. Plaintiff filed and served a substantially
identical action against Pilot Travel Centers LLC -- Newanforbi v. Pilot Travel Centers LLC,
Case No. STK-CV-UWT-2026-0007649 -- in the Superior Court of California, County of San
Joaquin. That action is in active litigation and arises from the same statute, the same theory, and
the same documentary pattern. Resolution of this matter before filing prevents it from being
docketed alongside a live, served case presenting identical claims.
2. Discovery will produce the background report. Upon service, Plaintiff will serve
document requests for the First Advantage screening report, UPS's employment screening
policies for California candidates, and all communications between UNITED PARCEL
SERVICE and First Advantage concerning Plaintiff's application. That discovery will confirm
what is pleaded on information and belief.
3. Fee exposure escalates immediately upon filing. The fee-shifting provision in Penal
Code section 290.46(j)(4)(A) makes this matter economically attractive to contingency
employment counsel -- a guaranty of fees upon judgment means no financial risk to retained
counsel. Once Plaintiff retains counsel, UPS's total exposure increases by the full amount of those
fees. Settling now eliminates that exposure entirely.
4. Pattern-and-practice risk. If UNITED PARCEL SERVICE uses First Advantage's
background reports systematically for California candidates, and those reports routinely include
sex offender registry hits that UPS uses as the basis for adverse action, discovery and UCL
litigation could expose a pattern-and-practice claim with class action potential. Pre-filing
resolution forecloses that risk.
VI.   THE DEMAND
To resolve all claims arising from the matters described herein without litigation, Plaintiff
demands the following:
SETTLEMENT PAYMENT: $85,000.00
(Eighty-Five Thousand U.S. Dollars)
Payment method: Wire transfer to Plaintiff's designated bank account, within seven (7)
calendar days of the execution of a mutually acceptable written settlement agreement. Wire
transfer instructions will be provided upon written acceptance of these terms.
In addition to the monetary payment, the following non-monetary terms are each material to
settlement:
(a) No re-application bar. Written confirmation that Plaintiff's name, identity, and registry status
shall not be used as a basis for denial of any future employment application with Federal
Express Corporation or any UPS-affiliated entity.

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
(b) Policy acknowledgment. Written acknowledgment, signed by an officer of United Parcel
Service of America, Inc., that California sex offender registry information is not a permissible
basis for employment decisions under California law.
(c) Neutral reference. A commitment that any future employer inquiry regarding Plaintiff's 2025
application to UNITED PARCEL SERVICE will receive no response other than confirmation
that no employment relationship was established.
(d) Confidentiality of amount only. The fact of settlement may be disclosed; only the dollar
amount will be confidential. No non-disparagement clause. Release limited to claims arising
from the July 2024 adverse action.
VII.   FORMAL LITIGATION HOLD NOTICE
This letter operates as formal notice of UPS's duty to preserve evidence under
Cedars-Sinai Medical Center v. Superior Court (1998) 18 Cal.4th 1 and applicable federal
authorities. UPS is directed to immediately suspend any auto-deletion, archive-purge, or
document-retention schedule that would result in the destruction, alteration, or loss of:
• All documents, e-mails, system entries, and communications concerning Plaintiff's application to
UNITED PARCEL SERVICE, the First Advantage background screening report for Plaintiff,
the pre-adverse action notice of March 10, 2025, all subsequent reminder notices, and the final
adverse action notice of July 31, 2024;
• All policies, procedures, training materials, and decision matrices used by UPS or UNITED
PARCEL SERVICE for California employment candidates flagged with sex offender registry
results on background reports, in effect at any time between January 1, 2024 and the present;
• All communications between UPS (including UNITED PARCEL SERVICE) and First
Advantage concerning California candidates with sex offender registry results; and
• All data identifying every California candidate against whom UPS took adverse action based on
sex offender registry information between January 1, 2024 and the present.
Failure to preserve will be the subject of a spoliation motion under Code of Civil
Procedure section 2023.030 and a request for adverse-inference instruction at trial.
VIII.   SETTLEMENT-COMMUNICATION PROTECTION
This letter is offered in compromise of a disputed claim and is inadmissible to prove
liability under California Evidence Code section 1152 and Federal Rule of Evidence 408. The
factual recitations herein are based on First Advantage's own transmitted notifications; nothing in
this letter limits Plaintiff's right to introduce those underlying documents as evidence at trial.
IX.   DEADLINE FOR RESPONSE
UPS must respond in writing or by email to bnn.cdla@gmail.com, on or before 5:00
p.m. Pacific Time on July 26, 2026. Absent a written acceptance of these terms or a
good-faith counter-offer by that deadline, the enclosed Draft Complaint will be filed
in the San Joaquin County Superior Court without further notice.

CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATION  --  Cal. Evid. Code § 1152  /  Fed. R. Evid. 408
X.   RESERVATION OF RIGHTS
Nothing in this letter waives, releases, or limits any claim, right, or remedy. All claims,
rights, and remedies are expressly reserved. This letter is not, and shall not be construed as, an
offer to settle for any amount less than that stated herein, nor as an admission of fact, law, or
comparative fault.
I look forward to your prompt response.
Very truly yours,
___________________________________
BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI
Plaintiff, In Pro Per

disclosure, and the toll charge, if any, for the telephone call is prepaid by or charged directly to you. 
• 
By requesting a copy be sent to a specified addressee by certified mail. ICRAs complying with requests for certified mailings 
shall not be liable for disclosures to third parties caused by mishandling of mail after such mailings leave the ICRAs. 
“Proper Identification” includes documents such as a valid driver’s license, social security account number, military identification 
card, and credit cards. Only if you cannot identify yourself with such information may INFOMART require additional information 
concerning your employment and personal or family history in order to verify your identity.  INFOMART will provide trained 
personnel to explain any information furnished to you and will provide a written explanation of any coded information contained in 
files maintained on you. This written explanation will be provided whenever a file is provided to you for visual inspection. You may 
be accompanied by one other person of your choosing, who must furnish reasonable identification. INFOMART may require you to 
furnish a written statement granting permission to INFOMART, to discuss your file in such person’s presence. 
All items of information in INFOMART’s file shall be available for inspection, except that the sources of information acquired solely 
for use in preparing an investigative consumer report and actually used for no other purpose will not be disclosed. Upon your 
request, INFOMART will also disclose the name, address and telephone number of any recipients of an investigative consumer 
report about you that INFOMART has furnished within the three-year period preceding the request. INFOMART will also disclose the 
dates, original payees, and amounts of any checks or charges upon which is based any adverse characterization of you, included in 
the file at the time of the disclosure. 
INFOMART may charge you a fee up to $8 for the disclosure and must notify you of any fee prior to the disclosure.  INFOMART may 
not impose a fee for providing you with a revised report after a reinvestigation of disputed information. You have the right to 
request that an ICRA provide the above information to you once during any 12-month period without charge if you certify in writing 
that you: (1) are unemployed and intend to apply for employment in the 60-day period beginning on the date the certification is 
made, (2) are a recipient of public welfare assistance, or (3) have reason to believe that the file on the consumer at the investigative 
consumer reporting agency contains inaccurate information due to fraud. 

 
 
NOTIFICACION IMPORTANTE 
INFOMART no garantiza la exactitud o veracidad de la información en canto al objeto de la investigación, sino que solamente 
copia la información de los archivos públicos con exactitud. La información generada a raíz del robo de identidad, incluyendo 
evidencia de actividad criminal, puede ser incorrectamente asociada con el consumidor objeto de este informe. El cliente está de 
acuerdo y certifica que al ordenar y usar este informe está en estricto cumplimiento de cualesquiera lees o regulaciones locales, 
estatales y federales que sean aplicables. 
En California, siendo una “agencia investigadora de información del consumidor” (ICRA, por sus siglas en inglés), INFOMART 
proveerá, a cualquier consumidor que busque obtener copia de un informe o que solicite revisar los archivos, una notificación 
sencilla y clara, escrita en inglés y español, detallando los términos y condiciones de su derecho a recibir toda divulgación. 
TERMINOS Y CONDICIONES DEL DERECHO DEL CONSUMIDOR A RECIBIR DIVULGACIONES BAJO EL CODIGO CIVIL DE CALIFORNIA 
Bajo el Código Civil de California, usted tiene derecho a averiguar, proveyendo identificación apropiada, la información sobre su 
persona que INFOMART mantiene en sus expedients, de las manera siguientes: 
• 
En persona, mediate inspección visual de su expedient durante horas de trabajo regulares y con aviso previo razonable. 
Usted también puede pedir copia de esta información en persona. INFOMART le cobrará solamente el cost actual de

• 
Un resumen de toda información contenida en el expediente de INFOMART sobre su persona que el Código Civil de

• 
Mediante solicitud de que una copia le sea enviada a un destinatario especifico por medio de correo certificado. Al cumplir 
con estas solicitudes que requieren el envio de información por correo certificado, las ICRA no serán responsables de

“Identificacion Apropiada” incluye documentos tales como una licencia de conducir válida, número de seguro social, tarjeta de

INFOMART le podrá cobra un cargo máximo de $8 por la divulgación y le debe notificar de cualquier cargo antes de la misma.

A Summary of Your Rights Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act 
 
 
 
The federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) promotes the accuracy, fairness, and privacy of information in the files of 
consumer reporting agencies.  There are many types of consumer reporting agencies, including credit bureaus and specialty agencies 
(such as agencies that sell information about check writing histories, medical records, and rental history records).  Here is a summary 
of your major rights under FCRA.  For more information, including information about additional rights, go to 
www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore or write to: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 1700 G Street NW, Washington, 
DC 20552. 
 
• 
You must be told if information in your file has been used against you.  Anyone who uses a credit report or another type 
of consumer report to deny your application for credit, insurance, or employment – or to take another adverse action against 
you – must tell you, and must give you the name, address, and phone number of the agency that provided the information. 
 
• 
You have the right to know what is in your file.  You may request and obtain all the information about you in the files of a 
consumer reporting agency (your “file disclosure”).  You will be required to provide proper identification, which may include 
your Social Security number.  In many cases, the disclosure will be free.  You are entitled to a free file disclosure if: 
 
o 
a person has taken adverse action against you because of information in your credit report; 
o 
you are the victim of identity theft and place a fraud alert in your file; 
o 
your file contains inaccurate information as a result of fraud; 
o 
you are on public assistance; 
o 
you are unemployed but expect to apply for employment within 60 days. 
 
In addition, all consumers are entitled to one free disclosure every 12 months upon request from each nationwide credit 
bureau and from nationwide specialty consumer reporting agencies.  See www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore for additional 
information. 
 
• 
You have the right to ask for a credit score.  Credit scores are numerical summaries of your credit-worthiness based on 
information from credit bureaus.  You may request a credit score from consumer reporting agencies that create scores or 
distribute scores used in residential real property loans, but you will have to pay for it.  In some mortgage transactions, you 
will receive credit score information for free from the mortgage lender. 
 
• 
You have the right to dispute incomplete or inaccurate information.  If you identify information in your file that is 
incomplete or inaccurate, and report it to the consumer reporting agency, the agency must investigate unless your dispute is 
frivolous.  See www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore for an explanation of dispute procedures. 
 
• 
Consumer reporting agencies must correct or delete inaccurate, incomplete, or unverifiable information.  Inaccurate, 
incomplete, or unverifiable information must be removed or corrected, usually within 30 days.  However, a consumer 
reporting agency may continue to report information it has verified as accurate. 
 
• 
Consumer reporting agencies may not report outdated negative information.  In most cases, a consumer reporting 
agency may not report negative information that is more than seven years old, or bankruptcies that are more than 10 years 
old. 
 
• 
Access to your file is limited.  A consumer reporting agency may provide information about you only to people with a valid 
need – usually to consider an application with a creditor, insurer, employer, landlord, or other business.  The FCRA specifies 
those with a valid need for access. 
 
• 
You must give your consent for reports to be provided to employers.  A consumer reporting agency may not give out 
information about you to your employer, or a potential employer, without your written consent given to the employer.  
Written consent generally is not required in the trucking industry.  For more information, go to 
www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
 

 
 
 
• 
You may limit “prescreened” offers of credit and insurance you get based on information in your credit report.  
Unsolicited “prescreened” offers for credit and insurance must include a toll-free phone number you can call if you choose to 
remove your name and address from the lists these offers are based on.  You may opt out with the nationwide credit bureaus 
at 1-888-567-8688. 
 
• 
The following FCRA right applies with respect to nationwide consumer reporting agencies: 
 
CONSUMERS HAVE THE RIGHT TO OBTAIN A SECURITY FREEZE 
 
You have a right to place a “security freeze” on your credit report, which will prohibit a consumer reporting agency 
from releasing information in your credit report without your express authorization.  The security freeze is designed to 
prevent credit, loans, and services from being approved in your name without your consent.  However, you should be aware 
that using a security freeze to take control over who gets access to the personal and financial information in your credit report 
may delay, interfere with, or prohibit the timely approval of any subsequent request or application you make regarding a new 
loan, credit, mortgage, or any other account involving the extension of credit. 
 
As an alternative to a security freeze, you have the right to place an initial or extended fraud alert on your credit file at no 
cost.  An initial fraud alert is a 1-year alert that is placed on a consumer’s credit file.  Upon seeing a fraud alert display on a 
consumer’s credit file, a business is required to take steps to verify the consumer’s identity before extending new credit.  If 
you are a victim of identity theft, you are entitled to an extended fraud alert, which is a fraud alert lasting 7 years. 
 
A security freeze does not apply to a person or entity, or its affiliates, or collection agencies acting on behalf of the person or 
entity, with which you have an existing account that requests information in your credit report for the purposes of reviewing 
or collecting the account.  Reviewing the account includes activities related to account maintenance, monitoring, credit line 
increases, and account upgrades and enhancements. 
 
• 
You may seek damages from violators.  If a consumer reporting agency, or, in some cases, a user of consumer reports or a 
furnisher of information to a consumer reporting agency violates the FCRA, you may be able to sue in state or federal court. 
 
• 
Identity theft victims and active duty military personnel have additional rights.  For more information, visit 
www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
 
States may enforce the FCRA, and many states have their own consumer reporting laws.  In some cases, you may have more 
rights under state law.  For more information, contact your state or local consumer protection agency or your state Attorney 
General.  For information about your federal rights, contact:

Un resumen de sus derechos en virtud de la Ley de Informe Justo de Crédito 
 
La Ley de Informe Justo de Crédito (Fair Credit Reporting Act, FCRA, por sus siglas en inglés), una ley federal, fomenta la 
exactitud, imparcialidad y privacidad de la información en los archivos de las agencias de informes del consumidor. Existen muchos 
tipos de agencias de informes del consumidor, incluidas las agencias de crédito (credit bureaus) y las agencias especializadas (como 
las agencias que venden información sobre el historial de extensión de cheques, registros médicos y registros de historial de alquiler). 
A continuación, se presenta un resumen de sus principales derechos en virtud de la FCRA. Para obtener más información, 
incluyendo información sobre derechos adicionales, visite www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore o escriba a: Consumer 
Financial Protection Bureau, 1700 G Street NW, Washington, DC 20552. 
 
• 
Deben notificarle si la información contenida en su archivo se ha utilizado en su contra. Todo aquel que utilice un 
informe de crédito u otro tipo de informe de consumidor para denegar su solicitud de crédito, seguro o empleo, o para 
emprender otra acción adversa en su contra, debe informarle y debe darle el nombre, la dirección y el número de teléfono de 
la agencia que proporcionó esa información. 
 
• 
Usted tiene derecho a saber lo que contiene su archivo. Usted puede solicitar y obtener toda la información registrada bajo 
su nombre en los archivos de una agencia de informe del consumidor (divulgación de su información). Usted deberá 
proporcionar una prueba de su identidad, que puede incluir su número de Seguro Social. En muchos casos, la divulgación de 
la información de su archivo será gratuita. Usted tiene derecho a recibir una copia gratuita de su archivo si: 
 
o 
Una persona ha emprendido una acción adversa en su contra debido a la información contenida en su informe de 
crédito. 
o 
Usted es víctima de un robo de identidad y coloca una alerta de fraude en su archivo. 
o 
Su archivo contiene información inexacta como resultado de fraude. 
o 
Usted recibe asistencia pública. 
o 
Usted está desempleado pero prevé solicitar empleo en un plazo de 60 días. 
 
Asimismo, todos los consumidores tendrán derecho a recibir una copia gratuita de la información registrada en su archivo 
cada 12 meses si así se lo solicitan a cada agencia de crédito a nivel nacional y a las agencias especializadas de informe del 
consumidor a nivel nacional. Para obtener más información, visite www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
 
• 
Usted tiene derecho a pedir su puntuación de crédito. Las puntuaciones de crédito son resúmenes numéricos de su 
solvencia crediticia basados en la información de las agencias de crédito. Usted puede solicitar su puntuación de crédito a las 
agencias de informes del consumidor que generan o distribuyen los puntajes utilizados en préstamos de bienes raíces 
residenciales, pero tendrá que pagar un cargo. En algunas transacciones hipotecarias, el prestamista le dará información sobre 
su puntuación de crédito gratuitamente. 
 
• 
Usted tiene derecho a impugnar la información incompleta o inexacta. Si usted identifica información en su archivo que 
es incompleta o inexacta, y la reporta a la agencia de informes del consumidor, la agencia debe investigar, a menos que su 
impugnación sea frívola. Para consultar una explicación sobre los procedimientos de impugnación, visite 
www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
 
• 
Las agencias de informes del consumidor deben corregir o eliminar la información inexacta, incompleta o no 
verificable. La información inexacta, incompleta o no verificable debe ser eliminada o corregida, por lo general en un plazo 
de 30 días. No obstante, si una agencia de informe del consumidor verifica la exactitud de la información, puede seguir 
reportándola. 
 
• 
Las agencias de informes del consumidor no pueden reportar información negativa desactualizada. En la mayoría de 
los casos, una agencia de informe del consumidor no puede reportar información negativa ocurrida hace más de siete años, ni 
quiebras ocurridas hace más de 10 años. 
 
• 
El acceso a su archivo es limitado. Una agencia de informe del consumidor puede proporcionar información sobre usted 
solamente a aquellas personas que realmente la necesiten — generalmente para considerar una solicitud presentada por usted 

 
ante un acreedor, asegurador, empleador, propietario de una vivienda en alquiler u otro negocio. La FCRA especifica quiénes 
son las personas que tienen una necesidad válida de acceso. 
 
• 
Usted debe otorgar su consentimiento para que se envíen sus informes a los empleadores. Una agencia de informe del 
consumidor no puede darle información sobre usted a su empleador, ni a un posible empleador si usted no da su 
consentimiento por escrito al empleador. Por lo general, el consentimiento escrito no es requerido en la industria del 
transporte de carga por camión. Para obtener más información, visite www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
 
• 
Usted puede limitar las ofertas "preseleccionadas" de crédito y seguro que recibe y que están basadas en la 
información de su informe de crédito. Las ofertas "preseleccionadas " de crédito y seguro no solicitadas deben incluir un 
número de teléfono gratuito al que usted puede llamar si desea eliminar su nombre y dirección de las listas en las que se 
basan estas ofertas. Puede solicitar su exclusión voluntaria de estas listas llamando a las agencias de crédito a nivel nacional 
al 1-888-5-OPTOUT (1-888-567-8688). 
 
• 
El siguiente derecho, en virtud de la FCRA, se aplica a las agencias de informe del consumidor a nivel nacional: 
 
LOS CONSUMIDORES TIENEN EL DERECHO A OBTENER UN CONGELAMIENTO DE SEGURIDAD 
  
Usted tiene derecho a colocar un "congelamiento de seguridad" en su informe de crédito, lo que prohibirá que una 
agencia de informes del consumidor entregue información sobre su informe de crédito sin su autorización expresa. El 
congelamiento de seguridad está diseñado para evitar que créditos, préstamos y servicios se aprueben en su nombre sin su 
consentimiento.  Sin embargo, usted debe saber que colocar un congelamiento de seguridad para controlar el acceso a la 
información personal y financiera en su informe de crédito podría retrasar, interferir o bloquear la aprobación a tiempo de 
peticiones o solicitudes posteriores que usted haga con respecto a un nuevo préstamo, crédito, hipoteca o cualquier otra 
transacción para obtener un crédito.    
  
Como alternativa a un congelamiento de seguridad, usted tiene derecho a colocar una alerta de fraude inicial o extendida en 
su archivo de crédito sin costo alguno. Una alerta de fraude inicial es un aviso que se coloca en el archivo de crédito del 
consumidor por un (1) año. Cuando hay una alerta de fraude en el archivo de crédito del consumidor, la empresa está 
obligada a tomar medidas para verificar la identidad de dicho consumidor, antes de concederle un crédito. Si usted es una 
víctima del robo de identidad, usted tiene derecho a colocar una alerta de fraude extendida, que es un aviso de fraude que 
dura 7 años. 
  
El congelamiento de seguridad no es aplicable a personas o entidades, ni a las subsidiarias o agencias de cobranza que actúen 
en nombre de dichas personas o entidades, con las cuales usted ya tiene una cuenta y que solicitan información sobre su 
informe de crédito con el fin de cobrarle o revisar su cuenta.   Revisar una cuenta significa realizar ciertas actividades como 
el mantenimiento, vigilancia, actualizaciones, mejoras y aumentos a la línea de crédito de dicha cuenta.  
 
• 
Usted puede obtener compensación de los infractores. Si una agencia de informes del consumidor o, en algunos casos, un 
usuario de informes del consumidor, o un proveedor de información a una agencia de informes del consumidor infringe la 
FCRA, es posible que usted pueda presentar una demanda ante una corte estatal o federal. 
 
• 
Las víctimas del robo de identidad y el personal militar en servicio activo tienen derechos adicionales. Para obtener más 
información, visite www.consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
 
Los estados tienen autoridad para hacer cumplir la FCRA, y muchos estados tienen su propia legislación sobre los informes de 
los consumidores. En algunos casos, usted puede tener más derechos en virtud de la ley estatal. Para obtener más información, 
comuníquese con su agencia estatal o local de protección del consumidor o con el Fiscal General estatal. Para obtener 
información sobre sus derechos federales, comuníquese con:

U.S.C. section 1681e(b)). The notice stated: "The purpose of this message is to notify you that
InfoMart, a consumer reporting agency, is reporting the criminal or other public record
information that may be adverse about you to: Randstad App." The notice further stated that the
"above listed employer has certified that it uses such public record information to determine your
eligibility for employment, promotion, reassignment, retention, placement and/or volunteering."
22. The InfoMart notice explicitly identified the information being reported as "criminal
or other public record information." The "other public record information" referenced in the
notice was sex offender registry information disclosed pursuant to Penal Code section 290.46 --
the only item of adverse information in the entire background report.

E. The Termination
24. On or about July 15, 2026 -- only two business days after the July 13, 2026
pre-adverse action notice -- Defendant Randstad terminated Plaintiff's employment by telephone.
25. Defendants terminated Plaintiff a mere two business days after InfoMart transmitted
the pre-adverse action notice on Monday, July 13, 2026, without affording Plaintiff a reasonable
opportunity to review and dispute the contents of the background report. No written adverse
action notice was provided to Plaintiff before, concurrent with, or after the termination.
26. The InfoMart report's "NEEDS APPROVAL, PER CLIENT CRITERIA" designation
confirms that Defendants had established predetermined screening criteria that automatically
flagged sex offender registry results for adverse action. The termination was not the product of an
individualized assessment of Plaintiff's qualifications, job duties, or fitness for the position; it was
the mechanical application of a categorical exclusion triggered by registry status alone.
F. The Statutory Prohibition
27. California Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j)(1), provides that "[a] person is
authorized to use information disclosed pursuant to this section only to protect a person at risk."
Subdivision (j)(2) further provides: "Except as authorized under paragraph (1) or any other
provision of law, use of any information that is disclosed pursuant to this section for purposes
relating to any of the following is prohibited: ... (E) Employment."
28. Subdivision (j)(4)(B) provides that "[a]ny other misuse of information disclosed
pursuant to this section is a misdemeanor," punishable by a fine not exceeding twenty-five

These criminal penalties confirm the Legislature's determination that the prohibition on
employment-related use of registry information reflects a fundamental public policy of the State
of California.
29. Subdivision (j)(5) provides that any use of information disclosed pursuant to Penal
Code section 290.46 for purposes relating to employment "shall make the user liable for the
actual damages, and any amount that may be determined by a jury or a court sitting without a
jury, not exceeding three times the amount of actual damage, and not less than two hundred fifty
dollars ($250), and attorney's fees, exemplary damages, or a civil penalty not exceeding
twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000)."
30. Defendants' termination of Plaintiff based on sex offender registry information
violated each of the foregoing provisions. The termination was not undertaken "to protect a
person at risk" within the meaning of subdivision (j)(1), and no other provision of law authorized
Defendants' use of the registry information for employment purposes. No exception to the
statutory prohibition applies to a CDL commercial driving placement.

damages will be established at trial.

systematic background screening protocol that categorically excluded individuals based on sex

38. California Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j)(2)(E), establishes a fundamental
public policy of the State of California prohibiting the use of sex offender registry information for
employment purposes. This public policy is: (a) tethered to a constitutional or statutory provision;
(b) designed to benefit the public at large rather than serve a purely private interest; (c)
well-established at the time of the termination; and (d) sufficiently substantial and fundamental.
(See Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167; Gantt v. Sentry Insurance (1992) 1
Cal.4th 1083, 1090.)

policy by basing the termination on sex offender registry information disclosed pursuant to Penal
Code section 290.46.

47. Article I, Section 1 of the California Constitution provides that all people have an
inalienable right to privacy. This right protects against the improper use of personal information
for purposes the law has declared off-limits. (See Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn. (1994)
7 Cal.4th 1.)
48. Plaintiff had a legally protected privacy interest in his sex offender registry
information, which the Legislature has expressly prohibited from use in employment decisions
through Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j)(2)(E). Plaintiff had a reasonable expectation
that this information would not be used for employment purposes, given the categorical statutory
prohibition.
49. Defendants' procurement, review, and use of Plaintiff's sex offender registry
information to terminate his employment constituted a serious invasion of Plaintiff's
constitutionally protected privacy interest. The invasion was not justified by any competing
interest, and the means employed were not the least intrusive available.

INSTRUCTIONS ON HOW TO COMPLETE THE COVER SHEET
To Plaintiffs and Others Filing First Papers. If you are filing a first paper (for example, a complaint) in a civil case, you must 
complete and file, along with your first paper, the Civil Case Cover Sheet contained on pages 1 and 2. This information will be used to 
compile statistics about the types and numbers of cases filed. You must complete items 1 through 6 on the sheet. In item 1, you must 
check one box for the case type that best describes the case. If the case fits both a general and a more specific type of case listed in 
item 1, check the more specific one. If the case has multiple causes of action, check the box that best indicates the primary cause of 
action. To assist you in completing the sheet, examples of the cases that belong under each case type in item 1 are provided on page 3 
of this form. A cover sheet must be filed only with your initial paper. Failure to file a cover sheet with the first paper filed in a civil case 
may subject a party, its counsel, or both to sanctions under rules 2.30 and 3.220 of the California Rules of Court. 
To Parties in Rule 3.740 Collections Cases. A "collections case" under rule 3.740 of the California Rules of Court is defined as an 
action for recovery of money owed in a sum stated to be certain that is not more than $35,000, exclusive of interest and attorney's fees, 
arising from a transaction in which property, services, or money was acquired on credit. A collections case does not include an action 
seeking the following: (1) tort damages, (2) punitive damages, (3) recovery of real property, (4) recovery of personal property, or (5) a 
prejudgment writ of attachment.  The identification of a case as a rule 3.740 collections case on this form means that it will be exempt 
from the general time-for-service requirements and case management rules, unless a defendant files a responsive pleading. A rule 
3.740 collections case will be subject to the requirements for service and obtaining a judgment in rule 3.740.
To Parties in Complex Cases. In complex cases only, parties must also use the Civil Case Cover Sheet to designate whether the 
case is complex. If a plaintiff believes the case is complex under rule 3.400 of the California Rules of Court, this must be indicated by 
completing the appropriate boxes in items 1 and 2. If a plaintiff designates a case as complex, the cover sheet must be served with the 
complaint on all parties to the action. A defendant may file and serve no later than the time of its first appearance a joinder in the 
plaintiff's designation, a counter-designation that the case is not complex, or, if the plaintiff has made no designation, a designation that 
the case is complex.

27. California Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j)(1), provides that "[a] person is
authorized to use information disclosed pursuant to this section only to protect a person at risk."
Subdivision (j)(2) further provides: "Except as authorized under paragraph (1) or any other
provision of law, use of any information that is disclosed pursuant to this section for purposes
relating to any of the following is prohibited: ... (E) Employment."
28. Subdivision (j)(4)(B) provides that "[a]ny other misuse of information disclosed
pursuant to this section is a misdemeanor," punishable by a fine not exceeding twenty-five

in that it was obtained through personal interviews and/or inquiry of public records for the
purpose of evaluating Plaintiff's eligibility for employment.
44. Defendants violated the Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act ("ICRAA")
in one or more of the following respects:
a. Defendants failed to provide Plaintiff with a clear and conspicuous written
disclosure, in a document consisting solely of the disclosure, that an investigative
consumer report would be obtained for employment purposes, as required by Civil Code
section 1786.16, subdivision (a)(2)(B);
b. Defendants failed to provide Plaintiff with a written adverse action notice, as
required by Civil Code section 1786.40, subdivision (b), prior to or concurrent with the
termination;
c. Defendants used the investigative consumer report for a purpose not permitted
under the ICRAA, specifically by relying on sex offender registry information that
California law categorically prohibits employers from using for employment purposes.

FOURTH CAUSE OF ACTION
Invasion of Privacy
(California Constitution, Article I, Section 1)
(Against All Defendants)
46. Plaintiff incorporates by reference paragraphs 1 through 32 as though fully set forth
herein.
47. Article I, Section 1 of the California Constitution provides that all people have an
inalienable right to privacy. This right protects against the improper use of personal information
for purposes the law has declared off-limits. (See Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn. (1994)
7 Cal.4th 1.)
48. Plaintiff had a legally protected privacy interest in his sex offender registry
information, which the Legislature has expressly prohibited from use in employment decisions
through Penal Code section 290.46, subdivision (j)(2)(E). Plaintiff had a reasonable expectation
that this information would not be used for employment purposes, given the categorical statutory
prohibition.
49. Defendants' procurement, review, and use of Plaintiff's sex offender registry
information to terminate his employment constituted a serious invasion of Plaintiff's
constitutionally protected privacy interest. The invasion was not justified by any competing
interest, and the means employed were not the least intrusive available.

54. The harm suffered by Plaintiff -- termination of employment based on registry
