Legislature has prescribed. (Common Cause v. Board of Supervisors (1989) 49 Cal.3d 432, 442.)
A public entity likewise "has a ministerial duty to comply with its own rules and regulations
where they are valid and unambiguous." (Kern County Hospital Authority v. Dept. of Corrections
& Rehabilitation (2023) 91 Cal.App.5th 1313, 1325.) Galzinski v. Somers (2016) 2 Cal.App.5th
1164 applied these principles to a law enforcement agency: even though the substance of a police
department's response to a citizen complaint was discretionary, mandamus lay to compel the
department to perform its procedural obligations—to conduct an investigation sufficient to
support a finding, and to make one of the enumerated findings. (Id. at pp. 1171-1173; accord, CV
Amalgamated LLC v. City of Chula Vista (2022) 82 Cal.App.5th 265, 283 [agency's "failure to
follow its own procedures provides the basis for the issuance of a traditional writ of mandate"].)
Here the procedural obligations arise not from a published internal procedure but from a
statute—a stronger footing still.
Accordingly, even assuming CHP retains fact-finding judgment concerning whether a
requestor is a victim of qualifying criminal activity, ordinary mandate reaches CHP's failure to
exercise that judgment under the controlling statutory framework, its failure to apply the
mandatory presumption, and action taken in derogation of statutory standards. (Common Cause, 
supra, 49 Cal.3d at p. 442; Cal. Correctional Peace Officers Assn. v. State Personnel Bd. (1995)
10 Cal.4th 1133, 1154.) The Court need not decide now whether the pleaded record compels
certification. It need decide only whether the Petition plausibly alleges that CHP failed to
perform, or lawfully exercise, duties section 679.10 imposes.
The Petition alleges the denial: (a) applied an unstated "standard" nowhere found in
section 679.10; (b) ignored the enumerated qualifying offenses the statute incorporates by
reference from 8 U.S.C. section 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii); (c) failed to address CHP's own detention
certificate reflecting that no accusatory pleading was filed—a material agency record submitted
with the request; (d) failed to address CHP's own dashcam recording; and (e) gave no explanation

they shall provide a written explanation for the denial of the Form I-918 Supplement B

The first sentence is a stand-alone command: the entity "shall provide a written
explanation for the denial." The second sentence adds a specific application: if the denial rests on
non-cooperation, the explanation must include details about the requests and the refusal. The
second sentence supplements the first; it does not replace it. (Manufacturers Life Ins. Co. v.
Superior Court (1995) 10 Cal.4th 257, 274; DuBois v. Workers' Comp. Appeals Bd. (1993) 5
Cal.4th 382, 388 ["[A] construction making some words surplusage is to be avoided."].)
The two-sentence structure is not accidental. The first sentence is the general rule: any
denial must be accompanied by a written explanation. The second sentence is a specific
application for cooperation-based denials. To read the second sentence as the only requirement
would mean that an agency could deny certification based on a failure to prove
victimization—the most common and most consequential category of denial—with no
explanation at all. That is precisely the result AB 1261 was enacted to prevent.
The legislative history removes any doubt. The Legislative Counsel's Digest of AB
1261—which "is printed as a preface to every bill considered by the Legislature" and is entitled to
great weight in construing the enactment (Jones v. Lodge at Torrey Pines Partnership (2008) 42
Cal.4th 1158, 1169-1170)—describes the requirement without qualification: "The bill would
require a certifying entity that does not certify the form regarding 'victim helpfulness' to provide a
written explanation for the denial of the certification." (Legis. Counsel's Dig., Assem. Bill No.
1261 (2023-2024 Reg. Sess.), Stats. 2023, ch. 679.) The Digest states the written-explanation
duty as a free-standing obligation attaching to every non-certification—not as a duty confined to
cooperation-based denials. Had the Legislature intended the narrower duty Respondent proposes,
the Digest would have said so. The Court may take judicial notice of the Digest as an official
legislative act. (Evid. Code, § 452, subd. (c).)

A legally adequate explanation need not resemble a judicial opinion or discuss every item
submitted. But it must state enough of the actual ground for denial to disclose whether CHP
rejected the request because it found no qualifying criminal activity, no substantially similar
activity, insufficient victim status, lack of helpfulness, or another legally permissible basis. CHP's
letter merely restates the ultimate conclusion and does not disclose the operative reasoned basis
for that conclusion. (Pet. ¶¶ 62, 82.) The ministerial character of the reason-giving duty is not in
serious dispute: like the duty to investigate and make findings enforced in Galzinski, the duty to
explain is a procedural obligation that does not depend on the merits of the underlying
certification decision. (Galzinski, supra, 2 Cal.App.5th at pp. 1171-1173; cf. Topanga Assn. for a
Scenic Community v. County of Los Angeles (1974) 11 Cal.3d 506, 514-515.) The second cause of

Respondent argues the presumption does not apply because Petitioner has not alleged that

help—placing the agency in sole control of whether the presumption ever operates. That is the
opposite of what a statutory presumption does.
The statute expressly makes refusal or failure to provide reasonably requested assistance
the relevant condition. The Petition alleges no request, refusal, or failure; it further alleges
affirmative provision of information through the citizen complaint, the POST complaint, the
DMV proceedings, and production of the dashcam transcript. (Pet. ¶¶ 7, 87.) CHP's denial letter
contains no finding of refusal or failure to cooperate and identifies no fact that could rebut the
presumption. (Pet. ¶ 62(f).) At minimum, those allegations plausibly require CHP to address the
presumption rather than silently disregard it. The failure to apply a controlling statutory
presumption is itself reviewable by mandamus. (Cf. Fukuda v. City of Angels (1999) 20 Cal.4th
805, 819.)
V.  THE FOURTH CAUSE OF ACTION STATES A CLAIM: AN ACTUAL
     CONTROVERSY EXISTS OVER THE CONSTRUCTION OF SECTION 679.10.
Respondent argues declaratory relief is "advisory" or "moot." (Dem. MPA at 17-20.)
Neither succeeds. The Petition asks the Court to declare the parties' rights with respect to a
concrete controversy: whether CHP's April 20, 2026 denial letter satisfies subdivision (i)(2). (Pet.
¶ 93(c).) That is an "actual controversy relating to the legal rights and duties of the respective
parties." (Code Civ. Proc., § 1060; Linda Vista Village San Diego Homeowners Assn., Inc. v.
Tecolote Investors, LLC (2015) 234 Cal.App.4th 166, 181.)

I. INTRODUCTION
On July 30, 2026, individual Respondents Gerardo Serrato (Captain/Commander), Gary
Paul (Lieutenant), and Eric Dutra (Sergeant) each filed a Notice of Joinder to Respondent
California Highway Patrol's Demurrer, a separate Demurrer, and a supporting Memorandum of
Points and Authorities. Each filing does two things. First, each individual Respondent joins and
adopts CHP's core theory that certifying Form I-918, Supplement B is a discretionary act beyond
the reach of ordinary mandamus under Code of Civil Procedure § 1085. Second, Respondents
Paul and Dutra each raise an individualized argument not previously briefed: that the Petition
fails to plead facts showing each of them personally qualifies as a “certifying official” within the
meaning of Penal Code § 679.10(b), and that each is therefore not a proper respondent.
Respondent Serrato's MPA does not independently challenge his certifying-official status but
rather acknowledges that Petitioner has alleged he is a certifying official and has attached the
denial letter he signed. (Serrato MPA at 2:20-24.)
As to the joinder-based arguments, Petitioner incorporates by reference in full the
arguments and authorities set forth in Petitioner's Opposition to Respondent CHP's Demurrer,
filed July 13, 2026, and the supporting Declaration of Petitioner. Those arguments apply with
equal force to the individual Respondents, who merely adopt CHP's positions without
independent analysis. Petitioner will not rebrief those arguments here.

As to the “not a certifying official” argument raised by Respondents Paul and Dutra, it is
independently meritless. As a threshold matter, the Petition does not merely support an inference
on this point — Pet. ¶¶ 14–16 each expressly allege, in the statute's own words, that the
respondent “is a 'certifying official' within the meaning of Penal Code § 679.10(b).” That
allegation must be accepted as true on demurrer, together with the specific supporting facts and
attached exhibits discussed below. Independent of that express allegation, the Petition also pleads
specific supporting facts — including two exhibits attached to and incorporated by reference in
the Petition itself — from which the Court can and must reasonably infer that each individual
Respondent is a certifying official under one or more of the four categories in § 679.10(b). The
Petition is not required to recite the statutory categories verbatim; it is required to plead facts,
which it does, and it does so twice over. If the Court nonetheless finds any allegation insufficient,
leave to amend should be granted because the deficiency, if any, is a readily curable pleading gap,
not a substantive defect.
II. STANDARD OF REVIEW
A demurrer tests whether the complaint states facts sufficient to constitute a cause of
action. (Code Civ. Proc., § 430.10, subd. (e).) In ruling on a demurrer, the court must “assume the
truth of all facts properly pleaded by the plaintiff, as well as those that are judicially noticeable.” (
Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311, 318.) The court “give[s] the complaint a reasonable
interpretation, reading it as a whole and its parts in their context.” (Ibid.) A complaint need not
plead facts in the precise language of the statute; it suffices if the facts alleged support a
reasonable inference that each element of the claim is met. (Quelimane Co. v. Stewart Title
Guaranty Co. (1998) 19 Cal.4th 26, 38-39 [“[w]e look to whether the factual allegations, liberally
construed, state a cause of action on any available legal theory”].)
“[A] demurrer should not be sustained without leave to amend if the complaint, liberally
construed, can reasonably be considered to state a cause of action on any theory, or if there is a

demurring party to show that the complaint does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of
action. (Ibid.)
On demurrer, the Court may also consider matters subject to judicial notice (Evid. Code, §
452) and documents incorporated by reference in the pleading. (Barnett v. Fireman's Fund Ins.
Co. (2001) 90 Cal.App.4th 500, 505 [“a demurrer reaches exhibits attached to or incorporated by
reference in the complaint”].) The Verified Petition incorporates fourteen exhibits, including the
April 20, 2026 denial letter (Exhibit 1), the dashcam transcript (Exhibit 5), the CHP arrest report
(Exhibit 6), and the Penal Code § 851.6 detention certificate (Exhibit 7). These are part of the
pleading and accepted as true on demurrer.
III. ARGUMENT
Penal Code § 679.10(b) defines “certifying official” as: (1) the head of the certifying
entity; (2) a person in a supervisory role who has been specifically designated by the head of the
certifying entity to issue Form I-918 Supplement B certifications on behalf of that agency; (3) a
judge; or (4) any other certifying official defined under § 214.14(a)(2) of Title 8 of the Code of
Federal Regulations. (Pen. Code, § 679.10, subd. (b)(1)-(4).)
The question on demurrer is not whether the Petition recites these categories verbatim. It
is whether the Petition alleges facts from which the Court can reasonably infer that each
individual Respondent falls within one or more of these categories. (Quelimane Co., supra, 19
Cal.4th at pp. 38-39.) Here, the Petition does more than support an inference: Pet. ¶¶ 14, 15, and
16 each expressly allege that the respondent “is a 'certifying official' within the meaning of Penal
Code § 679.10(b)” — using the statute's own operative phrase. As shown below, the Petition also
independently pleads the specific supporting facts for each Respondent, backed by exhibits

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES 
Respondent Gary Paul (“Lt. Paul”) joins in Respondent California Highway Patrol’s 
(“CHP”) Demurrer to the Petition for Writ of Mandate as to all causes of action in the petition on 
the ground that the petition does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action.  (See 
Code Civ. Proc. § 430.10, subd. (e).)   
Specifically, CHP demurs to the Petition for these reasons:  (1) CHP possesses no 
ministerial duty to certify Petitioner’s Form I-918, Supplement B, U Nonimmigrant Status 
Certification (“Form B”) (see CHP’s Demurrer at 11-13); (2) Petitioner has no clear, present and 
beneficial right to the performance of a ministerial duty (see CHP’s Demurrer at 13-15); (3) CHP 
has no ministerial duty to provide a written explanation for its certification denial in the form 
demanded by Petitioner (see CHP Demurrer at 15-16); (4) the rebuttable presumption of 
helpfulness is not applicable on the facts alleged (see CHP’s Demurrer at 16-17); and (5) 
Petitioner is not entitled to his requested declaratory relief because he seeks advisory opinions on 
purely legal questions, declaratory relief cannot unwind a past administrative decision, and 
because Petitioner is not entitled to a writ of ordinary mandate, mooting the declaration Petitioner 
seeks (see CHP’s Demurrer at 17-20).    
These reasons are relevant to Lt. Paul’s defenses and demurrer because the basis for 
Petitioner’s requested relief, as articulated in his petition, is the same as to all Respondents, 
including the individual Respondents.  Further, the relief sought by CHP would benefit Lt. Paul, 
as Petitioner alleges that Lt. Paul is a “certifying official” within the meaning of Penal Code 
section 679.10(b).  For these reasons, Lt. Paul joins CHP’s Demurrer to the Petition for Writ of 
Mandate as to all causes of action in the petition, and adopts the points and authorities filed in 
support of CHP’s Demurrer. 
Lt. Paul demurs to the petition for one additional reason:  Petitioner has not stated facts 
sufficient to allege that Lt. Paul is a “certifying official” within the meaning of Penal Code 
section 679.10(b).  Specifically, the petition alleges that Lt. Paul “is a CHP supervisory official 
with responsibility for processing the certification request.”  (Pet., ¶ 15.)  However, Section 
679.10(b) provides that a certifying official is (1) the head of the certifying entity; (2) a person in

named individual Respondents, in their official capacities, to perform mandatory,
non-discretionary duties owed to Petitioner under California Penal Code section 679.10 (as
amended by AB 1261, Stats. 2023, ch. 679, eff. Jan. 1, 2024). The duties at issue are the duties of
a state law-enforcement "certifying entity" and "certifying official" to: (a) certify a Form I-918,

2. On April 9, 2026, Petitioner submitted to CHP a verified, pre-completed Form I-918,
Supplement B, together with an eight-page supporting legal-and-evidentiary memorandum, a
verbatim transcript of CHP's own dashcam recording of the underlying incident, the CHP
arrest-investigation report, CHP's own Penal Code section 851.6 detention certificate
reclassifying the arrest as "a detention only, not an arrest" for "insufficient grounds for making a
criminal complaint," and additional documentary exhibits. CHP File No. 390.18437.17620. POST
Case No. PUBLIC-26-000371.
3. On April 20, 2026—eleven days after submission—Respondent G. Serrato, Captain and
Commander of the CHP Dublin Area, denied the certification request in a five-sentence letter that
nowhere identifies which element of Penal Code section 679.10 or 8 U.S.C. section
1101(a)(15)(U) Petitioner allegedly fails, nowhere engages with the dashcam evidence in CHP's
own custody, and nowhere reconciles its conclusion with CHP's own prior section 851.6
determination that the underlying arrest lacked legal justification. The denial states only that the
incident "does not meet the standard of qualifying criminal activity identified in Section 679.10 of
the California Penal Code," "does not meet the standards of the Immigration and Nationality Act
Section 101(a)(15)(U)(iii)," and "found no substantially similar qualifying criminal activity as
defined in Section 679.10(d) PC."
4. Petitioner is a victim of multiple enumerated qualifying offenses listed in 8 U.S.C.
section 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) and incorporated by reference into Penal Code section 679.10: false
imprisonment/unlawful criminal restraint, felonious assault/battery, obstruction of justice, and
perjury. CHP's own contemporaneous documentary record—the dashcam audio-video recording,
the arrest report, and the section 851.6 detention certificate—establishes these offenses on its

ROADMAP FOR THE COURT
7. This Petition presents three documentary propositions that, if accepted, compel writ
relief without requiring this Court to make any contested factual determination:
First, CHP's own dashcam audio-video recording (Exhibit 5) contradicts
CHP's own sworn arrest report (Exhibit 6) on four discrete material points—the
asserted odor of alcohol, slurred speech, confusion/disorientation, and "beverage
present." The contradictions are not matters of interpretation; they are absences (the

(the cup actually contained urine, as Officer Melano expressly identified by name). These

imprisonment, obstruction of justice, and perjury under Penal Code section 118.
Second, CHP's own Penal Code section 851.6 detention certificate (Exhibit 7)
reclassified the arrest as "a detention only, not an arrest" for "insufficient grounds
for making a criminal complaint." This is CHP's own contemporaneous formal
determination, four days after the incident, that the restraint was without legal
justification. The April 20, 2026 denial nowhere reconciles its "no qualifying criminal
activity" conclusion with CHP's own contrary determination.
Third, Penal Code section 679.10(h) creates a rebuttable presumption of
victim helpfulness when the victim has not refused or failed to provide reasonably
requested information or assistance. Petitioner's documented cooperation—the citizen
complaint that initiated the investigation, the POST complaint, the DMV proceedings, and
the production of the dashcam transcript—is uncontradicted. CHP's denial letter contains
no finding of refusal or failure to cooperate and identifies no fact that could rebut the
presumption. The presumption therefore stands unrebutted as a matter of law.
8. The relief sought is targeted and modest: vacate the conclusory denial; require
Respondents to reconsider under the correct legal standards; and require any future denial to
comply with the written-reasons mandate of section 679.10(g). This Petition does not ask this
Court to compel a particular outcome on the certification merits; it asks this Court to compel a
lawful process.

9. This Court has jurisdiction over this action pursuant to Article VI, section 10 of the
California Constitution and Code of Civil Procedure section 1085, which authorize the superior
court to issue writs of mandate to compel performance of an act "which the law specially enjoins,
as a duty resulting from an office, trust, or station" by any "tribunal, corporation, board, or
person."
10. Venue lies in this County under Code of Civil Procedure section 393(b). This
action is brought against a state law-enforcement agency and against public officers for acts done
by them in virtue of their offices. Under Code of Civil Procedure section 393(b), the proper
county is "the county where the cause, or some part of the cause, arose." The cause—or, at a
minimum, a substantial part of it—arose in Alameda County because: (a) the underlying
November 1, 2024 incident on which the certification request is based occurred on Interstate 580
East in Livermore, Alameda County; (b) the forcible handcuffing, transport, and involuntary
blood draw all occurred at the CHP Dublin Area Office, 4999 Gleason Drive, Dublin, Alameda
County; (c) Petitioner's certification request was submitted to a CHP investigator at the CHP
Dublin Area Office in Alameda County; and (d) the April 20, 2026 denial letter at issue in this
petition was authored, signed, and issued by the Commander of the CHP Dublin Area, on CHP
Dublin Area letterhead, from the CHP Dublin Area office in Alameda County.
11. Petitioner has no plain, speedy, and adequate remedy in the ordinary course of
law. Penal Code section 679.10 does not provide an administrative appeal, an internal grievance
process, or any other agency-level remedy by which a denial of certification may be reviewed.
The federal U-visa adjudication conducted by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services is not
an adequate substitute remedy because USCIS lacks any authority to certify or to compel a state
certifying entity to certify on Form I-918, Supplement B, and a U-visa petition cannot be filed
without a properly executed Supplement B. Mandamus is the traditional, and here the exclusive,
remedy. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1086.)

STATUTORY AND LEGAL FRAMEWORK
A. Ordinary Writ of Mandate Under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1085
18. Code of Civil Procedure section 1085 authorizes the issuance of a writ of mandate by
any court "to any inferior tribunal, corporation, board, or person, to compel the performance of an
act which the law specially enjoins, as a duty resulting from an office, trust, or station." The
traditional elements are: (a) a clear, present, and ministerial duty in the respondent; (b) a clear,
present, and beneficial right in the petitioner to performance of that duty; and (c) the absence of a
plain, speedy, and adequate alternative remedy in the ordinary course of law.
19. "Shall" creates a ministerial duty enforceable by writ. A statutory directive in
mandatory form imposes a ministerial duty, the breach of which is enforceable by writ. (See Gov.
Code § 14 ["shall" is mandatory, "may" is permissive]; Haggis v. City of Los Angeles (2000) 22
Cal.4th 490, 498-499 ["shall" is ordinarily mandatory for purposes of Government Code section
815.6]; Common Cause v. Board of Supervisors (1989) 49 Cal.3d 432, 443 ["shall" creates a

[discretionary immunity does not apply to ministerial acts].)
20. Mandate lies to correct abuse of discretion. Although a court will not substitute its
judgment for an agency's on a purely discretionary decision, mandate lies (a) to compel an agency
to exercise its discretion at all where it has refused to do so; (b) to compel an agency to apply the
correct legal standard; and (c) to set aside a decision that reflects a failure to proceed in the
manner required by law, or that is arbitrary, capricious, or wholly unsupported by the record. (See
Saleeby v. State Bar (1985) 39 Cal.3d 547, 562 [in traditional mandamus, court determines
whether agency action was arbitrary, capricious, or without evidentiary support, and whether it
failed to conform to the law]; Carloss v. County of Alameda (2015) 242 Cal.App.4th 116
[decision is abuse of discretion if arbitrary, capricious, entirely lacking in evidentiary support, or
without reasonable or rational basis as a matter of law]; SN Sands Corp. v. City and County of
San Francisco (2008) 167 Cal.App.4th 185, 189 [same]; Western/California, Ltd. v. Dry Creek
Joint Elementary Sch. Dist. (1996) 50 Cal.App.4th 1461, 1496-1497 [same]; Bunnett v. Regents
of University of California (1995) 35 Cal.App.4th 843, 848.)
21. An agency decision that ignores the agency's own contrary evidence and prior
determinations is arbitrary and capricious as a matter of law. A decision is arbitrary and
capricious if it fails to address relevant evidence, fails to articulate a rational connection between
the facts found and the decision made, or is so devoid of factual support as to be irrational. A
decision that ignores the agency's own exculpatory evidence and contradicts the agency's own
prior contemporaneous determinations is, by definition, both arbitrary and contrary to the
substantial-evidence rule under section 1085.

23. The list of "qualifying criminal activity" in 8 U.S.C. section 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii) is

I-918, Supplement B—signed by a certifying official of a federal, state, or local law-enforcement

24. The certifying agency does not adjudicate the U-visa itself. As the U.S. Department of
Homeland Security and the California Attorney General have repeatedly explained, the Form
I-918, Supplement B is a factual certification only; USCIS independently conducts all eligibility,
background, and adjudicatory determinations and has sole authority to grant or deny the visa. The
certifier merely attests to the agency's factual knowledge of victimization and helpfulness.

26. Mandatory certification. Section 679.10 directs that, upon request of a victim of
qualifying criminal activity, a certifying entity "shall" complete and certify Form I-918,
Supplement B when the statutory elements are met. The Legislature's use of "shall" imposes a
mandatory, ministerial duty enforceable by writ of mandate. (Haggis, supra, 22 Cal.4th at pp.
498-499; Common Cause, supra, 49 Cal.3d at p. 443.)
27. Rebuttable presumption of helpfulness (subdivision (h)). Section 679.10(h) creates
a "rebuttable presumption that the victim is helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to be helpful" in
the detection, investigation, or prosecution of the qualifying criminal activity if the victim has not
refused or failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested by the certifying
entity. The presumption operates against the certifying entity and may be overcome only by
evidence of refusal or failure to cooperate. An agency that fails to apply a controlling statutory
presumption commits legal error reviewable by mandamus.
28. Thirty-day processing deadline (subdivision (j)). Section 679.10(j) requires that a
certifying entity "shall process" a Form I-918, Supplement B certification request within 30 days
of the request, with shorter deadlines in specified circumstances.
29. No prosecution required (subdivision (k)). Section 679.10(k) provides that "[a]
current investigation, the filing of charges, closing of a case, and a prosecution or conviction are
not required for the victim to request and obtain the Form I-918 Supplement B certification."
Whether a prosecution has occurred is therefore legally irrelevant to the certification
determination, and any denial that rests, expressly or implicitly, on the absence of charges or
prosecution is contrary to law.
30. Reason-giving requirement (subdivision (g)) — AB 1261's central procedural
reform. Section 679.10(g), as amended by AB 1261, requires that a certifying entity that does not

The Legislature expressly imposed a procedural duty of meaningful explanation precisely to
forestall conclusory, pro-forma, or boilerplate refusals that frustrate both the requester's ability to
understand the basis for denial and any reviewing court's ability to evaluate the agency's
reasoning. The duty to provide written, specific reasons is itself ministerial: it does not depend on
the merits of the underlying certification decision.
31. Limited grounds for withdrawal (subdivision (l)). A certifying official may
withdraw a certification only if the victim refuses to provide information and assistance
reasonably requested. No comparable cabining provision exists for an initial denial precisely
because the Legislature anticipated that the presumption of helpfulness and the reason-giving
requirement together would constrain denial discretion.
32. Attorney General guidance. The California Attorney General has issued Information
Bulletins (most recently DLE-2024-05) instructing all state and local law enforcement
agencies—including CHP—that under AB 1261 they "shall process" certification requests within
the statutory timeline; that the rebuttable presumption of helpfulness applies; that no prosecution
is required; that the reason-giving requirement is a substantive procedural obligation that
conclusory letters do not satisfy; and that certification shall not be denied on grounds such as the
victim's criminal record, immigration history, or the absence of filed charges. The Attorney
General's interpretation of section 679.10 is entitled to substantial weight.

A. The Government Claims Act Does Not Apply
65. The Government Claims Act (Gov. Code, § 810 et seq.) governs claims "for money or
damages" against public entities. (Gov. Code, § 905.) This Petition seeks no money or damages.
It seeks only a peremptory writ of mandate vacating an unlawful denial, an order compelling
lawful reconsideration, and declaratory relief concerning the parties' rights under Penal Code
section 679.10. Equitable relief of this kind is not subject to the Act's claim-presentation
requirement. (See Loehr v. Ventura County Community College Dist. (1983) 147 Cal.App.3d
1071, 1080-1081 [claims for relief other than damages not subject to Government Claims Act];

because USCIS lacks any authority to certify or to compel a state certifying entity to do so;
without a properly executed Form I-918, Supplement B, a U-visa petition cannot be filed.

I.
CALIFORNIA LAW MANDATES CERTIFICATION

California Penal Code § 679.10 imposes affirmative, non-discretionary obligations on state 
law enforcement agencies—including CHP—to process U visa certification requests. Specifically:
Mandatory Processing: Under § 679.10(j), a certifying entity “shall process a Form I-918 
Supplement B certification within 30 days of request.” This is not a discretionary guideline; 
it is a legislative mandate.
Rebuttable Presumption of Helpfulness: Under § 679.10(h), there is a “rebuttable 
presumption that the victim is helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to be helpful” if the 
victim has not refused or failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested 
by law enforcement. I have not refused any such request. To the contrary, I have 
affirmatively cooperated at every stage.
No Prosecution Required: Under § 679.10(k), “a current investigation, the filing of 
charges, closing of a case, and a prosecution or conviction are not required for the victim to 
request and obtain the Form I-918 Supplement B certification.” The CHP’s investigation 
need not be complete—nor need it result in prosecution—for the certification to issue.
Limited Grounds for Withdrawal: Under § 679.10(l), a certifying official “may only 
withdraw the certification if the victim refuses to provide information and assistance when 
reasonably requested.” No such refusal has occurred here.
The California Attorney General’s Information Bulletin No. DLE-2024-05, issued to all 
state and local law enforcement agencies, reaffirms these obligations and encourages agencies to 
“be vigilant in identifying and supporting immigrant crime victims who may be eligible for U 
visas.”
II.
THE STATUTORY ELEMENTS ARE SATISFIED
To obtain a U visa certification, three elements must be established: (1) the petitioner is a 
victim of qualifying criminal activity; (2) the petitioner possesses information concerning the 
criminal activity; and (3) the petitioner has been helpful, is being helpful, or is likely to be helpful 
in the investigation or prosecution. Each element is met here.
A.
Qualifying Criminal Activity
On November 1, 2024, on Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County, CHP 
Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez (#023295) and Jose Melano (#023054) subjected me to criminal 
conduct constituting multiple qualifying offenses under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii), including:
False Imprisonment / Unlawful Criminal Restraint (Cal. Penal Code § 236)—I was 
unlawfully arrested, handcuffed, and detained; the arrest was subsequently reclassified 
as a “detention” in a revised report, an implicit acknowledgment that the initial restraint 
was without legal justification;
Felonious Assault / Battery (Cal. Penal Code § 242)—an involuntary blood draw was 
performed on my person based on a misrepresented warrant, constituting an unlawful 
application of force;

Obstruction of Justice (analogous to Cal. Penal Code §§ 118, 182)—the officers 
fabricated sworn arrest reports that are directly contradicted by the CHP’s own 
dashcam recording, constituting the creation of false evidence under penalty of perjury; 
and
Perjury (Cal. Penal Code § 118)—false statements in sworn reports contradicted by 
objective dashcam evidence.
Each of these offenses is independently enumerated as qualifying criminal activity under 
the VTVPA. The dashcam transcript—objective, contemporaneous evidence in CHP’s own 
custody—corroborates these allegations and directly contradicts the officers’ written reports.
B.
Possession of Information
As the direct victim and sole civilian percipient witness to the November 1, 2024 incident, I 
possess firsthand information regarding every aspect of the qualifying criminal activity. I have 
gathered and preserved key evidence, including the dashcam transcript, the arrest report, and the 
certificate of detention—all of which I have made available to CHP through this complaint process.
C.
Helpfulness
I have been helpful, am currently being helpful, and am likely to continue being helpful in 
the investigation of this criminal activity. My cooperation includes: filing the citizen complaint that 
initiated this investigation (File No. 390.18437.17620); filing a separate complaint with the 
Commission on Peace Officer Standards and Training (POST Case No. PUBLIC-26-000371); 
participating in DMV administrative proceedings related to the incident; gathering and preserving 
the dashcam transcript as objective evidence; and presenting all evidence to CHP and related 
agencies. At no time have I refused or failed to provide information or assistance reasonably 
requested by any investigating entity.
Under § 679.10(h), these facts create a rebuttable presumption of helpfulness that can only 
be overcome by evidence that I have refused to cooperate. No such evidence exists.
III.
SUBSTANTIAL PHYSICAL AND MENTAL ABUSE
I have suffered substantial physical and mental abuse as a direct result of the qualifying 
criminal activity, including: physical pain from forcible handcuffing and an involuntary blood 
draw; the trauma and humiliation of an unlawful arrest and incarceration; extended detention

IV.
IMPORTANT CLARIFICATIONS FOR THE CERTIFYING OFFICIAL
I respectfully call your attention to several points the Department of Homeland Security 
and the California Attorney General have emphasized for certifying officials:

Signing the certification does not grant a visa. The Form I-918 Supplement B is not a 
visa approval. It is a factual certification that the individual is or was a victim of qualifying 
criminal activity and has been helpful. USCIS independently adjudicates the visa petition, 
conducts a full background check, and makes all eligibility determinations. The certifying 
official’s signature carries no immigration consequences standing alone.
This certification concerns the officers’ conduct, not the outcome of the complaint. 
The standard is whether the petitioner is a victim of qualifying criminal activity and has 
been helpful—not whether the investigation has concluded or discipline has been imposed. 
California law is explicit that no prosecution, conviction, or even a pending investigation is 
required.
CHP has a public-safety interest in certifying. As the DHS U Visa Law Enforcement 
Resource Guide emphasizes, certifying U visa petitions builds trust within communities, 
encourages crime reporting, and strengthens law enforcement’s ability to detect, 
investigate, and prosecute criminal activity. CHP’s cooperation here advances these goals.

A.
False Imprisonment / Unlawful Criminal Restraint (Cal. Penal Code § 236)
Penal Code § 236 defines false imprisonment as “the unlawful violation of the personal 
liberty of another.” The evidence establishes each component:
The arrest lacked probable cause. The dashcam transcript (Exhibit A) reveals that the 
sole basis for the traffic stop was a welfare check on a lawfully parked vehicle. The only

The Petitioner exhibited no objective signs of impairment. Throughout the encounter, 
the Petitioner correctly identified his location as Livermore (Exhibit A, 01:00:41); read

highway signs approximately 50 yards away (Exhibit A, 01:00:44); coherently explained

fatigued (Exhibit A, 01:01:21); and estimated 30 seconds at 43 seconds on the Modified 
Romberg Balance test—well within normal parameters (Exhibit A, 01:08:40–01:08:45). 
Critically, neither officer verbalized detecting any odor of alcohol from the Petitioner’s 
person or breath at any point during the encounter, as confirmed by the complete dashcam 
audio.
The arrest was triggered solely by the PAS refusal. The dashcam recording captures the 
critical exchange: Officer Meza-Gonzalez explicitly advised the Petitioner, “You’re not 
required to do this” (Exhibit A, 01:10:54), referring to the preliminary alcohol screening 
test. When the Petitioner exercised his lawful right to decline, Meza-Gonzalez immediately 
placed him under arrest. (Exhibit A, 01:11:15–01:11:33.) An arrest based solely on the 
exercise of a right the officer explicitly acknowledged was voluntary constitutes false 
imprisonment.
CHP itself admitted the arrest was unjustified. The Detention Certificate (Exhibit C) 
officially recharacterizes the incident as “a detention only, not an arrest” and certifies 
“insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint.” No criminal charges were ever 
filed. This is CHP’s own contemporaneous determination that the Petitioner was restrained 
without lawful justification.
B.
Felonious Assault / Battery (Cal. Penal Code § 242)
Battery under California law is any willful and unlawful use of force or violence upon the 
person of another. Cal. Penal Code § 242. The Petitioner was subjected to two distinct batteries:
Forcible handcuffing without probable cause. At 01:11:33, Officer Meza-Gonzalez 
placed handcuffs on the Petitioner and transported him to the CHP Dublin Area Office. 
(Exhibit A, 01:11:33; Exhibit B, p. 5.) Because the arrest itself was without probable cause
—as CHP later conceded—the physical restraint constitutes an unlawful application of 
force.
Involuntary blood draw via misrepresented warrant. After the Petitioner exercised his 
right to refuse chemical testing, Officer Melano told him: “If you don’t do it we’re gonna 
get it anyways” (Exhibit A, 01:37:36). A warrant was obtained based on the fabricated CHP 
report, and at approximately 0238 hours, phlebotomist Aziza Ghaleb extracted two vials of 
blood from the Petitioner’s right arm at the CHP Dublin Area Office. (Exhibit B, p. 5.) 
Because the warrant was procured through material misrepresentations in the sworn report
—specifically, the fabricated “strong distinct odor of an alcoholic beverage” that the 
dashcam proves was never observed—the blood draw constitutes a forcible bodily 
intrusion based on fraudulent process.
C.
Obstruction of Justice / Fabrication of Evidence
Obstruction of justice is an enumerated qualifying crime under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)
(iii). The evidence of fabrication is extensive and directly provable through a comparison of the 
CHP report (Exhibit B) against the dashcam transcript (Exhibit A):
- 3 -

Fabrication #1: “Strong distinct odor of an alcoholic beverage.” The CHP report states 
that Officer Meza-Gonzalez “could smell the distinct odor of an alcoholic beverage 
emitting from within the vehicle” and “from Newanforbi’s breath and person.” (Exhibit B, 
pp. 4–5.) The dashcam transcript contains no contemporaneous verbalization of any 
alcohol odor at any point. The only odor discussed by either officer during the encounter 
was the odor of urine from the cup. (Exhibit A, 00:58:51–00:59:04.) This is not a matter of 
interpretation—it is a direct, provable contradiction between a sworn written statement and 
the objective audio recording.
Fabrication #2: “Slurred” speech. The CHP report characterizes the Petitioner’s speech 
as “Slurred.” (Exhibit B, p. 2.) The dashcam audio recording captures the Petitioner 
speaking coherently and articulately throughout the encounter. He identifies his location, 
reads distant highway signs, explains his professional background, and engages in 
extended, fluent conversation with both officers. The audio flatly contradicts the “slurred” 
characterization.
Fabrication #3: The Petitioner “seemed very confused and disoriented.” The CHP 
report describes the Petitioner as “very confused and disoriented.” (Exhibit B, p. 4.) The 
dashcam shows the Petitioner correctly identifying his location as Livermore (Exhibit A, 
01:00:41), accurately reading highway signs (Exhibit A, 01:00:44), explaining his origin 
(Oakland) and destination (Stockton), and providing a coherent account of his professional 
practices as a CDL holder. (Exhibit A, 01:01:21–01:01:56.)
Fabrication #4: “Beverage present: Yes.” The CHP report checks “BEVERAGE 
PRESENT: YES” (Exhibit B, p. 2), directly implying an alcoholic beverage was found in 
the vehicle. In fact, the only liquid found was the cup of urine, which Officer Melano 
definitively identified as such on the dashcam. No alcoholic beverage container was found 
containing alcohol—the “Mike’s Hard Lemonade” can referenced at 01:00:09 was 
described as empty, and the Petitioner denied consuming it.
These fabrications are not minor discrepancies—they are the material misrepresentations 
upon which the entire arrest, the warrant for the involuntary blood draw, the parole hold, the 
booking at Santa Rita Jail, and the DMV suspension were predicated. They were made under 
penalty of perjury in a sworn law enforcement report. The dashcam evidence in CHP’s own 
custody proves they are false.
D.
Perjury (Cal. Penal Code § 118)
The sworn statements in the CHP 202 report (Exhibit B) that are contradicted by the 
dashcam recording (Exhibit A) independently constitute perjury under California Penal Code § 
118. Officer Meza-Gonzalez’s report was prepared under penalty of perjury and submitted to 
secure a search warrant from a magistrate. The false statements regarding the odor of alcohol, the 
Petitioner’s speech, and his demeanor were material—they formed the factual predicate for the 
warrant, the arrest, and all subsequent proceedings.
IV.
ELEMENT TWO: PETITIONER POSSESSES INFORMATION CONCERNING 
THE CRIMINAL ACTIVITY
- 4 -

The Petitioner is the direct victim and the sole civilian percipient witness to every aspect of 
the qualifying criminal activity. He possesses:
Firsthand knowledge of the entire encounter, from initial contact through booking at Santa 
Rita Jail; the dashcam transcript (Exhibit A), which he obtained, authenticated, and 
produced—constituting the objective evidence that proves the fabrications in the CHP 
report; the CHP arrest report (Exhibit B), the Detention Certificate (Exhibit C), and the 
DMV records (Exhibit G), all of which he has analyzed, preserved, and made available to 
CHP and other investigating entities; and a detailed sworn declaration (Exhibit D) setting 
forth the full scope of physical and mental harms sustained.
This element is satisfied beyond any reasonable question. The Petitioner is not merely a 
passive victim—he is the individual who identified, preserved, and produced the key exculpatory 
evidence (the dashcam transcript) that proves the criminal activity occurred.
V.
ELEMENT THREE: PETITIONER HAS BEEN, IS BEING, AND IS LIKELY TO 
BE HELPFUL
The helpfulness requirement under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(i)(III) and California Penal 
Code § 679.10(b) is broadly construed. The Petitioner’s cooperation is extensive and ongoing:
(1) Filing of the CHP Citizen Complaint. Petitioner filed the citizen complaint that 
initiated CHP File No. 390.18437.17620—the very investigation Sergeant Dutra has been 
assigned to conduct. Without this complaint, there would be no investigation.
(2) POST Complaint. Petitioner filed a separate complaint with the Commission on Peace 
Officer Standards and Training, which was forwarded to CHP on March 23, 2026, under 
Case No. PUBLIC-26-000371. This expanded the investigative record available to CHP.
(3) Preservation and Production of the Dashcam Transcript. Petitioner obtained, 
transcribed, and produced the complete CHP dashcam recording (Exhibit A)—the single 
most important piece of evidence proving the criminal activity. This evidence is in CHP’s 
own custody but would not have been meaningfully analyzed or compared against the 
officers’ report without the Petitioner’s initiative.
(4) DMV Administrative Proceedings. Petitioner participated in the DMV APS hearing 
on January 24, 2025, preserving his rights under penalty of perjury and creating an 
additional official record of the incident.
(5) Government Tort Claim. Petitioner filed a sworn government tort claim with the 
California Department of General Services within the statutory period, initiating formal 
investigation of the officers’ conduct at the state level.
(6) No Refusal to Cooperate. At no point has the Petitioner refused or failed to provide 
information or assistance reasonably requested by any investigating entity. Under 
California Penal Code § 679.10(h), this creates a rebuttable presumption that the Petitioner 
is helpful.

VI.
SUBSTANTIAL PHYSICAL AND MENTAL ABUSE
While the “substantial physical or mental abuse” determination is ultimately made by 
USCIS—not the certifying official—the evidentiary record before CHP confirms the severity of 
the harm, which contextualizes the certification:
Physical harm: Forcible handcuffing and an involuntary blood draw (two vials extracted 
from the right arm by phlebotomist Aziza Ghaleb at the CHP Dublin Area Office). (Exhibit 
B, p. 5.)
Extended detention: Following the false arrest, a parole hold was instituted based on the 
fabricated report, extending the Petitioner’s detention from the initial arrest through 
booking at Santa Rita Jail, where he was held from Friday until the following Wednesday 
without arraignment. (Exhibit D, ¶ 5.) During this period, the Petitioner was confined with 
individuals accused of violent crimes including homicide, creating conditions he feared for 
his personal safety. (Exhibit D, ¶ 5.)
Complete loss of livelihood: The false arrest report triggered DMV administrative 
suspension proceedings. Following the APS hearing on January 24, 2025, the Petitioner’s 
Class A commercial driving license was suspended for one full year (February 20, 2025 
through February 19, 2026), disqualifying him from commercial driving. (Exhibit G.) The 
pay stubs (Exhibit E) document that the Petitioner was earning between approximately 
$900 and $2,800 per week as a commercial truck driver in the months before the incident. 
The Petitioner estimates total lost wages during the suspension period at approximately 
$112,000. (Exhibit D, ¶ 4.)
Severe emotional distress: The Petitioner’s sworn declaration details ongoing anxiety, 
panic attacks, flashbacks, a deteriorated sense of self-worth, humiliation in his spiritual and 
social community, and strained family relationships. (Exhibit D, ¶¶ 6–10.)
VII.
THE CRITICAL DASHCAM-TO-REPORT CONTRADICTIONS: A SIDE-BY-
SIDE ANALYSIS
Because the fabrication evidence is the foundation of the obstruction of justice and perjury 
elements, the following side-by-side comparison is provided for the certifying official’s 
convenience:
1. Odor of Alcohol
CHP Report (Exhibit B, p. 4): “I could smell the distinct odor of an alcoholic beverage 
emitting from within the vehicle.” Also: “the strong distinct odor of an alcoholic beverage 
coming from Newanforbi’s breath and person.”
Dashcam (Exhibit A): Neither officer verbalizes detecting any odor of alcohol at any point 
during the encounter. The only odor discussed is urine from the cup. (00:58:51–00:59:04.) 
Melano’s later comment about sanitizing gloves references “piss everywhere”—not 
alcohol. (01:23:26.)
2. Speech

CHP Report (Exhibit B, p. 2): Characterizes Petitioner’s speech as “Slurred.”
Dashcam (Exhibit A): Audio captures the Petitioner speaking coherently throughout. He 
spells his last name on request (“N-E-W-W-A-N-F-O-R-B-I” at 00:59:57), discusses 
alternator mechanics with officers (01:44:21–01:45:37), and engages in extended articulate 
conversation about his CDL training and truck driving practices (01:01:21–01:01:56).
3. Demeanor / Orientation
CHP Report (Exhibit B, p. 4): Claims Petitioner “seemed very confused and disoriented.”
Dashcam (Exhibit A): Petitioner correctly identifies his location as Livermore (01:00:41); 
reads distant highway signs (“Isabella Avenue, Portola Avenue” at 01:00:44); knows his 
origin (Oakland), destination (Stockton), and route; and provides a cogent explanation of

4. Beverage Present
CHP Report (Exhibit B, p. 2): Checks “BEVERAGE PRESENT: YES.”
Dashcam (Exhibit A): The only liquid found was urine in a cup. An empty Mike’s Hard

observed it to contain any liquid.
VIII.
THE LEGAL STANDARD FOR CERTIFICATION
California Penal Code § 679.10 imposes a mandatory obligation on CHP as a state law 
enforcement certifying entity. The statute requires certification when three elements are met: (1) 
the petitioner was a victim of a qualifying crime; (2) the petitioner possesses information 
concerning the criminal activity; and (3) the petitioner has been helpful, is being helpful, or is likely 
to be helpful in the detection, investigation, or prosecution of the criminal activity. All three are 
satisfied here, as demonstrated above.
The following legal points are emphasized for the certifying official’s consideration:
No prosecution or conviction is required. Section 679.10(k) provides that “[a] current 
investigation, the filing of charges, closing of a case, and a prosecution or conviction are not 
required for the victim to request and obtain the Form I-918 Supplement B certification.” 
The fact that CHP declined to file charges against the Petitioner—and indeed conceded the 
arrest was unjustified—is irrelevant to the certification determination. What matters is 
whether the officers’ conduct constituted qualifying criminal activity against the Petitioner.
Helpfulness is presumed. Section 679.10(h) creates “a rebuttable presumption that the 
victim is helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to be helpful” if the victim has not refused or 
failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested. The Petitioner has never 
refused any request for cooperation.
Certification must be processed within 30 days. Section 679.10(j) requires the certifying 
entity to process this request within 30 days of receipt.
- 7 -

Denial must be in writing with specific reasons. If CHP determines it cannot certify, § 
679.10(g) requires a “written explanation of the specific reasons for the denial.” A 
generalized or conclusory refusal does not satisfy this statutory obligation.
Signing the certification does not grant a visa. The Form I-918 Supplement B is a factual 
certification, not an immigration decision. USCIS independently adjudicates the petition, 
conducts a full background check, and makes all eligibility determinations. The certifying 
official’s signature carries no immigration consequences standing alone and does not 
prejudice any ongoing investigation. As the DHS U Visa Law Enforcement Resource 
Guide makes clear, the certification is simply a statement by the certifying official that, 
based on the facts known to the agency, the petitioner is or was a victim of qualifying 
criminal activity and has been helpful.
IX.
CONCLUSION
The evidentiary record before CHP is overwhelming and largely self-proving. The 
dashcam recording—CHP’s own evidence—establishes that Officers Meza-Gonzalez and Melano 
subjected the Petitioner to false imprisonment, felonious assault, and obstruction of justice on 
November 1, 2024. CHP’s own Detention Certificate confirms the arrest lacked justification. The 
Petitioner has cooperated extensively with every available investigative channel and has never 
refused any request for assistance.
Every statutory element for U visa certification is satisfied. The Petitioner respectfully 
requests that Sergeant Dutra, as the designated certifying official, review the enclosed Form I-918 
Supplement B and the supporting evidence, and execute the certification in accordance with 
California Penal Code § 679.10 and 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U).

The purpose of this bulletin is to update information provided in Information Bulletin 2020‐DLE‐01, dated 
April 1, 2020, titled “Update to Information Bulletin No. 2015‐DLE‐04: New and Existing State and Federal 
Laws Protecting Immigrant Victims of Crime.” Information Bulletin 2020‐DLE‐01 offered a detailed summary 
of a then new state law, Assembly Bill (AB) 917 (Stats. 2019, Ch. 576), enacted into law and effective on 
January 1, 2020, which required agencies that investigate or prosecute criminal matters to assist crime 
victims without authorized immigration status in applying for a U nonimmigrant visa (U visa) – a federal 
immigration visa set aside for victims of crime who have suffered substantial mental or physical abuse 
because of criminal activity, and who are willing to assist federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies 
or government officials in the investigation of that criminal activity.1 
On October 10, 2023, Governor Gavin Newsom signed the Immigrant Rights Act, Assembly Bill (AB) 1261 
(Stats. 2023, Ch. 679), into law, effective on January 1, 2024. AB 1261 provides additional affirmative 
obligations for law enforcement officials when responding to requests for U visa certifications. The United 
States Department of Homeland Security, United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) 
requires these certifications in order to grant a qualifying immigrant a U visa. 
In addition to providing guidance on the newly enacted AB 1261 this bulletin answers relevant questions 
regarding U Visa eligibility, and encourages state and local law enforcement agencies and officials to be 
vigilant in identifying and supporting immigrant crime victims who may be eligible for U visas. These visas 
are an important tool for encouraging the cooperation of witnesses; investigating, prosecuting, and 
convicting criminals; and increasing public safety. 
California Law Regulating U Visa Certifications by Law Enforcement—Effective January 1, 2024 
AB 1261 amends California Penal Code sections 679.10 and 679.11 and adds section 679.13 to the Penal 
Code. Significantly, the amendments require that certifying state and local agencies and officials: 
 Complete U visa certifications, upon request, for direct victims, indirect victims, and bystander or 
witness victims.

Questions and Answers Regarding U Visa Certifications 
1. Who is eligible for a U visa? 
Eligibility for U visas is governed by the Victims of Trafficking and Violence Protection Act (VTVPA) and 
determined by USCIS. Under those federal provisions, individuals without authorized immigrant status may 
be eligible for a U visa if they: (1) are victims of specified qualifying crimes (discussed below), (2) have 
suffered substantial physical or mental abuse as a result of having been a victim of criminal activity, (3) have 
specific knowledge and details of a qualifying crime committed within the United States, (4) are currently 
assisting, have previously assisted, or are likely to be helpful in the detection, investigation, or prosecution 
of the qualifying crime; and (5) are admissible to the United States, and if they are not admissible, they may 
apply for a waiver of inadmissibility. Victims may apply for a U visa even if they are no longer in the United 
States. Individuals presently in removal proceedings or with final orders of removal can also apply.

2. What is a qualifying crime? 
Under the relevant state and federal laws, qualifying crimes include rape, torture, human trafficking, incest, 
domestic violence (including violations of domestic violence restraining orders), sexual assault, abusive 
sexual conduct, prostitution, sexual exploitation, female genital mutilation, being held hostage, peonage, 
perjury, involuntary servitude, slavery, kidnaping, abduction, unlawful criminal restraint, false 
imprisonment, blackmail, extortion, manslaughter, murder, felonious assault, witness tampering, 
obstruction of justice, fraud in foreign labor contracting, stalking, and other related crimes which include 
any similar activity where the elements of the crime are substantially similar to the above specified 
offenses. 
California law, consistent with federal law, states that a qualifying crime includes the attempt, 
conspiracy, or solicitation to commit any of the specified and other related offenses. 
Bystanders who suffer unusually direct injury as a result of a qualifying crime may be considered eligible 
victims as well. An example provided by USCIS includes a pregnant woman who suffered a miscarriage as a 
result of trauma she experienced witnessing a violent crime.3 
3. Is an arrest, prosecution, or conviction necessary to certify a U visa petition? 
No. California’s Immigrant Victims of Crime Equity Act makes clear that a current investigation, the filing of 
charges, and a prosecution or conviction are not required to sign the law enforcement certification. Many 
situations exist where an immigrant victim reports a crime, but an arrest or prosecution cannot take place 
due to evidentiary or other circumstances. For example, the perpetrator may have fled the jurisdiction, 
cannot be identified, or has been deported by federal law enforcement officials. In addition, neither a plea 
agreement nor a dismissal of a criminal case affects a victim’s eligibility. Furthermore, a law enforcement 
certification is valid regardless of whether the crime that is eventually prosecuted is different from the 
crime that was investigated, as long as the individual is a victim of a qualifying crime and meets the other 
requirements for U visa eligibility.

3 Preamble at Federal Register, Vol. 72, No. 179, p. 53016‐53017 (Sept. 17, 2017).

Update to Information Bulletin 2020‐DLE‐01 
Page 5 
4. Can an agency deny a U visa certification request based on timeliness? 
No. There is no statute of limitations that bars immigrant crime victims from applying for a U visa. Law 
enforcement agencies’ duty to sign a certification is not time‐limited, even if the investigation or case is 
already closed. 
5. Will certifying a U visa petition automatically grant the victim an immigration benefit? 
No. Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies cannot legally grant or guarantee an immigrant 
crime victim a U visa or any other type of immigration status by signing a U visa certification (Form I‐918 
Supplement B). Instead, U visa petitions are adjudicated by USCIS, which conducts a full review of the 
victim’s petition and a thorough background check of the petitioner before approving or denying the 
petition. USCIS will also make the determination as to whether the victim has met the “substantial physical 
or mental abuse” standard on a case‐by‐case basis during its adjudication of the petition. Additionally, 
USCIS makes the determination of the applicant’s admissibility to the United States or eligibility for a waiver 
of inadmissibility. 
By signing a certification, the law enforcement official states: (1) under penalty of perjury, that the 
individual is or has been a victim of one of the qualifying crimes, and (2) the remaining information provided 
in the certification is true and correct to the best of the certifying official’s knowledge. Without a 
completed U visa certification, victims will not be eligible for a U visa. 
6. If a certifying agency denies a U visa certification request, what information must the agency 
provide? 
There is a rebuttable presumption that a victim is helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to be helpful, if the 
victim has not refused or failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested by law 
enforcement. To comply with the rebuttable presumption of helpfulness in the VTVPA, the reason for denial 
of certification should be clearly articulated and specific (i.e., non‐cooperative because of three unreturned 
phone calls on dates X, Y, and Z). Further, any denials of certification should be based upon issues within a 
particular law enforcement agency’s jurisdiction/investigation; each law enforcement agency should focus 
exclusively on its investigation to determine cooperation and should make a determination based on its 
investigation regardless of whether there is an investigation, referral, and/or prosecution by another law 
enforcement agency. 
Recommendations and Additional Resources for Law Enforcement 
Attorney General Rob Bonta is committed to seeking justice for every crime victim in California regardless of 
the victim’s immigration status. Undocumented immigrants are often among the most vulnerable victims of 
crime across California. Fear of deportation is a significant deterrent to reporting crime for many 
undocumented immigrants. As such, the Attorney General encourages all agencies and officials subject to 
California’s new law to immediately establish and implement a U visa certification policy and protocol that 
is consistent with California law and the guidance provided in this law enforcement bulletin. As such, a U 
visa certification policy and protocol may address the following:

1. Ensuring decisions are made as soon as possible within the 30‐day or 7‐day windows, especially in 
urgent cases (i.e., where a qualifying family member will otherwise lose eligibility). 
2. An appeals process for certification denials through which (1) an individual other than the initial 
supervisor that approved the “denial” reviews the certification to ensure impartiality and (2) the 
appeals process is made public to provide transparency. 
3. A review of the entire police report and file to independently consider whether or not all potential 
victims are eligible for certification (i.e., some police reports do not always list all potential victims 
and sometimes categorize victims as witnesses). 
4. Signing single‐sided I‐918B U Visa Certification forms with a signature and date clearly written in 
blue ink, and providing the original signature to the requestor. 
5. A consistent way of handling when parents of minors under 16 years of age have effectively 
cooperated with law enforcement by making the minor available to law enforcement or encouraged 
the minor’s cooperation with law enforcement, and may also be eligible for obtaining certification if 
they have also cooperated with law enforcement in the investigation of the crime(s). 
The USCIS web site includes useful information regarding U visa eligibility, qualifying criminal activities, and 
applying for a U visa. See https://www.uscis.gov/humanitarian/victims‐of‐criminal‐activity‐u‐nonimmigrant­
status. The Form I‐918 Supplement B Certification can be found here: http://www.uscis.gov/i‐918. 
We look forward to working with you to ensure that California continues to set an example across the 
nation for building and preserving the relationship of trust between our peace officers and the communities 
we are sworn to serve, including immigrant communities.

Exhibit A. Respondent's demurrer argues that Petitioner's factual allegations are

Penal Code section 679.10, subdivision (i)(2), which is squarely at issue on the demurrer to the

LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
AB 1261, Santiago. Crime: witnesses and informants.
Existing state law requires, upon request by specified persons, that a certifying official from a
certifying entity, as defined, certify “victim helpfulness” or “victim cooperation” on specified federal
supplemental forms relating to immigration when the person was a victim of a qualifying criminal
activity or human trafficking, and has, is, or is likely to be helpful or cooperative regarding the
investigation or prosecution of that qualifying criminal activity, as specified.
This bill would specify that a person submitting those forms does not have to be present in the
United States at the time of filing, and would require the certifying entity to forward the form to the
victim or other specified individuals without requiring the victim to provide government-issued
identification. The bill would require a certifying entity that does not certify the form regarding
“victim helpfulness” to provide a written explanation for the denial of the certification. The bill
would require a certifying entity to certify that form for direct victims, indirect victims, and
bystander or witness victims, as specified. The bill would prohibit a certifying entity from refusing to
complete either of those forms for specified reasons, including, among others, the informant’s
criminal history information or immigration history. The bill would require the certifying entities to
process those forms within 7 days if the victim asserts a qualifying family member of the victim will
lose eligibility for specified immigration statuses within 60 days. By imposing additional duties on
local law enforcement, this bill would impose a state-mandated local program.
Existing federal law provides a petition form to request temporary immigration benefits for a person
who is a witness or informant, as specified.
This bill would authorize a certifying official from a certifying entity, as defined, to certify that a

person is a witness or informant on that federal petition form when the person is an informant with
reliable information about an important aspect of a crime or pending commission of a crime, the
person is willing to share that information with law enforcement officials or become a witness in
court, and the person’s presence in the United States is important and leads to the successful
investigation or prosecution of that crime.
The California Constitution requires the state to reimburse local agencies and school districts for
certain costs mandated by the state. Statutory provisions establish procedures for making that
reimbursement.

costs mandated by the state, reimbursement for those costs shall be made pursuant to the statutory
provisions noted above.

If you are serving a domestic violence, elder abuse, or gun violence restraining order. 
If you have a civil harassment, workplace violence, or school violence restraining order based on a credible threat of
violence or stalking.
Give this form and a copy of all the court papers you need served to the sheriff or marshal, including a copy of a fee 
waiver (if you have one). You can turn in your papers in person or send them electronically. 
You should get a form back from the sheriff. 
If the sheriff was able to serve your court papers, you should receive a form (called a proof of service). Make sure 
you get a copy from the sheriff and file it with the court. Note that if there is a court stamp at the top right corner 
of the first page, it has already been filed and you do not need to file it with the court. 
If the sheriff was unable to serve your court papers, you should receive a form (sometimes called declaration of due 
diligence) that tells you that service was unsuccessful and will give details about when the sheriff tried to serve the 
person. If the sheriff was unable to serve your papers, you can ask a lawyer or court’s self-help center about your 
next steps.
To find your local court self-help center, go to selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/. Self-help center staff will not act as your lawyer 
but may be able to give you information to help you decide what to do in your case. Services are free.

Any order submitted does not have a judge’s signature or other representation of a judge’s signature; clerk’s

MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES 
Respondent Gerardo Serrato (“Capt. Serrato”) joins in Respondent California Highway 
Patrol’s (“CHP”) Demurrer to the Petition for Writ of Mandate as to all causes of action in the 
petition on the ground that the petition does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of 
action.  (See Code Civ. Proc. § 430.10, subd. (e).)   
Specifically, CHP demurs to the Petition for these reasons:  (1) CHP possesses no 
ministerial duty to certify Petitioner’s Form I-918, Supplement B, U Nonimmigrant Status 
Certification (“Form B”) (see CHP’s Demurrer at 11-13); (2) Petitioner has no clear, present and 
beneficial right to the performance of a ministerial duty (see CHP’s Demurrer at 13-15); (3) CHP 
has no ministerial duty to provide a written explanation for its certification denial in the form 
demanded by Petitioner (see CHP Demurrer at 15-16); (4) the rebuttable presumption of 
helpfulness is not applicable on the facts alleged (see CHP’s Demurrer at 16-17); and (5) 
Petitioner is not entitled to his requested declaratory relief because he seeks advisory opinions on 
purely legal questions, declaratory relief cannot unwind a past administrative decision, and 
because Petitioner is not entitled to a writ of ordinary mandate, mooting the declaration Petitioner 
seeks (see CHP’s Demurrer at 17-20).  
These reasons are relevant to Capt. Serrato’s defenses and demurrer because the basis for 
Petitioner’s requested relief, as articulated in his petition, is the same as to all Respondents, 
including the individual Respondents.  Further, the relief sought by CHP would benefit Capt. 
Serrato, as Petitioner alleges that Capt. Serrato is a “certifying official” within the meaning of 
Penal Code section 679.10(b) and has attached to his petition the certification denial letter signed 
by Capt. Serrato.  For these reasons, Capt. Serrato joins CHP’s demurrer to the Petition for Writ 
of Mandate as to all causes of action in the petition, and adopts the points and authorities filed in 
support of CHP’s Demurrer. 
Capt. Serrato therefore respectfully requests that the Court sustain his demurrer without 
leave to amend.

California. Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi, a commercial truck driver holding a Class A

Case No. RJ68845) -- the officers opened the vehicle without consent or warrant, identified the

initial suspicion had dissipated, arrested Plaintiff within eighteen seconds of his exercise of the
statutory right to decline a voluntary preliminary alcohol screening test, and then generated sworn
statements containing material representations that are contradicted by the same recording in the
CHP's own custody.
2. After the arrest, Officer Meza-Gonzalez executed under penalty of perjury a DS-367
Officer's Statement and a CHP Arrest-Investigation Report, both of which were used to obtain a
blood-draw warrant from a magistrate, to initiate a one-year administrative suspension of
Plaintiff's commercial driving privileges, and to refer criminal charges to the Alameda County
District Attorney. The DS-367 and arrest report contain at least four representations that are
materially contradicted by the dashcam recording: a claimed "strong distinct odor of an alcoholic
beverage" that neither officer ever verbalizes on the recording; a characterization of Plaintiff's
speech as "slurred" when the recording captures extended coherent conversation; a claim that
Plaintiff was "very confused and disoriented" when the recording shows him correctly identifying
his location and reading distant signage; and a checked box for "Beverage Present: Yes" when the
only liquid the officers found was, in Officer Melano's own contemporaneous words on the
recording, "piss." Four days later, CHP itself issued a Penal Code section 851.6 Detention
Certificate reclassifying the event as "a detention only, not an arrest" for "insufficient grounds."
The Alameda County District Attorney declined to file any charges.
3. Plaintiff brings five claims against Defendants in their individual capacities: judicial
deception in support of a blood-draw warrant; deliberate fabrication of evidence; unlawful arrest
without probable cause; unlawful warrantless entry into a private vehicle; and unlawful search.

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. Plaintiff Was Lawfully Parked and Asleep
11. On the evening of October 31, 2024, and into the early hours of November 1, 2024,
Plaintiff was driving a rented gray Tesla Model Y eastbound on Interstate 580. Feeling fatigued,
he exited active travel lanes and parked on the right shoulder just west of the Isabel Avenue exit
in Livermore, Alameda County. He then rested in the driver's seat. He was not driving. No officer
observed him in volitional movement of the vehicle.
12. Plaintiff is a professional commercial truck driver. Pulling off the road to rest when
fatigued is consistent with federal Hours-of-Service principles and with CHP's own public safety
guidance to drowsy motorists.
B. The Officers' Pre-Contact Hypothesis
13. At approximately 00:54:36, the CHP patrol vehicle's dashcam recording activated as it
came to a stop behind Plaintiff's parked Tesla. The recording ran continuously through
approximately 01:57:10, capturing the entirety of the encounter.

evidence, no hot pursuit -- was present or articulated. The door was opened because Officer

screening ("PAS") test was voluntary: "You're not required to do this." That advisement is legally
accurate. Under California Vehicle Code section 23612(i), a PAS is a preliminary investigative

containing statements that are deliberately or recklessly false, or that omit material facts, if the
application -- stripped of the false statements and supplemented with the omitted facts -- would
not support probable cause. Franks v. Delaware, 438 U.S. 154, 155-56 (1978); Chism v.

Santa Clara, 307 F.3d 1119, 1126 (9th Cir. 2002).

(42 U.S.C. § 1983 -- Against Defendant Melano and DOES 1-10)
53. Plaintiff re-alleges paragraphs 1 through 36.
54. A warrantless entry into a constitutionally protected area is presumptively
unreasonable absent consent or a recognized exception. Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573,
585-90 (1980); Collins v. Virginia, 584 U.S. 586, 592-93 (2018). The interior of a passenger
vehicle is a constitutionally protected area.
55. At 00:56:43, Defendant Melano opened the front passenger-side door of Plaintiff's
vehicle while Plaintiff was asleep. No consent was given. No warrant existed. No exigent
circumstance was present. The officers' own words on the recording preceding the entry ("It's a
rental," "It wasn't here earlier," "I think it's booze") reflect investigative interest, not a response to
an observable medical emergency. Even if a welfare rationale had been present, the community
caretaking exception does not authorize warrantless entry absent an imminent threat to safety.
Caniglia v. Strom, 593 U.S. 194, 197-99 (2021).
56. The right to be free from warrantless entry into a vehicle absent consent, exigency, or
an applicable exception was clearly established before November 1, 2024. Payton, 445 U.S. at
585-90; Collins, 584 U.S. at 592-93; Caniglia, 593 U.S. at 197-99.

paragraphs 35-36.

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. Plaintiff Was Lawfully Parked and Asleep
11. On the evening of October 31, 2024, and into the early hours of November 1, 2024,
Plaintiff was driving a rented gray Tesla Model Y eastbound on Interstate 580. Feeling fatigued,
he exited active travel lanes and parked on the right shoulder just west of the Isabel Avenue exit
in Livermore, Alameda County. He then rested in the driver's seat. He was not driving. No officer
observed him in volitional movement of the vehicle.
12. Plaintiff is a professional commercial truck driver. Pulling off the road to rest when
fatigued is consistent with federal Hours-of-Service principles and with CHP's own public safety
guidance to drowsy motorists.
B. The Officers' Pre-Contact Hypothesis
13. At approximately 00:54:36, the CHP patrol vehicle's dashcam recording activated as it
came to a stop behind Plaintiff's parked Tesla. The recording ran continuously through
approximately 01:57:10, capturing the entirety of the encounter.

H. The Blood-Draw Warrant and Forced Extraction
29. Based on the DS-367 and arrest report, a magistrate authorized a warrant for the
involuntary extraction of Plaintiff's blood. Plaintiff was transported to the CHP Dublin Area
office, where a blood sample was forcibly drawn pursuant to that warrant. A compelled blood
draw is a significant bodily intrusion within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Missouri v.
McNeely, 569 U.S. 141, 148 (2013).
30. If the four contradicted representations identified in paragraph 26 are set aside, and if
the omitted facts identified in paragraph 27 are restored, the warrant application would have
reflected: a commercial driver parked and asleep on a highway shoulder; a cup identified by the
investigating officer as urine; coherent, oriented conversation; no verbalized alcohol odor; and
refusal of a test the officer had just described as voluntary. Whether those facts, standing alone,
would have supported probable cause for a blood-draw warrant is a question that should be
resolved on a developed record, not on the pleadings.

Jail in Dublin, California. A parole hold was placed based on the arrest report, extending
Plaintiff's custodial confinement beyond the initial arrest.
