Fourth Amendment -- Unlawful Warrantless Entry
(42 U.S.C. § 1983 -- Against Defendant Melano and DOES 1-10)
54. Plaintiff re-alleges paragraphs 1 through 37.
55. A warrantless entry into a constitutionally protected area is presumptively
unreasonable absent consent or a recognized exception. Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573,
585-90 (1980); Collins v. Virginia, 584 U.S. 586, 592-93 (2018). The interior of a passenger
vehicle is a constitutionally protected area.
56. At 00:56:43, Defendant Melano opened the front passenger-side door of Plaintiff's
vehicle while Plaintiff was asleep. No consent was given. No warrant existed. No exigent
circumstance was present. The officers' own words on the recording preceding the entry ("It's a
rental," "It wasn't here earlier," "I think it's booze") reflect investigative interest, not a response to
an observable medical emergency. Even if a welfare rationale had been present, the community
caretaking exception does not authorize warrantless entry absent an imminent threat to safety.
Caniglia v. Strom, 593 U.S. 194, 197-99 (2021).
57. The right to be free from warrantless entry into a vehicle absent consent, exigency, or

adverse action. See Nieves v. Bartlett, 587 U.S. 391, 398-99 (2019); Ballentine v. Tucker, 28

expressly non-mandatory constitutes constitutionally protected conduct. See Camara v. Municipal
Court, 387 U.S. 523, 528-33 (1967). Plaintiff's refusal of the PAS test -- a test that Officer
Meza-Gonzalez had just expressly advised was voluntary ("You're not required to do this" at
dashcam timestamp 01:10:54) -- was such an exercise, and refusal was itself a form of expressive
conduct communicating Plaintiff's non-consent to a discretionary investigative procedure.

Officer Meza-Gonzalez arrested Plaintiff. That temporal proximity, together with the absence on
the recording of any newly discovered probable cause between the moment of refusal and the

been. 587 U.S. at 407. Here, Plaintiff had refused an expressly voluntary investigative procedure

immunity shields government officials only where their conduct does not violate clearly

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 arising from an arrest on
November 1, 2024, on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California. Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi, a commercial truck driver holding a Class A

only cup in the vehicle as containing urine, continued the investigation after the basis for their
initial suspicion had dissipated, arrested Plaintiff within eighteen seconds of his exercise of the
statutory right to decline a voluntary preliminary alcohol screening test, and then generated sworn
statements containing material representations that are contradicted by the same recording in the
CHP's own custody.
2. After the arrest, Officer Meza-Gonzalez executed under penalty of perjury a DS-367
Officer's Statement and a CHP Arrest-Investigation Report, both of which were used to obtain a
blood-draw warrant from a magistrate, to initiate a one-year administrative suspension of
Plaintiff's commercial driving privileges, and to refer criminal charges to the Alameda County
District Attorney. The DS-367 and arrest report contain at least four representations that are
materially contradicted by the dashcam recording: a claimed "strong distinct odor of an alcoholic
beverage" that neither officer ever verbalizes on the recording; a characterization of Plaintiff's
speech as "slurred" when the recording captures extended coherent conversation; a claim that
Plaintiff was "very confused and disoriented" when the recording shows him correctly identifying
his location and reading distant signage; and a checked box for "Beverage Present: Yes" when the
only liquid the officers found was, in Officer Melano's own contemporaneous words on the
recording, "piss." Four days later, CHP itself issued a Penal Code section 851.6 Detention
Certificate reclassifying the event as "a detention only, not an arrest" for "insufficient grounds."
The Alameda County District Attorney declined to file any charges.
3. Plaintiff brings six claims against Defendants in their individual capacities: judicial
deception in support of a blood-draw warrant; deliberate fabrication of evidence; unlawful arrest
without probable cause; unlawful warrantless entry into a private vehicle; unlawful search; and

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. Plaintiff Was Lawfully Parked and Asleep
11. On the evening of October 31, 2024, and into the early hours of November 1, 2024,
Plaintiff was driving a rented gray Tesla Model Y eastbound on Interstate 580. Feeling fatigued,
he exited active travel lanes and parked on the right shoulder just west of the Isabel Avenue exit

observed him in volitional movement of the vehicle.
12. Plaintiff is a professional commercial truck driver. Pulling off the road to rest when
fatigued is consistent with federal Hours-of-Service principles and with CHP's own public safety
guidance to drowsy motorists.

came to a stop behind Plaintiff's parked Tesla. The recording ran continuously through

H. The Blood-Draw Warrant and Forced Extraction
29. Based on the DS-367 and arrest report, a magistrate authorized a warrant for the
involuntary extraction of Plaintiff's blood. Plaintiff was transported to the CHP Dublin Area
office, where a blood sample was forcibly drawn pursuant to that warrant. A compelled blood
draw is a significant bodily intrusion within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Missouri v.
McNeely, 569 U.S. 141, 148 (2013).
30. If the four contradicted representations identified in paragraph 26 are set aside, and if
the omitted facts identified in paragraph 27 are restored, the warrant application would have
reflected: a commercial driver parked and asleep on a highway shoulder; a cup identified by the
investigating officer as urine; coherent, oriented conversation; no verbalized alcohol odor; and
refusal of a test the officer had just described as voluntary. Whether those facts, standing alone,
would have supported probable cause for a blood-draw warrant is a question that should be

65. To state a First Amendment retaliation claim, a plaintiff must allege (i)
constitutionally protected activity; (ii) an adverse action; and (iii) a causal connection. Nieves v.
Bartlett, 587 U.S. 391, 398-99 (2019); Ballentine v. Tucker, 28 F.4th 54, 62 (9th Cir. 2022).
66. Plaintiff engaged in protected activity. Under California Vehicle Code section
23612(i), a PAS test is a voluntary investigative tool for drivers not on DUI probation. Refusal
carries no statutory consequence. Officer Meza-Gonzalez confirmed its voluntary nature at
timestamp 01:10:54: "You're not required to do this." The exercise of a statutory right to refuse a
voluntary investigative procedure is constitutionally protected conduct. Ballentine, 28 F.4th at 62;
Camara v. Municipal Court, 387 U.S. 523, 528-33 (1967).
67. Defendants took an adverse action. At timestamp 01:11:15, Plaintiff declined the PAS
test. Eighteen seconds later, at timestamp 01:11:33, Officer Meza-Gonzalez placed Plaintiff under
arrest. No new evidence of impairment was observed or articulated between the refusal and the
arrest.

seconds -- supports an inference of causation. That inference is reinforced by Officer
Meza-Gonzalez's own statement at timestamp 01:11:03, captured on the dashcam recording: "If

INTRODUCTION

November 1, 2024, on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California. Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi, a commercial truck driver holding a Class A

initial suspicion had dissipated, arrested Plaintiff within eighteen seconds of his exercise of the
statutory right to decline a voluntary preliminary alcohol screening test, and then generated sworn
statements containing material representations that are contradicted by the same recording in the
CHP's own custody.
2. After the arrest, Officer Meza-Gonzalez executed under penalty of perjury a DS-367
Officer's Statement and a CHP Arrest-Investigation Report, both of which were used to obtain a
blood-draw warrant from a magistrate, to initiate a one-year administrative suspension of
Plaintiff's commercial driving privileges, and to refer criminal charges to the Alameda County
District Attorney. The DS-367 and arrest report contain at least four representations that are
materially contradicted by the dashcam recording: a claimed "strong distinct odor of an alcoholic
beverage" that neither officer ever verbalizes on the recording; a characterization of Plaintiff's
speech as "slurred" when the recording captures extended coherent conversation; a claim that
Plaintiff was "very confused and disoriented" when the recording shows him correctly identifying
his location and reading distant signage; and a checked box for "Beverage Present: Yes" when the
only liquid the officers found was, in Officer Melano's own contemporaneous words on the
recording, "piss." Four days later, CHP itself issued a Penal Code section 851.6 Detention
Certificate reclassifying the event as "a detention only, not an arrest" for "insufficient grounds."
The Alameda County District Attorney declined to file any charges.
3. Plaintiff brings six claims against Defendants in their individual capacities: judicial
deception in support of a blood-draw warrant; deliberate fabrication of evidence; unlawful arrest
without probable cause; unlawful warrantless entry into a private vehicle; unlawful search; and

49. The Fourth Amendment requires probable cause for a warrantless arrest. Probable
cause exists when the facts and circumstances known to the officer at the time are sufficient for a
prudent person to believe that the suspect has committed a crime. Devenpeck v. Alford, 543 U.S.
146, 152 (2004).

certain FSTs due to ground conditions; and Plaintiff had exercised his statutory right under
Vehicle Code section 23612(i) to decline a voluntary PAS test. No new observation or evidence
intervened between the PAS refusal and the arrest. Plaintiff's exercise of the statutory right to
refuse the PAS test could not itself supply the probable cause that was otherwise absent. Thomas
v. Dillard, 818 F.3d 864, 884-85 (9th Cir. 2016) (refusal to consent to a search cannot create
reasonable suspicion or establish probable cause). Moreover, officers evaluating probable cause
may not disregard facts tending to dissipate it. Sialoi v. City of San Diego, 823 F.3d 1223, 1233

toy; applying United States v. Lopez, 482 F.3d 1067 (9th Cir. 2007)). Here, Officer Melano's
contemporaneous identification of the cup's contents as urine was a fact tending to dissipate the

voluntary investigative procedure is constitutionally protected conduct. Ballentine, 28 F.4th at 62;
Camara v. Municipal Court, 387 U.S. 523, 528-33 (1967).

test. Eighteen seconds later, at timestamp 01:11:33, Officer Meza-Gonzalez placed Plaintiff under

INSTRUCTIONS FOR ATTORNEYS COMPLETING CIVIL COVER SHEET FORM JS 44
Authority For Civil Cover Sheet
The JS 44 civil cover sheet and the information contained herein neither replaces nor supplements the filings and service of pleading or other papers as 
required by law, except as provided by local rules of court.  This form, approved by the Judicial Conference of the United States in September 1974, is 
required for the use of the Clerk of Court for the purpose of initiating the civil docket sheet.  Consequently, a civil cover sheet is submitted to the Clerk of 
Court for each civil complaint filed.  The attorney filing a case should complete the form as follows: 
I.(a) 
Plaintiffs-Defendants.  Enter names (last, first, middle initial) of plaintiff and defendant.  If the plaintiff or defendant is a government agency, use   
only the full name or standard abbreviations. If the plaintiff or defendant is an official within a government agency, identify first the agency and then 
the official, giving both name and title.
   (b)
County of Residence.  For each civil case filed, except U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county where the first listed plaintiff resides at the 
time of filing. In U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county in which the first listed defendant resides at the time of filing. (NOTE: In land 
condemnation cases, the county of residence of the "defendant" is the location of the tract of land involved.) 
   (c)
Attorneys.  Enter the firm name, address, telephone number, and attorney of record.  If there are several attorneys, list them on an attachment, noting  
in this section "(see attachment)". 
II.   
Jurisdiction.  The basis of jurisdiction is set forth under Rule 8(a), F.R.Cv.P., which requires that jurisdictions be shown in pleadings.  Place an "X" 
in one of the boxes. If there is more than one basis of jurisdiction, precedence is given in the order shown below. 
United States plaintiff.  (1) Jurisdiction based on 28 U.S.C. 1345 and 1348.  Suits by agencies and officers of the United States are included here. 
United States defendant.  (2) When the plaintiff is suing the United States, its officers or agencies, place an "X" in this box. 
Federal question.  (3) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1331, where jurisdiction arises under the Constitution of the United States, an amendment 
to the Constitution, an act of Congress or a treaty of the United States. In cases where the U.S. is a party, the U.S. plaintiff or defendant code takes 
precedence, and box 1 or 2 should be marked. 
Diversity of citizenship.  (4) This refers to suits under 28 U.S.C. 1332, where parties are citizens of different states.  When Box 4 is checked, the  
citizenship of the different parties must be checked.  (See Section III below; NOTE: federal question actions take precedence over diversity  
cases.) 
III.   
Residence (citizenship) of Principal Parties.  This section of the JS 44 is to be completed if diversity of citizenship was indicated above.  Mark this 
section for each principal party. 
IV. 
Nature of Suit.  Place an "X" in the appropriate box.  If there are multiple nature of suit codes associated with the case, pick the nature of suit code  
that is most applicable.  Click here for: Nature of Suit Code Descriptions. 
V.  
Origin.  Place an "X" in one of the seven boxes. 
Original Proceedings.  (1) Cases which originate in the United States district courts. 
Removed from State Court.  (2) Proceedings initiated in state courts may be removed to the district courts under Title 28 U.S.C., Section 1441.   
Remanded from Appellate Court.  (3) Check this box for cases remanded to the district court for further action.  Use the date of remand as the filing 
date. 
Reinstated or Reopened.  (4) Check this box for cases reinstated or reopened in the district court.  Use the reopening date as the filing date. 
Transferred from Another District.  (5) For cases transferred under Title 28 U.S.C. Section 1404(a).  Do not use this for within district transfers or
multidistrict litigation transfers. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Transfer.  (6) Check this box when a multidistrict case is transferred into the district under authority of Title 28 U.S.C. 
Section 1407. 
Multidistrict Litigation – Direct File.  (8) Check this box when a multidistrict case is filed in the same district as the Master MDL docket.  
PLEASE NOTE THAT THERE IS NOT AN ORIGIN CODE 7.  Origin Code 7 was used for historical records and is no longer relevant due to  
changes in statute. 
VI.  
Cause of Action.  Report the civil statute directly related to the cause of action and give a brief description of the cause.  Do not cite jurisdictional  
statutes unless diversity.  Example: U.S. Civil Statute: 47 USC 553 Brief Description: Unauthorized reception of cable service. 
VII.  
Requested in Complaint.  Class Action.  Place an "X" in this box if you are filing a class action under Rule 23, F.R.Cv.P. 
Demand.  In this space enter the actual dollar amount being demanded or indicate other demand, such as a preliminary injunction. 
Jury Demand.  Check the appropriate box to indicate whether or not a jury is being demanded. 
VIII.   Related Cases.  This section of the JS 44 is used to reference related cases, if any.  If there are related cases, insert the docket  
numbers and the corresponding judge names for such cases. 
Date and Attorney Signature.  Date and sign the civil cover sheet.

Commercial Driver's License (License No. F7953179, with doubles/triples and tank vehicle

2. The administrative record establishes an extraordinary result: the State destroyed
Plaintiff's livelihood on the basis of an arrest that the arresting agency itself formally repudiated
under Penal Code section 849(b)(1), through a hearing that refused to analyze binding California
Supreme Court authority, ignored objective audio-video evidence, and was presided over by a
decisionmaker who functioned as a prosecuting advocate rather than a neutral adjudicator. No
criminal accusatory pleading of any kind was ever filed. The Alameda County District Attorney
declined to prosecute. The California Highway Patrol ("CHP") formally reclassified the encounter
as "a detention only, not an arrest." Yet the DMV, through Defendant Candelaria in APS Case
No. 34739340, sustained a one-year Commercial Driver's License ("CDL") suspension on the
same arrest—and through Defendant Gordon, continues to enforce it.
3. Plaintiff, a law-abiding professional truck driver, made the responsible decision to rest
rather than drive while fatigued. He had commenced his employment with Centerline Drivers,
LLC on October 30, 2024—just two days before the November 1, 2024 CHP
encounter—assigned to the Lily Transportation/Toyota Dedicated route in San Ramon,
California, at a regular rate of $33.35 per hour and premium rate of $50.03 per hour. For his
decision to rest, Plaintiff lost his career through a process that ignored the law, the evidence, and
basic fairness. The DMV's actions have left him unemployed, unable to work in the only field for
which he is trained and credentialed, and suffering severe financial and emotional hardship. His
documented damages exceed $326,000 and continue to accrue daily.
4. Plaintiff continues to suffer irreparable harm each day the suspension remains in effect.

(a) On November 1, 2024, at approximately 12:55 a.m., Plaintiff was asleep in the

(b) CHP Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez (Badge No. 023295) and Jose Melano

C. The Arrest Was Statutorily Unauthorized Under Mercer v. DMV
19. Under California Penal Code section 836(a)(1), a warrantless misdemeanor arrest
requires that the offense be committed in the officer's presence. No officer observed Plaintiff
driving. Plaintiff was asleep in a stationary vehicle, engine off, keys out of the ignition.
20. Officer Meza-Gonzalez cited CVC section 40300.5 as authority to arrest without
observing driving. No statutory exception applied: there was no accident; Plaintiff posed no flight
risk; there was no imminent destruction of evidence; and the vehicle was parked entirely on the
unpaved dirt shoulder, not a "roadway" within the meaning of CVC section 530. The CHP's own
arrest report describes the location of the field evaluation as "Dirt shoulder."
21. The California Supreme Court adjudicated this precise scenario in Mercer v.
Department of Motor Vehicles, 53 Cal.3d 753, 760–762 (1991), holding that a warrantless DUI
arrest under CVC section 40300.5 is unlawful where the vehicle was not observed in "volitional
movement" and was parked off the traveled roadway. Under Mercer, the arrest of Plaintiff was
unlawful at its inception.

E. The Refusal Suspension Cannot Stand Absent a Lawful Arrest
27. The APS suspension imposed on Plaintiff was a refusal suspension under California
Vehicle Code section 13353, not a chemical-test result suspension under section 13353.2.
Defendant Candelaria's Notification of Findings and Decision is expressly captioned
"ADMINISTRATIVE PER SE - .08% BAC Refusal," and the decision's "Admonition and
Refusal" section sustains the suspension on the ground that Plaintiff "refused to voluntarily

CVC section 13353(a)(1), by its own text, predicates a refusal suspension on the driver having

or 23154." The lawful-arrest predicate is not a technicality; it is the statutory foundation of the
refusal-suspension scheme. (See Music v. Department of Motor Vehicles, 221 Cal.App.3d 841,
850 (1990) [refusal suspension requires lawful arrest]; Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d at 760–762

respondent—embeds the structural defect that the California Court of Appeal has by now held
unconstitutional on three separate occasions. The notice's next-sentence disclaimer, that the

2024), the Fifth District held that when a hearing officer actually acts as an advocate, the
violation constitutes "structural error" requiring no showing of actual prejudice—placing the

reversed yet another APS suspension on the same due process ground—in a case expressly
naming Defendant Gordon personally as respondent, placing him on individualized notice
approximately four months before Plaintiff's hearing.

embedded in being personally named as respondent in Clarke v. Gordon, Defendant Gordon took
no adequate corrective action. The DMV's hearing framework as applied to Plaintiff in January
2025 operated in the very form the Court of Appeal has twice in the preceding thirty-three
months—and once in the preceding four months—declared unconstitutional. Defendant
Candelaria's conduct at Plaintiff's hearing exemplifies the advocacy condemned in those
decisions: she adopted the arresting officer's narrative wholesale without independent scrutiny,
declined to acknowledge exculpatory evidence, and issued a decision affirmatively defending the

shield officials from liability for violating clearly established rights. The following principles

release reclassifies the event as a "detention only" by mandatory statutory language (Pen. Code
sections 849(c), 849.5); (e) a refusal suspension under CVC section 13353 requires a "lawful
arrest" as a statutory predicate (Music v. DMV (1990)); and (f) the DMV's dual-role APS

April 2022, reinforced as "structural error" by Knudsen in April 2024, and reaffirmed in

hearing officer in January 2025—nearly three years after the dual-role framework had been

named in an appellate reversal on the same ground—could have believed that dismissing all of

In the Serrato Order, Judge Krishnan (1) granted Plaintiff's application to proceed in
forma pauperis, (2) screened the complaint pursuant to 28 U.S.C. section 1915(e), and (3)
concluded that the operative complaint "is sufficient" to proceed past the section 1915 screening
stage. The Court ordered the Clerk to issue summons and directed service of process by the
United States Marshal.
RELEVANCE TO THE PENDING OBJECTIONS
The Serrato Order is relevant to this Court's de novo review of the Findings and
Recommendations for the following reasons:
First, the Serrato Order arises from the same November 1, 2024 incident that is the factual
foundation of this action. Although the instant case challenges the constitutional architecture of
the DMV administrative per se hearing rather than the CHP officers' roadside conduct, both cases
depend on the same predicate: whether the November 1, 2024 arrest was lawful and whether the
sworn CHP report was truthful. Judge Krishnan evaluated the dashcam contradictions, the
fabrication allegations, and the Penal Code section 851.6 detention certificate -- the same
documentary record on which this action's "lawful arrest" and jurisdictional arguments rest -- and
found them sufficient.
Second, the Findings and Recommendations in this case expressly relied on the pendency
of recommended dismissal in a companion case as additional support for denying leave to amend.
See F&R at 9 (citing Newanforbi v. California, 2026 WL 1067541 (E.D. Cal. Apr. 20, 2026)).
The Serrato Order materially undermines that cross-reference. A coordinate Article III court has
now examined substantially overlapping factual allegations and concluded they state a sufficient
claim. The inference that Plaintiff's litigation pattern reflects frivolousness rather than legitimate
pursuit of distinct legal theories is no longer sustainable.

INTRODUCTION
Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi, proceeding pro se, timely files these Objections to
Magistrate Judge Chi Soo Kim's Findings and Recommendations (ECF No. 6, filed June 15,
2026), pursuant to 28 U.S.C. section 636(b)(1) and Local Rule 304. The Magistrate Judge
recommends denying Plaintiff's in forma pauperis application, dismissing the First Amended
Complaint without leave to amend, and closing the case.
De novo review of the Findings and Recommendations is required as to each objection. 28
U.S.C. section 636(b)(1)(C); United States v. Reyna-Tapia, 328 F.3d 1114, 1121 (9th Cir. 2003)

OBJECTIONS TO MAGISTRATE JUDGE'S FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
(en banc). As set forth below, the Findings and Recommendations contain three categories of
fundamental error that, if adopted, would deny Plaintiff his day in court on substantial
constitutional claims for which three California appellate courts provide substantial support on
the same due process theory: (1) the Findings and Recommendations misapplied the section
1915(e) screening standard by weighing evidence and resolving fact-sensitive immunity and
standing questions against the pleader; (2) the Findings and Recommendations applied
out-of-circuit authority to bypass the Ninth Circuit's required functional analysis of quasi-judicial
immunity; and (3) the Findings and Recommendations denied leave to amend without identifying
any deficiency that could not be cured by additional factual allegations drawn from the hearing
transcript, the dashcam audio, and the agency record.
These Objections are organized to give the District Judge multiple independent paths to
decline adoption. Even if the Court is unpersuaded on any single merits theory, the First
Amended Complaint at minimum states a non-frivolous, amendable claim and cannot be
dismissed at the section 1915 screening stage.
STANDARD OF REVIEW AT THE SECTION 1915(e) SCREENING STAGE
Before turning to the specific objections, Plaintiff respectfully reminds the Court of the
procedural posture that governs every issue below. At the section 1915(e) screening stage, the
court must (1) accept all well-pleaded factual allegations as true, (2) construe the pleadings of a
pro se litigant liberally, and (3) deny dismissal without leave to amend only when futility is clear
on the face of the complaint. Hebbe v. Pliler, 627 F.3d 338, 342 (9th Cir. 2010) (pro se pleadings
construed liberally); Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1130 (9th Cir. 2000) (en banc) (leave to
amend mandatory absent clear futility); Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319, 325 (1989)
(frivolousness standard is narrow).
The Findings and Recommendations did not apply these standards. The Findings and

A short organizing principle runs through these Objections. At minimum, the First

acknowledged Plaintiff's financial eligibility and dismissed only on a facial-merit theory built on

Absolute Immunity to Defendant Candelaria (Count I)

Analysis. The Supreme Court has held that the applicability of absolute immunity to non-judicial
officers turns on a functional analysis of the nature of the acts performed, not on the title of the
officer. Butz v. Economou, 438 U.S. 478, 512 (1978); Forrester v. White, 484 U.S. 219, 227-30
(1988). The Ninth Circuit applies this functional test by examining whether the official (1)

allegations state a plausible claim. Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). Three appellate
courts examining the identical type of APS hearing concluded that the hearing officer performed

OBJECTION II
The Magistrate Judge Erred in Treating Plaintiff's Mercer / CVC
Section 13353(a)(1) 'Lawful Arrest' Theory as Frivolous
A. The Mercer Question Is at Minimum a Substantial Legal Dispute. California
Vehicle Code section 13353(a)(1) makes the lawfulness of the arrest a statutory predicate to any
refusal suspension. Music v. Department of Motor Vehicles, 221 Cal. App. 3d 841, 851 (1990). 
Mercer v. Department of Motor Vehicles, 53 Cal. 3d 753, 768-69 (1991), requires observed
volitional movement of the vehicle to support a warrantless DUI arrest in the absence of a
qualifying statutory exception. The First Amended Complaint plausibly alleges that the vehicle
was stationary, the engine was off, and Plaintiff was asleep on a dirt shoulder when the CHP
officers made contact, and that no qualifying exception applied (FAC paragraphs 15-20). That
presents, at a minimum, a substantial legal dispute that is not properly resolved against Plaintiff at
the section 1915 screening stage.
B. The Findings and Recommendations Misapplied California Vehicle Code Section
40300.5. The Findings and Recommendations cited California Vehicle Code section 40300.5 to
bypass the Mercer observed-volitional-movement requirement. F&R at 6 & n.1. But section
40300.5 applies only when specified statutory prerequisites are present, including a traffic

suspension under Penal Code section 849(b). Plaintiff argues that the 'lawfully arrested' predicate

state law. Federal courts have original jurisdiction over such claims. 28 U.S.C. section 1331. The

court rather than through state administrative channels, and that choice does not render the federal
action a 'pretext.'

Merely the Hearing Outcome. The First Amended Complaint does not merely seek to relitigate
the DMV's factual findings. It challenges the structural merger of prosecutorial and adjudicative
functions -- a systemic constitutional deficiency for which Plaintiff seeks relief broader than
ordinary administrative review of one hearing outcome. A mandamus action under California
Code of Civil Procedure section 1094.5 reviews whether the agency's findings are supported by
the weight of the evidence; it does not restructure the hearing process itself or address the
constitutional architecture of the dual-role framework. The declaratory and injunctive relief
sought in Counts II and III -- including structural reform of that framework -- goes beyond what
mandamus review provides, which is precisely what section 1983 is designed for.

officers' own recorded words, the contradiction the First Amended Complaint alleges, and so that
the Court has a direct record on which to evaluate the Findings and Recommendations' Footnote 2
treatment of that contradiction.
IV. ONGOING PROFESSIONAL CONSEQUENCES AND CDL EMPLOYABILITY
15. I am a professional holder of a California Class A Commercial Driver's License. My
CDL carries doubles, triples, and tank vehicle endorsements. Prior to the suspension imposed in
Case Number 34739340, my Class A CDL was the basis of my livelihood as a long-haul and
intrastate commercial driver.

in the DMV record as a refusal-related suspension under CVC § 13353. A refusal-related
suspension by a Class A CDL holder is reportable through the Commercial Driver License
Information System ('CDLIS') maintained pursuant to 49 C.F.R. Part 384, and a chemical-test
refusal is reportable to the federal Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse maintained by the Federal

TIMELINESS OF THE PETITION
12. This Petition is timely because the Decision is void ab initio for want of subject-matter
jurisdiction. A void administrative order has no force or effect from the moment of its issuance
and may be set aside at any time, by direct or collateral attack, without regard to ordinary
limitations periods. (Code Civ. Proc., § 473(d).) The void character of the Decision is
independent of, and prior to, any analysis of legal error within an exercise of jurisdiction; it arises
from the complete statutory destruction of the Administrative Per Se framework's "lawful arrest"
predicate before the hearing was ever convened. The governing legal framework and its
application to the record are set forth in paragraphs 13 and 14 below.
13. California law distinguishes categorically between an order that is "void" — one
rendered without jurisdiction over the subject matter or in complete excess of statutory authority

American Contractors Indemnity Co. (2004) 33 Cal.4th 653, 660; Abelleira v. District Court of
Appeal (1941) 17 Cal.2d 280, 287–288.) A void order "has no force or effect" and may be set
aside at any time by direct or collateral attack. (Code Civ. Proc., § 473(d); Heidary v. Yadollahi
(2002) 99 Cal.App.4th 857, 862; Rochin v. Pat Johnson Manufacturing Co. (1998) 67
Cal.App.4th 1228, 1239.) These principles apply with equal force to administrative orders
rendered in excess of statutory authority. (Pittman v. State Personnel Bd. (1965) 233 Cal.App.2d
26, 31–32.) An order rendered in clear absence of all jurisdiction cannot be insulated from review
by an ordinary limitations period; to hold otherwise would convert procedural deadlines into a
license for state agencies to act ultra vires with impunity.
14. The Decision is void in this categorical sense. The Administrative Per Se
refusal-suspension framework of Vehicle Code section 13353(a)(1) requires, as a jurisdictional
and statutory predicate, that the driver have been "lawfully arrested." On November 5, 2024 —
more than two months before the January 24, 2025 hearing — the Dublin CHP issued a formal
Detention Certificate releasing Petitioner under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for "insufficient
grounds for making a criminal complaint." By operation of Penal Code sections 849(c) and 849.5,
the encounter "shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention only." That statutory effect is
mandatory, automatic, and non-discretionary; no exercise of agency discretion can override it.
Respondent Candelaria nevertheless convened the APS hearing and sustained the refusal
suspension, exercising adjudicative power over a subject matter that did not legally exist at the
time of the hearing. (See Stump v. Sparkman (1978) 435 U.S. 349, 356–357 [adjudicative action
in clear absence of all jurisdiction is void].) The Decision was void at the moment of its issuance
and remains void today. The thirty-four-day limitations period of Vehicle Code section 13559(a)
confers no finality on an order rendered in clear absence of all jurisdiction and cannot bar this
Petition.

STANDARD OF REVIEW
25. Because the Decision affects a fundamental vested right—Petitioner's commercial
driving privilege, which is also his means of livelihood—this Court exercises its independent
judgment on the evidence. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1094.5(c); Berlinghieri v. DMV, 33 Cal.3d 392,
396–398 (1983); Daniels v. DMV, 33 Cal.3d 532, 536 (1983).) The Court determines whether the
agency proceeded without, or in excess of, jurisdiction; whether there was a fair trial; and whether
there was a prejudicial abuse of discretion, which is established if the agency has not proceeded in
the manner required by law, the order is not supported by the findings, or the findings are not
supported by the weight of the evidence. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1094.5(b).)
FIRST CAUSE OF ACTION
Want of Statutory Predicate — No "Lawful Arrest"
(Veh. Code, § 13353(a)(1); Code Civ. Proc., § 1094.5(b))
26. Petitioner incorporates paragraphs 1 through 25 as though fully set forth herein.
27. Vehicle Code section 13353(a)(1) predicates a refusal suspension on the driver having
been "lawfully arrested for any offense allegedly committed in violation of Section 23140, 23152,
or 23154." The "lawful arrest" predicate is jurisdictional and statutory, not merely procedural.
(Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753, 760–762 (1991); Music v. DMV, 221 Cal.App.3d 841, 850
(1990).)
28. The Decision is captioned "ADMINISTRATIVE PER SE - .08% BAC Refusal" and is
sustained under the refusal framework of section 13353. By operation of Penal Code sections
849(b)(1), 849(c), and 849.5, the November 1, 2024 taking into custody "shall not be deemed an

On 11/01/2024 at approximately 0055 hours, I was on duty, in full tan California Highway Patrol (CHP) uniform, driving a 
fully marked CHP patrol vehicle (1633363). My partner, Officer Melano ID 023054, was seated in the right front passenger 
of my patrol vehicle, also in full tan CHP uniform. We were traveling eastbound on I-580, just west of Isabel Avenue, when 
we came upon a Gray Tesla Model Y (S/V) on the right shoulder of I-580, just west of Isabel Avenue. I proceeded to park 
my patrol vehicle right behind the Tesla on the right shoulder to make a welfare check on the Tesla. I conducted a 
passenger side approach of the Tesla and observed a black male adult seated in the driver seat of the Tesla. The subject 
was asleep, and I noticed the subject was wearing an orange 21 + wrist band on his right wrist. I knocked on the right front 
passenger side window of the Tesla and the subject woke up. The subject seemed very confused and disoriented. I 
contacted the subject through the open right passenger side door and I could smell the distinct odor of an alcoholic 
beverage emitting from within the vehicle. I asked the subject if he was okay, and he related yes. The subject related he 
was on a parking lot, and I proceeded to informed him he was not in a parking lot, and he was on the side of the freeway. I 
asked the subject how long he had been parked on the side of the freeway and he related approximately 7 minutes. I asked 
him if he was alone, and he related yes. I asked him if he drove to that location and he related yes, from a party in Oakland. 
I asked the subject if he had consumed any alcoholic beverages, and he related no. I conducted a DUI evaluation on the 
subject and at 0112 hours, I placed the subject (Newanforbi) under arrest for a violation of California Vehicle Code section 
23152(a), driving while under the influence of alcohol, per 40300.5 VC.

You are hereby notified that your privilege to operate a motor vehicle will be suspended or revoked effective 30 days from the issue date of this order as shown 
below, and until you pay a $125 reissue fee and file proof of financial responsibility as shown on the reverse.
For additional information call (916) 657-0214.
TEMPORARY DRIVER LICENSE
This document must be carried with you and shall serve as your temporary California driver license. It is subject to the same class(es) and all restrictions as your permanent 
driver license. This temporary driver license does not provide you with any driving privileges if you do not have a California driver license or your license is 
expired, suspended, revoked, canceled, or denied. It expires at midnight 30 days from the issue date of this order shown below.
This action is taken under authority of California Vehicle Code (CVC) §§13353,13353.1,13353.2 and 13389 because you were arrested or detained for driving under the 
influence of alcohol and/or drugs and:
BAC 0.01% PAS, Breath, 
Blood or Urine Test 
DUI Probation
You completed a PAS, breath, blood, or urine test and the officer believes the results will show 0.01% BAC or more. If the laboratory 
results show your BAC was less than 0.01%, this suspension will be set aside. Your driver license will be reissued to you if you do 
not have another suspension or revocation in effect.
You completed a breath test with 0.08% BAC or more, or you completed a blood or urine test and the officer believes the results will 
show 0.08% BAC or more. If the laboratory results show that your BAC is less than 0.08%, this suspension or revocation will be set 
aside. Your driver license will be reissued to you if you do not have another suspension or revocation in effect.
BAC 0.08% Breath, Blood, 
or Urine Test
BAC 0.04 % Breath, Blood 
or Urine Test while driving a 
Commercial Vehicle
You completed a breath test with 0.04% BAC or more, or you completed a blood or urine test and the officer believes the results will 
show 0.04% BAC or more. If the laboratory results show that your BAC is less than 0.04%, this suspension or revocation will be set 
aside. Your driver license will be reissued to you if you do not have another suspension or revocation in effect.
Chemical Test Refusal
You refused to submit to, or failed to complete, a chemical test of the alcohol and/or drug content of your blood.
COMMERCIAL DISQUALIFICATION
A commercial disqualification action will be taken due to any of the following: if you refused a chemical test, if you had a 0.04% BAC or more while operating 
a commercial motor vehicle as defined in CVC §15210 or while transporting hazardous materials, or held a commercial driver license and were driving any 
vehicle when you had a 0.08% BAC or more.
HEARING INFORMATION
YOU HAVE 10 DAYS FROM RECEIPT OF THIS NOTICE TO REQUEST A HEARING TO SHOW THAT THE SUSPENSION OR REVOCATION IS NOT JUSTIFIED. 
The suspension or revocation will not be stayed (delayed) unless you request a hearing within 10 DAYS from the issue date of this order and DMV cannot 
provide a hearing before the effective date of the suspension or revocation and make a determination. Hearings are conducted only to determine questions of 
fact as described on the reverse. Your need for a license cannot be considered at a hearing. If you want a hearing or have questions regarding this matter, contact 
the DMV at (916) 657-0214. A telephone hearing will be conducted unless you request an in-person hearing. Before the hearing you may see or obtain copies of the 
department’s evidence. You must request copies of the department’s evidence at least 10 DAYS prior to the date set for commencement of the hearing in 
order to receive them prior to the hearing date. If you want the information released to someone else, give them signed permission. You have the right to have 
a sign or language interpreter present at your hearing. If you require the service of an interpreter, immediately notify DMV of the need for such service. 
During the hearing you may present oral testimony and/or other evidence. Testimony is taken under oath or affirmation, and the hearing is recorded. You may be 
represented by legal counsel, or you may represent yourself. The arresting officer(s) may be subpoenaed in this matter, if it is determined that his or her testimony is 
needed. If you wish to question the arresting officer(s), you have the right to have subpoenas issued on your behalf. You may subpoena any other witness(es) you feel 
may help your case, and you have the right to cross-examine any opposing witness(es). Blank subpoenas may be obtained on the internet at the following address 
http://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/dmv/detail/forms/formsds or provided to you by the hearing officer upon request prior to the hearing. You are responsible for service of 
your subpoena(s) and any witness fee required by law. After the hearing, the hearing officer shall make findings and render a decision.

HEARING ISSUES
Chemical test results of 0.01% or more BAC while on DUI probation; 0.04% or more BAG in a commercial motor vehicle; or 0.08% 
or more BAC.
• Did the peace officer have reasonable cause to believe you were driving a motor vehicle in violation of CVC §§23152,23153, 
or 23154?
• Were you lawfully detained while on DUI probation or lawfully arrested?
• Were you driving a motor vehicle when you had: 0.01% BAC or more by weight of alcohol while on DUI probation; 0.04% BAC 
or more by weight of alcohol while driving a commercial vehicle; or 0.08% BAC or more by weight of alcohol?
Refusal to submit to or failure to complete a chemical test.
• Did the peace officer have reasonable cause to believe you were driving a motor vehicle in violation of CVC §§23152, 23153, 
or 23154?
• Were you lawfully detained while on DUI probation, or lawfully arrested?
• Were you told that your driving privilege would be suspended, or revoked for one, two, or three years if you refused to submit 
to, or failed to complete a chemical test?
• Did you refuse or fail to complete a chemical test, or PAS test (DUI Probation), after being requested to do so by a peace officer?
APPEAL RIGHTS
Following the hearing decision, you may request a department review in writing within 15 days from the date on the bottom of the 
notice telling you the results of your hearing. The fee for the department review is $120. You may also appeal a DMV decision by 
filing a writ of mandamus at the superior court in your county of residence within 30 days from the date on the bottom of the notice 
telling you the results of your hearing.
PENALTIES
Chemical test results of 0.01% or more BAC while on DUI probation; 0.04% or more BAC in a commercial motor vehicle; or 0.08% 
or more BAC. (CVC §§13353.2 and 13353.3)
• First Offense of driving with a BAC of 0.08% or more or 0.04% or more BAC in a commercial motor vehicle will result in a 
4-month suspension, or a 1-year suspension if 0.01% or more BAC while on DUI probation.
• Second or Subsequent Offense, within 10 years of a separate violation of driving under the influence, including such a 
charge reduced to reckless driving, or vehicular manslaughter, or violation of CVC §23140, which resulted in a conviction, or 
separate administrative determination that you were driving with a BAC of 0.01% or more while on DUI probation, or a BAC 
of 0.08% or more or a BAC of 0.04% or more in a commercial motor vehicle at any age, or you refused a test, will result in 
a 1-year suspension.
Refusal to submit to or failure to complete a chemical test or a preliminary alcohol screening. (CVC §§13353 and 13353.1)
• First Offense will result in a 1-year suspension, or a 2-year revocation if on DUI probation.
• Second Offense, within 10 years of a separate violation of driving under the influence, including such a charge reduced 
to reckless driving, or vehicular manslaughter, or a violation of CVC §23140, which resulted in a conviction, or separate 
administrative determination that you were driving with a BAC of 0.01% or more while on DUI probation, or a BAC of 0.08% or 
more or a BAC of 0.04% or more in a commercial vehicle at any age, or you refused a test, will result in a 2-year revocation, 
or a 3-year revocation while on DUI probation.
• Three or More Offenses within 10 years of any combination of the above violations, convictions or separate administrative 
determinations will result in a 3-year revocation.
ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
An administrative review will automatically be conducted. You will be notified in writing only if the suspension or revocation is set 
aside. Before the suspension or revocation can be ended and a driver license issued or returned to you, a $125 reissue fee must be 
paid to DMV (CVC §14905), and you must file proof of financial responsibility by a California Insurance Proof Certificate (SR 22/1P), 
$35,000 cash deposit, or surety bond, or self insurer certificate (CVC §16430). You must maintain proof of financial responsibility 
for three years. If you drive while your driving privilege is suspended or revoked, you may be arrested and, if convicted, jailed and/ 
or fined and your vehicle can be impounded or sold.

DUI Probation Violations: Indicate below how you determined the driver was on DUI probation.
On 11/01/2024 at approximately 0055 hours, I was on duty, in full tan California Highway Patrol (CHP) uniform, driving a 
fully marked CHP patrol vehicle (1633363). My partner, Officer Melano ID 023054, was seated in the right front passenger 
of my patrol vehicle, also in full tan CHP uniform. We were traveling eastbound on I-580, just west of Isabel Avenue, when 
we came upon a Gray Tesla Model Y (S/V) on the right shoulder of I-580, just west of Isabel Avenue. I proceeded to park 
my patrol vehicle right behind the Tesla on the right shoulder to make a welfare check on the Tesla. I conducted a 
passenger side approach of the Tesla and observed a black male adult seated in the driver seat of the Tesla. The subject 
was asleep, and I noticed the subject was wearing an orange 21 + wrist band on his right wrist. I knocked on the right front 
passenger side window of the Tesla and the subject woke up. The subject seemed very confused and disoriented. I 
contacted the subject through the open right passenger side door and I could smell the distinct odor of an alcoholic 
beverage emitting from within the vehicle. I asked the subject if he was okay, and he related yes. The subject related he 
was on a parking lot, and I proceeded to informed him he was not in a parking lot, and he was on the side of the freeway. I 
asked the subject how long he had been parked on the side of the freeway and he related approximately 7 minutes. I asked 
him if he was alone, and he related yes. I asked him if he drove to that location and he related yes, from a party in Oakland. 
I asked the subject if he had consumed any alcoholic beverages, and he related no. I conducted a DUI evaluation on the 
subject and at 0112 hours, I placed the subject (Newanforbi) under arrest for a violation of California Vehicle Code section 
23152(a), driving while under the influence of alcohol, per 40300.5 VC.

provide a hearing before the effective date of the suspension or revocation and make a determination. Hearings are conducted only to determine questions of

represented by legal counsel, or you may represent yourself. The arresting officer(s) may be subpoenaed in this matter, if it is determined that his or her testimony is

Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI, appearing in propria persona, brings this action
against Defendants DIANA CANDELARIA, in her individual capacity, and STEVE GORDON,
Director of the California Department of Motor Vehicles, in his official capacity, and alleges as
follows:
INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 challenging the process by
which Defendant Diana Candelaria, a California Department of Motor Vehicles Driver Safety
Hearing Officer, suspended Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi's Class A Commercial Driver's

License for one year and imposed a three-year SR-22 financial-responsibility requirement that
continues to burden Plaintiff today. Plaintiff brings claims for damages against Candelaria in her
individual capacity, and claims for prospective declaratory and injunctive relief against Defendant
Steve Gordon, Director of the California DMV, in his official capacity under Ex parte Young,
209 U.S. 123 (1908).
2. The suspension rests on an administrative-per-se refusal hearing conducted on January
24, 2025, in which Candelaria operated simultaneously as the DMV's evidence-gatherer,
advocate, and adjudicator -- a dual-role framework that three separate California Court of Appeal
decisions had condemned before Plaintiff's hearing. Candelaria's written decision sustained the
suspension without addressing a formal Penal Code section 851.6 Detention Certificate issued by
the arresting agency itself, reclassifying the underlying arrest as "a detention only, not an arrest"
for "insufficient grounds"; without addressing the California Supreme Court's requirement of
observed volitional movement in Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991); and without addressing
objective dashcam evidence materially contradicting the sworn officer's statement on which the
suspension was based. The decision stated that "no evidence was presented to the contrary" when,
in fact, contrary evidence had been presented in writing and at the hearing.
3. Although the one-year suspension period has expired, Plaintiff continues to suffer
present adverse effects: a three-year SR-22 requirement running through approximately February
2028, a $125.00 reissue fee, and continuing commercial-driving-record consequences that affect
his employability. These ongoing burdens are traceable to Candelaria's decision and redressable
by prospective relief against Gordon. Plaintiff seeks compensatory and punitive damages against
Candelaria, declaratory and injunctive relief against Gordon, and attorney's fees under 42 U.S.C.
section 1988.

13353 through 13389 and with supervision of DMV Driver Safety Hearing Officers. He is sued in

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. The November 1, 2024 Arrest and Its Aftermath
12. On November 1, 2024, at approximately 12:54 a.m., Plaintiff was parked and asleep in
a rented vehicle on the right shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County. CHP
Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez and Jose Melano approached, opened the vehicle without
consent, and arrested Plaintiff for suspected driving under the influence. The encounter was
captured on the officers' dashcam recording (CHP Case No. RJ68845).
13. Following the arrest, Officer Meza-Gonzalez executed a sworn DS-367 Officer's
Statement and CHP Arrest-Investigation Report. Those documents contain representations that
are materially contradicted by the dashcam recording -- including a claimed "strong distinct odor

his location, and a checked box for "Beverage Present: Yes" when the only liquid the officers
found was, in Officer Melano's own words on the recording, "piss." The contradictions between
the sworn statements and the recording are the subject of the related Ngwa Nforbi v.
Meza-Gonzalez & Melano action pending in this District.
14. On November 5, 2024, the Dublin CHP issued a Detention Certificate under Penal
Code section 851.6, reclassifying the event as "a detention only, not an arrest" and releasing
Plaintiff under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for "insufficient grounds for making a criminal
complaint." The Alameda County District Attorney declined to file any charges.
B. The DMV APS Process and
Plaintiff's Written Defense
15. The DS-367 executed by Officer Meza-Gonzalez triggered automatic
administrative-per-se suspension proceedings under Vehicle Code sections 13353 et seq. Plaintiff
timely requested a hearing.
16. On December 4, 2024, the DMV issued a Notice of Hearing Appointment (Form DS
2304, Rev. 05/2023) setting the hearing for January 24, 2025 before Defendant Candelaria via
Microsoft Teams. The same notice imposed a commercial-driving restriction on Plaintiff's
Temporary License pending the hearing outcome.
17. Form DS 2304 states, verbatim: "The Hearing Officer will develop the facts and
render a final decision on your matter." That sentence describes the merger of investigative,
advocacy, and adjudicative functions within a single officer -- the structural configuration that

for Discovery identifying the dashcam evidence, the contradictions in the DS-367, the Detention
Certificate, and controlling authority including Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991). Plaintiff
also placed the Detention Certificate and a dashcam transcript into the administrative record.
C. The January 24, 2025 Hearing
19. On January 24, 2025, Defendant Candelaria presided over Plaintiff's APS hearing. At
the hearing, Candelaria gathered and marshaled evidence on behalf of the DMV, offered the
DMV's documentary exhibits, ruled on Plaintiff's objections to those exhibits, evaluated Plaintiff's
testimony, and issued the ultimate decision on the merits -- all within the same proceeding and
without a separate advocate presenting the DMV's case.
20. Plaintiff appeared and testified under penalty of perjury. He presented the Detention
Certificate, referenced the dashcam evidence, and argued the authority cited in his December 9
submission.
D. The February 11, 2025 Written Decision
21. On February 11, 2025, Candelaria issued a written Notification of Findings and
Decision in APS Case No. 34739340, sustaining a one-year suspension of Plaintiff's Class A CDL
(Feb. 20, 2025 through Feb. 19, 2026) and imposing: (a) a $125.00 reissue fee under Vehicle
Code sections 14904 and 14906; and (b) a three-year SR-22 financial-responsibility requirement
under Vehicle Code section 16430.

that is inconsistent with the record, which contained Plaintiff's written submission, the Detention

23. The decision treated the DS-367 as dispositive without engaging with the contrary
evidence in the record. The practical effect was that the officer's sworn statement was treated as
conclusive regardless of what the driver presented.
E. The Dual-Role Framework:
Three Appellate Condemnations Before Plaintiff's Hearing
24. By the date of Plaintiff's hearing, three published California Court of Appeal decisions
had condemned the DMV's practice of appointing hearing officers who act simultaneously as
advocates and adjudicators in APS proceedings: California DUI Lawyers Ass'n v. DMV, 77
Cal.App.5th 517 (2022); Knudsen v. DMV, 101 Cal.App.5th 186 (2024); and Clarke v. Gordon,
104 Cal.App.5th 1267 (2024). Clarke names Defendant Gordon personally as respondent. The
pattern of dual-role conduct described in those decisions -- marshaling evidence, offering
exhibits, overruling objections, and deciding the merits -- is consistent with Candelaria's conduct
at Plaintiff's hearing.
25. On information and belief, the dual-role framework condemned in those decisions
remained in operational effect at the time of Plaintiff's hearing, as reflected in the DMV's own
Form DS 2304, and remains in effect today. Defendant Gordon, as Director of the DMV, has not
restructured hearing-officer functions, revised Form DS 2304, or implemented training or
oversight adequate to prevent the recurrence of the dual-role configuration.

F. The Lawful-Arrest Predicate
26. The APS refusal-suspension framework requires, as a statutory predicate, that the
driver have been "lawfully arrested." Cal. Veh. Code section 13353(a)(1). At the time of
Plaintiff's hearing, the lawful-arrest predicate was contested by at least two independent factors:
(a) no officer had observed Plaintiff in volitional movement of the vehicle, raising a question
under Mercer, 53 Cal.3d at 760-62; and (b) the CHP's own Detention Certificate had reclassified
the event as "a detention only, not an arrest" under Penal Code section 849(b)(1), with the
statutory consequence that the event "shall not be deemed an arrest" under Penal Code sections
849(c) and 849.5.
27. Candelaria's written decision did not address either factor. Whether the lawful-arrest
predicate was satisfied is a contested question that Candelaria's decision left unresolved.
G. Ongoing Consequences
28. The one-year suspension period (Feb. 20, 2025 through Feb. 19, 2026) has expired.
But the following consequences of Candelaria's decision remain in effect:
(a) SR-22 requirement. Candelaria's decision imposed a three-year SR-22
financial-responsibility mandate under Vehicle Code section 16430, running through

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action for damages under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 against
Defendant DIANA CANDELARIA, a Driver Safety Hearing Officer employed by the California
Department of Motor Vehicles ("DMV"), sued in her individual capacity; and for prospective
declaratory and injunctive relief under Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908), against Defendant
STEVE GORDON, Director of the California DMV, sued in his official capacity. Acting under
color of state law, Defendant Candelaria deprived Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI of a
constitutionally protected property interest -- his Class A Commercial Driver's License (No.
F7953179) -- through an administrative-per-se proceeding that was constitutionally deficient in at
least three independently sufficient ways, each traceable directly to Defendant Candelaria's own
written decision.
2. The underlying facts are simple, documented, and largely undisputed. On November 1,
2024, Plaintiff -- a professional commercial truck driver -- was arrested by California Highway
Patrol ("CHP") officers on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California, on a suspicion of driving under the influence that the officers' own contemporaneous
dashcam recording refutes. Four days later, on November 5, 2024, the CHP itself issued a formal
Penal Code section 851.6 Detention Certificate reclassifying that taking-into-custody as "a
detention only, not an arrest," and releasing Plaintiff under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for
"insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint." The Alameda County District Attorney,
to whom charges had been referred, declined to file any accusatory pleading. Both the arresting
agency and the prosecuting authority formally repudiated the arrest as lacking any evidentiary
basis.
3. Notwithstanding the Detention Certificate, the DMV proceeded with a Vehicle Code
section 13353 administrative-per-se refusal-suspension hearing. That hearing took place on
January 24, 2025, via Microsoft Teams, before Defendant Candelaria. On February 11, 2025,

continue through approximately February 2028.
4. Candelaria's decision is constitutionally infirm on at least three independent grounds,
each of which -- standing alone -- states a claim upon which relief can be granted:
(a) STRUCTURAL BIAS. Candelaria adjudicated Plaintiff's suspension within the
DMV's dual-role framework in which the same officer functions as both prosecuting
advocate for the Department and adjudicator of the Department's own case. The DMV's
own written Notice of Hearing Appointment (Form DS 2304) served on Plaintiff confirms
the dual role verbatim: "The Hearing Officer will develop the facts and render a final
decision on your matter." This structural merger of investigative, advocacy, and
adjudicative functions has by the date of Plaintiff's hearing been condemned in three
separate California Court of Appeal decisions, including one in which Defendant Gordon
was personally named as respondent.
(b) DENIAL OF A FAIR HEARING. Candelaria refused to conduct the reasoned,
evidence-based inquiry the Fourteenth Amendment requires. Presented with (i) the CHP's
own section 851.6 Detention Certificate, (ii) the CHP dashcam recording in which the
officers themselves identified the suspected "alcoholic beverage" as urine, and (iii)
binding California Supreme Court authority in Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991),
Candelaria issued a written decision that mentioned none of them, ratified the fabricated
sworn statement of the arresting officer as if it were irrebuttable, and characterized the
record as one in which "no evidence was presented to the contrary" when in fact contrary

(c) CLEAR ABSENCE OF STATUTORY JURISDICTION. The APS refusal framework
requires, as a jurisdictional predicate, that the driver have been "lawfully arrested." Cal.
Veh. Code section 13353(a)(1). By the time of the January 24, 2025 hearing, that
predicate had been destroyed as a matter of law by (i) Mercer's requirement of observed
volitional movement, unmet on the officers' own account; and (ii) the mandatory statutory
command of Penal Code sections 849(c) and 849.5 that, upon issuance of a section 851.6
Detention Certificate, "the arrest shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention only."
Candelaria proceeded anyway, exercising adjudicative power over a subject matter that, as
a matter of California law, did not exist.
5. Candelaria's structural dual role was not incidental to her decision. By the date of
Plaintiff's hearing, three published California Court of Appeal decisions had squarely condemned
it: California DUI Lawyers Ass'n v. DMV, 77 Cal.App.5th 517 (2022); Knudsen v. DMV, 101
Cal.App.5th 186 (2024); and Clarke v. Gordon, 104 Cal.App.5th 1267 (2024). Clarke names
Defendant Gordon personally as the responsible official. Defendant Gordon has actual notice of
the constitutional infirmity; he has failed to remedy it; and the framework in the form condemned
by the Court of Appeal remains in operational effect, causing continuing, present adverse effects
to Plaintiff -- including the ongoing SR-22 encumbrance and the ongoing
commercial-driving-record consequences of the suspension -- that Ex parte Young empowers this
Court to redress.
6. The consequences of Candelaria's decision have been -- and continue to be -- severe.
Plaintiff is a professional Class A CDL truck driver. The one-year suspension of his commercial
driving privileges immediately terminated his employment. The three-year SR-22 filing
requirement continues to encumber him today; it is a punitive, high-risk financial-responsibility
filing that would not exist absent Candelaria's decision, and it prevents Plaintiff from obtaining

condemning the DMV dual-role framework, and it provides no basis for the DMV to

defense fails on the functional analysis the Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit require.
125. The Supreme Court has held that the applicability of absolute immunity to

219, 227-30 (1988). The Ninth Circuit applies this functional test by examining whether the
official (1) performed an adjudicative function, (2) within a proceeding with adequate procedural
safeguards, and (3) whether there were sufficient checks on the official's authority. Cleavinger v.
Saxner, 474 U.S. 193, 202 (1985). Officials performing functions traditionally associated with

INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action for damages under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 against
Defendant DIANA CANDELARIA, a Driver Safety Hearing Officer employed by the California
Department of Motor Vehicles ("DMV"), sued in her individual capacity; and for prospective
declaratory and injunctive relief under Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908), against Defendant
STEVE GORDON, Director of the California DMV, sued in his official capacity. Acting under
color of state law, Defendant Candelaria deprived Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI of a
constitutionally protected property interest -- his Class A Commercial Driver's License (No.
F7953179) -- through an administrative-per-se proceeding that was constitutionally deficient in at
least three independently sufficient ways, each traceable directly to Defendant Candelaria's own
written decision.
2. The underlying facts are simple, documented, and largely undisputed. On November 1,
2024, Plaintiff -- a professional commercial truck driver -- was arrested by California Highway
Patrol ("CHP") officers on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California, on a suspicion of driving under the influence that the officers' own contemporaneous
dashcam recording refutes. Four days later, on November 5, 2024, the CHP itself issued a formal
Penal Code section 851.6 Detention Certificate reclassifying that taking-into-custody as "a
detention only, not an arrest," and releasing Plaintiff under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for
"insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint." The Alameda County District Attorney,
to whom charges had been referred, declined to file any accusatory pleading. Both the arresting
agency and the prosecuting authority formally repudiated the arrest as lacking any evidentiary
basis.
3. Notwithstanding the Detention Certificate, the DMV proceeded with a Vehicle Code
section 13353 administrative-per-se refusal-suspension hearing. That hearing took place on
January 24, 2025, via Microsoft Teams, before Defendant Candelaria. On February 11, 2025,

binding California Supreme Court authority in Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991),
Candelaria issued a written decision that mentioned none of them, ratified the fabricated
sworn statement of the arresting officer as if it were irrebuttable, and characterized the
record as one in which "no evidence was presented to the contrary" when in fact contrary

E. The Non-Discretionary Statutory Effect of the
Detention Certificate Under California Law
36. The consequences of a Penal Code section 849(b)(1) release, followed by a section
851.6 Detention Certificate, are non-discretionary and dispositive as a matter of California law:
(a) Penal Code section 849(c) provides: "Thereafter, the arrest shall not be deemed an
arrest, but a detention only."
(b) Penal Code section 849.5 provides in materially identical terms for cases in which no
accusatory pleading is filed: "the arrest shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention
only."
(c) Penal Code section 851.6(a) mandates that the releasing agency "shall issue to that
person a certificate . . . describing the action as a detention."

1. This is a civil rights action for damages under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 against
Defendant DIANA CANDELARIA, a Driver Safety Hearing Officer employed by the California
Department of Motor Vehicles ("DMV"), sued in her individual capacity; and for prospective
declaratory and injunctive relief under Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908), against Defendant

color of state law, Defendant Candelaria deprived Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI of a
constitutionally protected property interest ~ his Class A Commercial Driver's License (No.
F7953179) -- through an administrative-per-se proceeding that was constitutionally deficient in at
least three independently sufficient ways, each traceable directly to Defendant Candelaria's own
written decision.
2. The underlying facts are simple, documented, and largely undisputed. On November I,
2024, Plaintiff - 
a professional commercial truck driver - was arrested by Califomia Highway
Patrol ("CHP") officers on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
Califomia, on a suspicion of driving under the influence that the officers' own contemporaneous
dashcam recording refutes. Four days later, on November 5, 2024, the CHP itself issued a formal
Penal Code section 851.6 Detention Certificate reclassifying that taking-into-custody as "a
detention only, not an arrest," and releasing Plaintiff under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for
"insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint." The Alameda County District Attorney,
to whom charges had been referred, declined to file any accusatory pleading. Both the arresting
agency and the prosecuting authority formally repudiated the arrest as lacking any evidentiary
basis.
3. Notwithstanding the Detention Certificate, the DMV proceeded with a Vehicle Code
section 13353 administrative-per-se refusal-suspension hearing. That hearing took place on
January 24, 2025, via Microsoft Teams, before Defendant Candelaria. On February 11, 2025,

124. To the extent Defendant Candelaria asserts quasi-judicial absolute immunity, the

Saxner, 474 U.S. 193, 202 (1985). Officials performing functions traditionally associated with
advocates are not entitled to absolute immunity. Swift v. Califomia. 384 F.3d 1184, 1191-92 (9th
Cir. 2004); Miller v. Gammie, 335 F.3d 889, 897 (9th Cir. 2003) (en banc).

Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI, appearing in propria persona, brings this First
Amended Complaint against Defendants DIANA CANDELARIA, in her individual capacity, and
STEVE GORDON, Director of the California Department of Motor Vehicles, in his official
capacity, and alleges as follows:
INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action for damages under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 against
Defendant DIANA CANDELARIA, a Driver Safety Hearing Officer employed by the California

Department of Motor Vehicles ("DMV"), sued in her individual capacity; and for prospective
declaratory and injunctive relief under Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908), against Defendant
STEVE GORDON, Director of the California DMV, sued in his official capacity. Acting under
color of state law, Defendant Candelaria deprived Plaintiff BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI of a
constitutionally protected property interest -- his Class A Commercial Driver's License (No.
F7953179) -- through an administrative-per-se proceeding that was constitutionally deficient in at
least three independently sufficient ways, each traceable directly to Defendant Candelaria's own
written decision.
2. The underlying facts are simple, documented, and largely undisputed. On November 1,
2024, Plaintiff -- a professional commercial truck driver -- was arrested by California Highway
Patrol ("CHP") officers on the shoulder of Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County,
California, on a suspicion of driving under the influence that the officers' own contemporaneous
dashcam recording refutes. Four days later, on November 5, 2024, the CHP itself issued a formal
Penal Code section 851.6 Detention Certificate reclassifying that taking-into-custody as "a
detention only, not an arrest," and releasing Plaintiff under Penal Code section 849(b)(1) for
"insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint." The Alameda County District Attorney,
to whom charges had been referred, declined to file any accusatory pleading. The Detention
Certificate and the District Attorney's declination constitute material contrary evidence bearing on
the lawfulness of the arrest that Defendant Candelaria's written decision did not address.
3. Notwithstanding the Detention Certificate, the DMV proceeded with a Vehicle Code
section 13353 administrative-per-se refusal-suspension hearing. That hearing took place on
January 24, 2025, via Microsoft Teams, before Defendant Candelaria. On February 11, 2025,
Candelaria issued a written Notification of Findings and Decision in APS Case No. 34739340
sustaining a one-year suspension of Plaintiff's Class A Commercial Driver's License (Feb. 20,
2025 through Feb. 19, 2026), imposing a $125.00 reissue fee under Vehicle Code sections 14904
and 14906, and imposing a three-year SR-22 financial-responsibility requirement under Vehicle

Code section 16430 that continues to burden Plaintiff to this day. Plaintiff's SR-22 filing became
effective May 18, 2026; accordingly, the three-year maintenance period extends through
approximately May 2029.
4. Candelaria's decision is constitutionally infirm on at least three independent grounds,
each of which -- standing alone -- states a claim upon which relief can be granted:
(a) DENIAL OF AN IMPARTIAL ADJUDICATOR. Candelaria adjudicated Plaintiff's
suspension within the DMV's hearing framework in which the same officer both develops the
evidentiary record and renders the final decision. Whether that framework operates consistently
with due process depends on whether the hearing officer conducts neutral fact development or
crosses the line into advocacy -- a distinction three separate California Court of Appeal decisions
had drawn before Plaintiff's hearing. The DMV's own written Notice of Hearing Appointment
(Form DS 2304) describes the combined role verbatim: "The Hearing Officer will develop the
facts and render a final decision on your matter." As alleged below, Candelaria's specific conduct
at Plaintiff's hearing crossed the line from neutral fact development into advocacy for the
Department's position.
(b) DENIAL OF A FAIR HEARING. Candelaria's written decision did not engage with
the material evidence and controlling authority Plaintiff placed in the record. Presented with (i)
the CHP's own section 851.6 Detention Certificate, (ii) the CHP dashcam recording in which the
officers themselves identified the suspected "alcoholic beverage" as urine, and (iii) binding
California Supreme Court authority in Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991), Candelaria issued a
written decision that addressed none of them, treated the officer's sworn statement as dispositive,
and characterized the record as one in which "no evidence was presented to the contrary" when in
fact contrary evidence had been presented in writing and at the hearing.
(c) FAILURE TO EVALUATE THE LAWFUL-ARREST PREDICATE. The APS

refusal framework, operating through Vehicle Code section 23612(a)(1)(A), requires that the
driver have been "lawfully arrested." Whether the arrest was lawful was a contested hearing issue:
Plaintiff presented the section 851.6 Detention Certificate, the Mercer volitional-movement
requirement, and the dashcam evidence -- each bearing directly on the lawfulness question.
Candelaria's written decision did not address any of them.
5. Whether Candelaria's conduct at Plaintiff's hearing crossed the line from neutral fact
development to advocacy is evaluated under the framework three published California Court of
Appeal decisions articulated before the date of Plaintiff's hearing: California DUI Lawyers Ass'n
v. DMV, 77 Cal.App.5th 517 (2022); Knudsen v. DMV, 101 Cal.App.5th 186 (2024); and Clarke
v. Gordon, 104 Cal.App.5th 1267 (2024). Clarke names Defendant Gordon personally as the
responsible official. Defendant Gordon has actual notice of the constitutional requirements; he
has failed to ensure compliance; and the consequences of a decision issued in a hearing that did
not comply continue to cause Plaintiff present, ongoing adverse effects -- including the ongoing
SR-22 encumbrance and the ongoing commercial-driving-record consequences of the suspension
-- that Ex parte Young empowers this Court to redress.
6. The consequences of Candelaria's decision have been -- and continue to be -- severe.
Plaintiff is a professional Class A CDL truck driver. The one-year suspension of his commercial
driving privileges immediately terminated his employment. The three-year SR-22 filing
requirement continues to encumber him today; it is a punitive, high-risk financial-responsibility
filing that would not exist absent Candelaria's decision, and on information and belief it has
materially restricted the pool of carriers willing to insure Plaintiff and has prevented him from
obtaining standard owners-coverage insurance on terms comparable to those available to drivers
not subject to the mandate. Plaintiff currently maintains California Auto Insurance Policy No.
11411043872 (Dairyland / Viking Insurance Company of Wisconsin), a California Named
Non-Owner SR-22 policy with an annual premium of $281.28, in force through May 18, 2027,
solely because Candelaria's February 11, 2025 decision imposes the three-year mandate.

7. This action is brought against Candelaria in her individual capacity for damages, and
against Gordon in his official capacity for prospective declaratory and injunctive relief under Ex
parte Young. Quasi-judicial absolute immunity, on the functional analysis the Supreme Court and
Ninth Circuit require, does not shield Candelaria from suit to the extent she performed conduct
outside the protected adjudicatory function; such conduct is not immunized merely because it
occurred in connection with a hearing. The Eleventh Amendment does not bar the Ex parte Young
claims against Gordon -- Plaintiff pleads ongoing constitutional violations with continuing,
present adverse effects, including the SR-22 encumbrance extending through approximately May
2029 and the continuing operation of the hearing framework that Gordon has been personally
noticed of and has failed to reform.
8. A related civil-rights action, Ngwa Nforbi v. Meza-Gonzalez & Melano (N.D. Cal.), is
pending in this District against the CHP officers whose conduct on November 1, 2024 gave rise
to the arrest. That action rests on the same dashcam recording and the same section 851.6
Detention Certificate that Defendant Candelaria's written decision did not address. The alias
relationship between Plaintiff's name in this action and the caption in that related action is
explained at paragraph 22, below.
9. Plaintiff respectfully seeks (a) compensatory and punitive damages against Defendant
Candelaria; (b) attorney's fees and costs pursuant to 42 U.S.C. section 1988 to the extent
recoverable; (c) a declaratory judgment against Defendant Gordon that the APS proceeding as
applied to Plaintiff violated the Fourteenth Amendment; and (d) a prospective injunction against
Defendant Gordon vacating Plaintiff's suspension, its associated financial-responsibility burdens,
and requiring that any future APS hearing involving Plaintiff be conducted by a neutral
decisionmaker who does not act as an advocate for the Department.
